and accountability but also provide enough scope and flexibility for creative 
development. Some of the very well -intended new policies meant for contributing in 
all-round development of country also had some undesirable impact on the process of 
acquiring required scientific items as per quality requirement of technical 
specification. 
2.17 The policy restrictions for procuring i tems, not produced / manufactured in the 
country, through global tender enquiry (GTE) have been affecting the procurement of 
essential items required in very small quantity for high end R&D. These restrictions 
have practically resulted in inaccessibility o f essential items for R&D. Expectation 
from user to develop products involving complex technologies defeats the research & 
development utilising these items.  That will only prove to be counterproductive since 
the demand for most of these specialised instr uments and materials required for R&D 
is very small. Therefore, it is not always financially viable to indigenise such items 
even if technology is developed after enormous efforts. The demand of the items may 
be assessed before intending for indigenous dev elopment and most competent 
ministry or department may be entrusted with responsibility of indigenisation. 
Therefore, it is urgent requirement that the procurement by R&D institutions should 
be exempted from restriction of global tender enquiries till it i s indigenised through 
suitable mechanism. 
2.18 Scientific research often requires precision instruments and specialised 
components where quality, performance and reliability are far more critical than cost. 
The current methods of procuring items based of l owest cost affects quality of 

30 
 
material and results in financial penalty in long terms. It is very difficult to ascertain 
on prevailing procurements platforms such as GeM. Moreover, original manufacturers 
of many such components often are not registered on such platforms which poses 
difficulty in acquiring items of requisite specification. While vendors may state to 
technically fulfilling procurement requirements, the quality and reliability of 
specialized scientific equipment falls short and there is requirement of well-structured 
mechanism to address such issues in shortest possible time.  
2.19 The General Financial Rules (GFRs) are expected to ensure transparency and 
equal opportunity in doing Government business. Unlike the infrastructure projects, 
R&D projects are of very small cost and specific in nature therefore, should not be 
treated like infrastructure projects. The current procedures and rules are time taking 
and inflexible that there is little scope adjustment to the rapidly developing scenario. 
There is a requirement of changes in the rules to make them flexible for R&D 
institutes. There should be sufficient financial autonomy available with the Unit 
Heads outside projects to meet exigencies. 
2.20 The Committee notes with concern the financial and administrative 
constraints that significantly impede the smooth functioning of BARC and other 
R&D institutions under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The 
Committee is given to understand that d espite rigorous technical scrutiny and 
approval of R&D projects, annual budgetary allocations often fall short because 
funding decisions are based on past spending patterns rather than the actual 
scientific requirements of ongoing or future research, adversely a ffecting long-
term basic research that underpins advanced technological development. The 
Committee further observes that the existing financial and administrative 
frameworks, while designed to ensure transparency and accountability , have 
over time become r igid, applying uniform rules across all sectors and leaving 
insufficient flexibility to accommodate the dynamic and creative nature of 
research and development. Procurement challenges arising from restrictions on 
Global Tender Enquiries (GTE), particularly  for specialized scientific 
instruments not manufactured domestically and needed in small quantities, have 
resulted in the inaccessibility of essential components, undermining high -end 
research where indigenisation is neither immediately feasible nor econo mically 
viable. Moreover, procurement procedures based solely on the lowest -cost 
criteria compromise the quality and reliability of scientific equipment, while 

31 
 
platforms such as GeM often lack original manufacturers of precision items, 
further complicating  timely and quality -assured procurement. The Committee 
also finds that applying the General Financial Rules (GFRs) uniformly to both 
infrastructure projects and R&D activities fails to account for the specific, small-
scale, and time -sensitive nature of res earch work, necessitating greater 
procedural flexibility and financial autonomy for research units. In light of these 
challenges, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry of Finance 
undertake a comprehensive review of the financial, administrati ve, and 
procurement frameworks governing R&D institutions under DAE, with reforms 
aimed at ensuring that funding allocations reflect actual research needs, 
introducing flexible R&D -specific financial procedures, exempting research 
institutions from GTE res trictions for items not manufactured domestically, 
establishing procurement mechanisms that prioritize quality and technical 
specifications over cost alone, and granting enhanced financial autonomy to unit 
heads to meet urgent and unforeseen research requirements. 
 
  

32 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS — AT A GLANCE 
CHAPTER –I 
TATA MEMORIAL CENTRE  
Cancer burden in India  
 The Committee notes with concern the increasing number of cancer cases 
in the country, particularly the significantly higher incidence reported  in the 
North-Eastern region of India . The Committee believes that it is essential to 
examine whether the ethnic groups of the Northeast are  genetically predisposed 
to specific types of cancers. To address this, the Committee recommends TMC 
to collaborate with the CSIR-Institute of Genomics and Integrative Biology 
(IGIB), which has been conducting extensive work in population and cancer 
genomics. Such collaborative research should aim to identify genomic signatures 
and risk factors unique to the North -Eastern population. The Committee feels 
that these insights will be critical for developing tailored cancer therapies, 
targeted prevention methods and early detection strategies for the northeastern 
population.                                                                                                     (Para 1.8) 
Notification of cancer as a documentable disease 
 The Committee notes with serious concern that only 19% of India’s 
population is currently covered by the population -based National Cancer 
Registry Programme. The Committee was given to understand that, at present, 
cancer registration in India is largely voluntary and that  hospitals and 
healthcare providers a re presently under no legal obligation to report cancer 
cases to public health authorities  because cancer is not a notifiable disease . As a 
result, existing cancer statistics are largely derived from extrapolations based on 
data from hospital -based and pop ulation-based registries. The Committee is of 
the considered opinion that effective prevention and control of cancer is possible 
only when the Government has accurate and comprehensive data on the 
incidence and prevalence of cancer in the country. The avai lability of real -time 
cancer statistics would enable timely epidemiological analysis and help identify 
priority areas for focused prevention and control efforts.  In view of the above, 

33 
 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
should declare cancer a mandatory documentable disease.                   (Para 1.12) 
Need for a nation-wide population based cancer registry  
 The Committee notes with serious concern that India still does not have a 
nationwide, population -based cancer re gistry. At present, the 52 population -
based cancer registries and approximately 243 hospital -based cancer registries 
together cover only about 19% of the country’s population. In the absence of a 
national-level database, it is impossible to accurately asse ss the true burden of 
cancer in the country.  The Committee finds it particularly worrying that a 
country with an advanced medical system like India lacks a unified national 
cancer registry, whereas many nations across the world maintain comprehensive 
nationwide cancer databases. For example, NORDCAN maintains cancer 
statistics for the Nordic countries, namely, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, 
Iceland, Greenland, and the Faroe Islands, providing a consolidated picture of 
incidence, prevalence, mortality, an d survival rates.  In view of the above, t he 
Committee recommends the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to establish 
a nationwide population -based cancer registry , with districts designated as 
nodal units. District-wide and state-wide registries should feed into a centralized 
national registry at the Union level. Maintaining a unified national database will 
provide an accurate and real -time picture of cancer incidence, prevalence, 
mortality, and survival. This, in turn, will significantly strengthen evid ence-
based policymaking and program interventions for the prevention and control 
of cancer.                                                                                                      (Para 1.15) 
TMC’s Hub-and-Spoke Model  
 The Committee commends TMC for developing a successful Hub -and-
Spoke model  for decentralized cancer care. The Committee is given to 
understand that establishing a model hub requires an initial investment of 
approximately ₹650 crore and recurring annual costs of about ₹120 crore,  while 
setting up a model spoke requires an initial investment of around ₹400 crore and 
annual recurring costs of about ₹40 crore. The Committee feels that it would be 
difficult for TMC to establish hubs and spokes across the entire country on its 
own. The Committee also understands that TMC’s existing infrastructure is 

34 
 
already overburdened, and the demand for cancer care has significantly 
outpaced its current capacity.                                                                    (Para 1.19) 
 The Committee in its 325 th Report titled ‘An expanded role for the 
Department of Atomic Energy in Cancer treatment in India through an 
enlarged network of the Tata Memorial Centre’  had recommended that TMC 
should take all the stakeholders on board related to c ancer treatment, and 
leverage some of the existing centres and upgrade them to TMC standards 
rather than building de novo centres. The Committee recommends that each of 
the 28 States should designate one government hospital with an existing 
oncology unit ( such as an SCI, RCC, AIIMS campus or major medical college) 
as the State Hub, supported by 1 -2 medical colleges or district hospitals as 
Spokes. Strengthening these centres should be funded jointly by the Centre and 
States through existing NPCDCS and relat ed schemes. The Committee further 
recommends that TMC act as the ‘national technical partner’ and collaborate 
with the States and provide requisite guidance, mentorship, wo rkforce training, 
and standardized clinical protocols required to deliver specialized cancer care.    
(Para 1.20)    
 The Committee had also previously recommended that a High Level 
Steering Committee headed by the Minister of State for Atomic Energy, the 
Chief Secretaries/Administrators of all the States and Union Territories as 
Members and Director, TMC as Member Secretary be constituted so that all the 
modalities related to the adoption and rolling out of the Hub and Spoke Model 
can be chalked out in a time bound manner. The Committee reiterates its earlier 
recommendation. The Committee  recommends the Department of Atomic 
Energy and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to provide full support, 
including enhanced budgetary allocations, policy backing, and greater financial 
autonomy to TMC to help it achieve this objective.                                (Para 1.21) 
Proton beam therapy  
 The Committee is given to understand that the superior precision of 
proton beam therapy and its significantly lower toxicity profile makes it 
particularly suitable fortumours located near vital body structures, tumours 
considered resistant toradiation and for paediatric patients who are highly 
vulnerable to long-term radiation-induced developmental complications. The 

35 
 
Committee, therefore,  recommends the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare to 
take proactive steps to expand access to proton beam therapy. Considering that 
TMC has already established a Proton Therapy Centre and has treated 636 
patients, including 95 children, the Committee further recommends that the 
Ministry collaborate with TMC to develop a national plan for setting up 
additional proton therapy centres in strategic regions of the country. Given 
TMC’s proven expertise and operational experience in commissioning and 
managing India’s first proton therapy facility, the Committee further 
recommends that the Ministry formally engage TMC as the principal technical 
partnerfor planning, commissioning, workforce capacity building, and 
establishing clinical protocols to ensure that these centres can effectively meet 
the growing needs of paediatric and other eligible cancer patients.      (Para 1.25) 
 The Committee, in its 387th Report, had earlier recommended TMC to 
take steps to expand access to Proton Beam Therapy (PBT) and Boron Neutron 
Capture Therapy (BNCT) which offer precise tumour targeting with fewer side 
effects, reducing long-term treatment costs.As regards Boron Neutron Capture 
Therapy, the Committee was informed that TMC is working with scientists in 
BARC's Reactor and Radiobiology groups and is looking into constructing 
reactor-based BNCT equipment for treating patients with recurrent Head and 
Neck and Brain tumours. The Committee was also informed that TMC is 
currently actively involved in discussions on the construction of such equipment, 
patient treatment rooms, and research laboratory facilities for patient treatment 
and the discovery/ generation of new pharmacological boronated compounds to 
make such treatment feasible and affordable in India. The activity is still in the 
stages of discussions and approval of the concept and design. BNCT therapy is 
already a mainstream treatment in countries like China and Japan; India should 
explore its adoption at the earliest. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
TMC expedite these discussions and ensure that this therapy becomes available 
in India at the earliest.                                                                                (Para 1.26) 
 The Committee observes that cancer treatment cannot follow a one-size-
fits-all approach and must be tailored to a patient’s unique molecular profile. 
The Committee notes with concern that India’s continued reliance on 
conventional radiotherapy and chemotherapy often results in suboptimal 
treatment, higher fatality rates, and unnecessary expenditure. In light of the 

36 
 
rising incidence of cancer in the country, the Committee stresses the urgent need 
to transition towards precision medicine, where therapies are based on 
individualized molecular characteristics, thereby improving clinical outcomes 
and reducing overall costs.The Committee therefore recommends the 
Department of Atomic Energy and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to 
prioritise the development and adoption of personalised oncology treatment 
regimens at scale. Future research efforts should focus on precision medicine, 
particularly gene-network-based precision oncology, to better understand 
tumour biology, analyse how patient-specific gene regulatory networks 
contribute to cancer, and ultimately enable the delivery of tailored therapies and 
drugs rather than uniform treatments for all patients.The Committee further 
emphasises that precision medicine must be made available at a population scale 
and urges the concerned Departments to provide necessary policy support and 
funding to facilitate this transition.The Committee also recommends that the 
cancer institutes under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare should 
collaborate with TMC and help achieve this transition.                         (Para 1.27) 
CSR funding  
 The Committee appreciates the welfare -oriented initiatives being 
undertaken by TMC, particularly in providing free treatment to paediatric 
cancer patients. The Committee notes that in 2024 –25, TMC spent 
approximately ₹74 crore on free treatment for paediatric patients, of which 
around ₹70 crore was sourced from non -governmental sources, including ₹45 
crore from CSR contributions. Considering the rising incidence of cancer in the 
coming years, the Committee observes that existing funding levels would be 
insufficient to meet the growing demand for free treatment. In view of this, the 
Committee recommends the Department of Public Enterprises  to direct Central 
Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) to allocate a portion of their CSR funds to 
TMC. This additional support will help ensure sustained provision of free 
treatment to paediatric and economically disadvantaged cancer patients.  
                                                                                                                      (Para 1.33) 
KEVAT 
 The Committee appreciates the Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) for 
conceptualizing and successfully rolling out the KEVAT program, India’s first 

37 
 
formal training initiative for patient navigation. The Committee notes that the 
role of patient navigators, though of ten overlooked, is integral to strengthening 
the entire healthcare continuum, particularly in complex domains such as 
cancer care, where patients and families face multiple barriers including lack of 
awareness, language challenges, financial constraints, e motional distress, and 
difficulty in navigating hospital systems. The Committee observes that patient 
navigators play a pivotal role in improving access to timely and equitable care 
by facilitating screening and early detection, supporting patients through  
hospital procedures, coordinating multidisciplinary care, ensuring treatment 
adherence, and providing psychosocial and end -of-life support. Their 
contribution in mobilizing financial assistance, arranging accommodation, 
improving referral pathways, and br idging communication gaps between 
healthcare providers and patients demonstrates their critical importance in 
addressing systemic and patient -level challenges. In view of the remarkable 
outcomes achieved by KEVAT, both within the TMC network and 
internationally, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare, in collaboration with the National Medical Commission should 
encourage universities, medical colleges, and healthcare institutions across the 
country to initiate dedicated courses on patient navigation.                  (Para 1.36) 
Designation of TMC as an Institution of National Importance 
 The Committee notes with concern that one of the most pressing 
challenges in strengthening cancer care delivery in India is the acute short age of 
trained oncology professionals. This deficit adversely affects early diagnosis, 
timely treatment, multidisciplinary care, and patient outcomes, particularly in 
Government cancer centres and institutions located in underserved regions. The 
Committee is given to understand that despite being the country's premier 
oncology training hub, TMC continues to face significant difficulties in 
recruiting specialised personnel  including oncologists, radiologists, pathologists, 
and allied health professionals, es pecially in its newer centres located outside 
Mumbai. The Committee observes that the demand for a skilled oncology 
workforce is rapidly outpacing supply, and incremental increases in intake of 
students alone will not adequately meet national requirements.  The Committee, 
in its 325th Report, had earlier recommended the Government of India to 

38 
 
consider conferring Institute of National Importance (INI) status on the Tata 
Memorial Centre (TMC)/Homi Bhabha National Institute, in view of its pivotal 
national role in cancer care, training, and research. Keeping in view the rising 
burden of cancer cases in the country and the growing demand for skilled 
oncology workforce, the Committee reiterates its above recommendation to 
designate TMC/HBNI as Institute of National Importance.                   (Para 1.40) 
CHAPTER –II 
BHABHA ATOMIC RESEARCH CENTRE (BARC) AND NUCLEAR 
POWER CORPORATION OF INDIA LIMITED (NPCIL) 
Nuclear Power Plants  
 The Committee notes that in the global discourse on energy, India stands 
at a critical juncture. India is currently faced with twin challenges, one is to fuel 
the rapid growth of the economy for the prosperity of the citizens and the second 
is to do so in a manner that is sustainable, reliable, and is in alignment with our 
climate commitments. The Committee believes that i n this complex landscape, 
nuclear power is not merely an alternative but an indispensable strategic 
imperative for India’s long -term ener gy security and low -carbon future . The 
Committee notes with concern that Jaitapur and Kovvada projects were 
announced as far back as 2010 and have not materialized yet. The Committee is 
of the view that these projects are crucial for achieving the national target of 100 
GW of nuclear capacity by 2047. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that 
all necessary measures should be undertaken to ensure their timely 
implementation in strict accordance with the proposed timelines.          (Para 2.8) 
India’s three stage nuclear programme 
 The Committee notes that India’s three -stage nuclear programme is 
inherently sequential, with each stage dependent on the fuel cycle of the 
preceding one, and that thorium is not a fissile material and cannot be used 
directly for power generation, as it must first be converted into uranium -233, 
which offers superior physical characteristics compared to uranium -235 and 
plutonium-239. While India plans to harness thorium -based energy in the third 
stage through advanced technologies such as Molten Salt Reactors and 

39 
 
Advanced Heavy Water Reactors, the Committee expresses concern that nuclear 
energy currently contributes only about 3 percent of India’s total electricity 
generation, in sharp contrast to countries like France where nuclear power 
accounts for nearly 67 percent. The Committee is of the considered view that 
India must substantially increase the share of nuclear energy to at least 10 
percent in the medium term and recomme nds that the Department of Atomic 
Energy, in consultation with relevant stakeholders, formulate a clear, time -
bound roadmap to achieve this target through planned capacity addition and 
phased commissioning of new reactors. Given India’s vast monazite depos its, the 
Committee further recommends that BARC and other R&D institutions under 
DAE intensify research focused on enabling the direct utilization of thorium for 
electricity generation and expediting the development, demonstration, and 
commercial readiness of thorium-based reactor technologies.               (Para 2.14) 
Challenges being faced by BARC 
 The Committee notes with concern the financial and administrative 
constraints that significantly impede the smooth functioning of BARC and other 
R&D institutions under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE). The 
Committee is given to understand that d espite rigorous technical scrutiny and 
approval of R&D projects, annual budgetary allocations often fall short because 
funding decisions are based on past spending patterns rather than the actual 
scientific requirements of ongoing or future research, adversely affecting long -
term basic research that underpins advanced technological development. The 
Committee further observes that the existing financial and administra tive 
frameworks, while designed to ensure transparency and accountability , have 
over time become rigid, applying uniform rules across all sectors and leaving 
insufficient flexibility to accommodate the dynamic and creative nature of 
research and developmen t. Procurement challenges arising from restrictions on 
Global Tender Enquiries (GTE), particularly for specialized scientific 
instruments not manufactured domestically and needed in small quantities, have 
resulted in the inaccessibility of essential compon ents, undermining high -end 
research where indigenisation is neither immediately feasible nor economically 
viable. Moreover, procurement procedures based solely on the lowest -cost 
criteria compromise the quality and reliability of scientific equipment, whil e 
platforms such as GeM often lack original manufacturers of precision items, 

40 
 
further complicating timely and quality -assured procurement. The Committee 
also finds that applying the General Financial Rules (GFRs) uniformly to both 
infrastructure projects and R&D activities fails to account for the specific, small-
scale, and time -sensitive nature of research work, necessitating greater 
procedural flexibility and financial autonomy for research units. In light of these 
challenges, the Committee strongly recom mends that the Ministry of Finance 
undertake a comprehensive review of the financial, administrative, and 
procurement frameworks governing R&D institutions under DAE, with reforms 
aimed at ensuring that funding allocations reflect actual research needs, 
introducing flexible R&D -specific financial procedures, exempting research 
institutions from GTE restrictions for items not manufactured domestically, 
establishing procurement mechanisms that prioritize quality and technical 
specifications over cost alone, a nd granting enhanced financial autonomy to unit 
heads to meet urgent and unforeseen research requirements.                (Para 2.20)

REPORT 
 
INTRODUCTION 
The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEF&CC) is the nodal 
agency in the administrative structure of the Central Government for planning, promoting, 
coordinating and overseeing environmental, ecological, forestry and wildlife policies and 
programmes. Its main activities include conservation and survey of natural resources including 
flora, fauna, forests, wildlife, aquatic bodies and water resources and eco-systems, prevention 
and control of pollution and management of hazardous substances. Other important activities 
include protection of the environment and forests, including their biodiversity, mitigation and 
adaptation to climate change through measures that include afforestation, regeneration of 
degraded areas, and adoption of cleaner technologies.  It also plays important role in promoting 
sustainable development and better environmental governance while protecting human, plants 
and animals life, health and welfare etc.  
1.2 These objectives are well supported by a set of legislative and regulatory measures, 
aimed at the preservation, conservation and protection of the environment. Besides the 
legislative measures, a National Conservation Strategy and Policy Statement on Environment 
and Development, 1992, National Forest Policy, 1988, a Policy Statement on Abatement of 
Pollution, 1992 and a National Environment Policy, 2006 also guide the Ministry’s work.  
1.3 The main tools used to discharge its mandate include, inter alia, conducting surveys; 
collecting, compiling and disseminating data and information; undertaking scientific research, 
extension services and analyses; carrying out impact assessment of developmental projects and 
programmes; regulating use of natural resources; undertaking regeneration programmes; 
extending technical, scientific, financial and administrative support to organisations and 
institutions in the subject fields; imparting education, training, building capacity and generating 
awareness among stakeholders and the public at large; and promoting international cooperation 
through bilateral, regional and multilateral initiatives in environment and ecology. 
1.4 The institutional set up of the Ministry includes a number of Directorates and Divisions 
assembled around the main thematic sectors of environment and ecology, forestry and wildlife, 
afforestation and eco-development. The Ministry has 20 Regional Offices; ten 
Attached/Subordinate Offices (e.g. Botanical, Zoological and Forests Surveys of India, 
Directorate of Forestry Education, Indira Gandhi National Forestry Academy, National Green 
Tribunal, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau etc.); Boards and Authorities (e.g. Central Pollution 
Control Board, National Biodiversity Authority, National Tiger Conservation Authority, Central 
Zoo Authority) and Autonomous Institutions (e.g. Indian Council for Forestry Research and 
Education, Wildlife Institute of India etc.). Provision has been made in the Demand for Grants 
for the year 2026-27 for its attached/ subordinate/ autonomous organisations and other bodies. 
Functioning and Activities of the Ministry 
1.5 The Mission of MoEF&CC is to plan, promote, co-ordinate and oversee the 
implementation of India’s environmental and forestry policies and programmes related to 
conservation of the country’s natural resources including its wetlands, lakes, rivers and coasts, 
its biodiversity, forests and wildlife, ensuring the welfare of animals, and the prevention, 
abatement and mitigation of pollution across various sectors. The Ministry addresses the 
impacts of climate change and adaptation needs across various sectors like health, food and 
water security etc. The Ministry maintains a robust regulatory regime for striking balance 
between development and conservation of environment and forests. The Ministry seeks to

ensure inclusive economic growth guided by the principles of sustainable development and 
enhancement of human well-being.

4.2 The Committee noted that the budget allocation for Central Sector Schemes was 
increased from ₹1060.56 crore in BE 2025-26 to ₹1451.52 crore at RE 2025-26 and desired to 
know the reasons for the same.  
4.3 The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the reasons for increase in allocation 
at RE 2025-26 under Central Sector Schemes was mainly due to major augmentation in one 
such Scheme i.e. Control of Pollution. The increase of budget of Control of Pollution Scheme is 
mainly due to allocation of ₹1020 crore to 82 cities in the year 2025-26 covered under National 
Clean Air Programme (NCAP) based on air quality performance in the year 2024-25 in line 
with the MoEFCC guidelines dated 25.8.2022. An amount ₹33.54 core was earmarked to 8 NE 
States under AAoP component for the year 2025-26. Further, R&D activities, National 
Outreach and Capacity Building programmes (₹6.5 crore), Awards for Swachh Vayu 
Sarvekshan for Wards (₹14.7 crore) were planned to be implemented along with administrative 
expenses in the year 2025-26.  All targeted cities under NCAP have prepared action plans for 
implementation of air quality improvement measures based on allocations made for FY 2025-
26. North Eastern State Pollution Control Board have prepared action plans for expenditure for 
allocated funds in FY 2025- 26. 
4.4 The Committee was further informed that the National Coastal Mission (NCM) scheme 
was launched with a budgetary outlay of ₹87.00 crore for a period of five years (FY 2021–
2026). The remaining ₹2.00 crore under the NCM was allotted in Budget Estimate (BE) 2025-
2026. However, the scheme has been extended for another six years from 2025 to 2031, with a 
budgetary allocation of ₹767 crore as National Coastal Mission 2.0 (NCM 2.0) on 16th May 
2025. Therefore, for preparatory work an additional budget of Rs 5.5 crore at RE stage was 
solicited in anticipation that the preparatory works and institutional work can be initiated. 
4.5 The Committee notes that although the budget allocation for Central Sector 
Schemes was increased from ₹1060.56 crore in BE 2025-26 to ₹1451.52 crore at RE 2025-
26, the Ministry could utilize only ₹888.22 crore (as on 31.01.2026). There has been less 
utilization of funds in three out of the four components viz. ‘Environmental Knowledge 
and Capacity Building’, ‘National Coastal Management Programme’ and ‘Control of 
Pollution’.  The Committee also took note that the major contributor for less utilization is

the ‘Control of Pollution’ Scheme.  The Committee recommends that all steps be taken to 
ensure utilization of funds allocated during 2025-26.

for ‘Control of Pollution’ scheme has been increased from ₹853.9 core to ₹1300 crore. 
Environmental pollution in the country poses a significant, ongoing threat to public health 
and environmental stability and hence, the funds allocated for its control must be 
optimally utilized.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must take 

10 
 
remedial measures, devise a robust monitoring system to monitor financial and physical 
progress of the works and ensure that the funds allocated under ‘Control of Pollution’ are 
thoroughly utilized in the next financial year, ensuring desired outcomes. 
5.6 The Committee observed that the Air quality in Delhi NCR remained in the 
category of poor and below during most part of October-February period of current 
financial year.  The Committee feels that there is a need of a sturdy plan to mitigate the 
air pollution and recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change, in coordination with the Govt. of NCR of Delhi, should chalk out a long term plan 
to overcome this long standing problem.

about only 60% expenditure i.e. ₹18.27 crore out of the RE allocation of ₹30.48 crore on 
Conservation of Natural Resources and Ecosystems. 
8. National Mission for a Green India 
8.1 The umbrella scheme of National Mission for a Green India includes two sub schemes 
as under: 
(i)  Green India Mission (GIM) - National Afforestation Programme (NAP): GIM is one of the 
eight Missions outlined under the National Action Plan on Climate Change which aims towards 
protecting, restoring and enhancing India’s forest cover and responding to Climate Change. It 
envisages a holistic view of greening and focuses on multiple ecosystem services along with 
carbon sequestration and emission reduction as co-benefit.  The scheme envisages to increase 

13 
 
forest/tree cover and improved quality of the existing forest cover, improve ecosystem services 
including biodiversity, hydrological services and carbon sequestration, to increase forest-based 
livelihood income of households living in and around the forests, to enhance annual CO2 
sequestration. 
(ii) Forest Fire Prevention and Management (FFPM):  The Ministry supports the eﬀorts of the 
States/ UTs in prevention and control of forest fires by providing financial assistance under the 
Centrally Sponsored   Scheme   namely   Forest   Fire Prevention and Management Scheme. 
Under the Scheme, the assistance is provided to the States/UTs for various forest fire prevention 
and management measures such as use of communication and information technology, creation 
and maintenance of fire lines in forest areas, engagement of fire watchers, creation of water 
storage structures in forest areas, strengthening of forest infrastructure, procurement of 
firefighting equipment, soil and moisture conservation works in high risk areas, awareness 
creation and such other activities. 
8.2 The Committee observed that in 2025-26, the BE allocation of ₹220.00 crore for 
‘National Mission for a Green India’ was reduced to ₹95.70 crore at RE i.e. a reduction of 
nearly 56%.  The Committee desired to know the reasons for this drastic reduction in allocation 
to the Mission and the impact of the reduction on the various schemes and programmes under 
the Mission.  The Committee was informed by the Ministry that the reduction in allocation 
under the National Mission for a Green India (GIM) from ₹220.00 crore (BE) to ₹95.70 crore 
(RE) in 2025–26 has implications. The cut slows afforestation and eco-restoration activities, 
reduces the area of degraded forests taken up for treatment, and delays new landscape-based 
interventions. Further, the reduced allocation constrains support to Joint Forest Management 
Committees (JFMCs), capacity building, micro-planning, and livelihood activities linked to 
non-timber forest produce (NTFP) and eco enterprises which may impact continuity of 
restoration efforts and may slow progress towards land degradation neutrality, climate 
resilience, and sustainable forest management objectives. 
8.3 As regards the targets set and physical and financial achievements of the various 
schemes and programs under the ‘National Mission for a Green India’ during 2025-26, the 
Committee was informed by the Ministry that funds have been released towards the committed 
liabilities of the States/UTs. During the FY 2025-26, amount of ₹56.40 crore has been allocated 
to the 08 States for creation (11499 ha) and maintenance work (15137).  
8.4 As regards the allocation of ₹212.50 crore in BE 2026-27, the Committee was informed 
that 18 States/UTs are actively involved in implementing the Mission’s activities. Of the 
proposed allocation of ₹212.50 crore for Umbrella scheme National Mission for a Green India, 
₹172.50 crore will be allocated for Green India Mission. The funds will be utilized for taking 
new eco-restoration targets in the existing States and moreover, the Mission will focus on 
expanding its operation to other States. Additionally, the States under GIM are in the process of 
revising their perspective plan in line with the revised Mission Document and accordingly, the 
funds will be utilized to streamline the overall implementation of Green India Mission as per 
the revised approach. 
8.5 The Committee observes that the BE 2025-26 allocation of ₹220.00 crore for 
National Mission for a Green India was reduced to ₹95.70 crore at RE stage, which is 
nearly 44 percent of the BE allocation.  Again, out of the reduced allocation of ₹95.70 
crore, the Ministry could utilise only ₹40.95 crore upto 31st January 2026 i.e. nearly 43 
percent of the RE allocation. The Ministry must work out a plan of action to expedite 
utilization of RE allocation. Full utilization of the available funds during the current 

14 
 
financial year should be ensured.  The Ministry has not provided any reason for the 
reduction in allocation at RE stage.  The Committee is of the view that though the 
reduction at RE adversely affected the activities under the scheme, but the Ministry also, 
on its own part, has not able to utilize the available funds to the desired extent till January 
month. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change to examine the slow progress of funds utilization under this scheme and take 
measures to ensure that such funds are not underutilized.

11. Project Tiger & Elephant 
11.1 The Ministry provides financial assistance to the States/UTs under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme Project Tiger & Elephant for the protection of elephants, their habitats & 
corridors, welfare of captive elephant and mitigation of human elephant conflict. 
11.2 The Committee noted that the BE allocation of ₹290.00 crore was reduced to ₹153.04 
crore in RE 2025-26.  The Ministry had been able to utilize ₹132.56 crore as on 31st January 
2026.  The Committee desired to know the reasons for the reduction and the impact of this 
reduction on the activities planned under this scheme during 2025-26.  In response, the 
Committee was informed by the Ministry that the reduction from BE ₹290.00 crore to RE 
₹153.04 crore during 2025–26 was largely procedural and transitional. The migration to the 
SNA-SPARSH architecture led to timing mismatches in releases, reconciliation, and 
expenditure booking, transitional administrative complexities due to merger of Project Tiger & 
Elephant. It was further informed that the RE is finalised in October, whereas the effective field 
expenditure cycle for wildlife activities gains momentum post-monsoon and peaks between 
December–January.   
11.3 As regards the impact of the reduction on the activities under the scheme, the 
Committee was informed that the activities like habitat restoration, conflict mitigation 
infrastructure were impacted.  However, Field-level implementation did not slow down. Habitat 
management, anti-poaching operations, conflict mitigation, and relocation processes continued 
as per approved APOs. By the middle of February 2026, the expenditure has already reached 
approximately ₹148 crore, demonstrating that utilisation capacity remains strong. The lower RE 

16 
 
therefore reflects timing and system-transition factors rather than lack of demand or 
implementation capacity. 
11.4 In response to a query regarding the mechanisms devised by the Ministry to ensure that 
funds allocation under the scheme are not underutilized, the Committee was informed of the 
following mechanisms :- 
(i) Project Elephant delinked from Project Tiger for administrative clarity. 
(ii) 50% release in two tranches. 
(iii) Early sanction of APOs. 
(iv) Dedicated monitoring through Wildlife and Project Elephant Divisions. 
(v) Regional Office inspections. 
(vi) Periodic evaluation through MEE. 
 
11.5 The Committee was further informed by the Ministry that States have already adopted 
the revised SNA-SPARSH architecture in 2025–26 and streamlined fund-flow mechanisms, and 
will endeavour to fully absorb the allocation during 2026–27 through improved financial 
planning and monitoring. However, the actual requirement is significantly higher, as the 
number of Tiger Reserves, tiger population, landscape coverage, and human–wildlife conflict 
incidents have all increased in recent years. The current allocation does not fully reflect the 
expanded mandate and growing field-level liabilities.  
11.6 The Committee also enquired about the reasons for reduction of the BE allocation of 
₹148.00 crore to ₹102.53 crore in RE 2025-26 for ‘Development of Wildlife Habitats’. The 
Committee was informed that Scheme was on-boarded to SNA SPARSH w.e.f. 01.7.2025 and it 
took time for the States to On-board in the Scheme and understand the modalities thereof. 
Accordingly, the actual expenditure has been made at slow pace, due to which the budget has 
been reduced and subsequently, the allocations to the States will be made as per Revised 
Estimates. 
11.7 Centrally-funded schemes are crucial for implementing national priorities, 
reducing inter-state inequalities, and ensuring uniform development.  The Committee 
finds the financial performance of the Ministry in ‘Project Tiger & Elephant’ satisfactory.  
The Committee is in agreement that the pace of expenditure had slowed down due to 
unavoidable administrative reasons.  The Committee also agrees that fund requirement 
under this scheme is significantly higher, as the number of Tiger Reserves, tiger 
population, landscape coverage, and human–wildlife conflict incidents have all increased 
in recent years.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should consider 
allocating additional funds to this head to address the rising demands of protection, 
relocation, and conflict mitigation. 
12. Need to reduce cases of Man-Animal conflict 
12.1 During the meeting held on 26th February 2025, the Ministry, while making 
presentation, informed the Committee that about 30% of Tigers were found inhabiting areas 
outside designated Tiger Reserves, leading to an increase in negative Human–Tiger interactions.  
Accordingly, a pilot initiative, tiger outside tiger reserves (TOTR), was undertaken by NTCA to 
address this human-tiger conflict.  Phase one was approved by CAMPA with an outlay of 88.7 
crore.  It was implemented across 40 high conflict divisions in nine States.  ₹36.15 crore was 
been disbursed to 40 divisions for the current financial year. 

17 
 
12.2 The Committee observes that although the Ministry informed that they had been 
making efforts very assiduously to reduce the cases of man-animal conflict, such incidents 
were increasing day by day.  The Committee feels that the number of tigers and leopards 
has increased as compared to the forest area, and hence there is a shortage of habitat for 
them. The Committee recommends that all possible steps should be taken to prevent these 
animals from entering populated areas so that they remain restricted to forest areas only. 
Suitable funds may be allocated to build rescue centers for tigers and leopards in the 
forest areas so that they do not leave the forest area. The Ministry may also come up with 
technological interventions to tackle this menace and to reduce the cases of man-animal 
conflicts.

13. Plantation of medicinal plants from CAMPA funds  
13.1 The Committee enquired from the Ministry plantation of medicinal plants is considered 
under CAMPA funds.  In response, the Ministry stated that National Authority, CAMPA 
considers Annual Plan of Operations (APO) furnished by States and UTs. States and UTs 
furnish Mandatory activities as per approvals (under Van Sanrakshan and Samvardhan 
Adhiniyam 1980) and terms and conditions contained therein. In such cases/proposals, if the 
plantation of Medicinal Plants is prescribed and placed in under Mandatory activities (refer 
section 6 (a) of CAF act 2016), they are liable to be approved. If plantation of medicinal plants 
is proposed by State /UT Government under rule 5 and 6 of CAF Rules 2018; and it is in 
consonance of prescriptions of Working Plan of concerned Forest division National Authority 
favorably considers it and conveys its decision to State /UT Govt. on merit of the proposal. 
Moreover, an explicit provision for enlisting medical plants’ species has also been created in the 
Online Digital APO portal for States and UTs to clearly mention them in their afforestation 
proposals.   
13.2 Further briefing the Committee on the subject during the meeting of the Committee held 
on 26.2.2026, Secretary of the Ministry stated as under: 
“Regarding the suggestion made by the Chair of using CAMPA Fund for medicinal 
plants, I don't see any issue in that except that CAMPA Fund is used actually in lieu of 
the forest area which has been diverted. So, wherever the degraded land is provided or 
the land is bought and provided to the forest department, these plants can be grown in 
such areas only provided the local conditions, the ecological conditions and the 
environmental conditions promote such medicinal plants. So those plantation activities 
which are a part of CAMPA can obviously be taken in.”  
13.3 Medicinal plants have been an integral part of traditional and modern healthcare 
systems due to their therapeutic potential and bioactive compounds. Medicinal plants 
offer natural, cost-effective remedies with fewer side effects for a wide range of health 
conditions, including chronic diseases, infections, and metabolic disorders.  In order to 
reach maximum benefits of these traditional plants, the availability of such plants 
becomes essential.  In view of this, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should make it mandatory that, in case of 
afforestation in degraded areas, at least 25 percent of the plantation from CAMPA funds 
should be of medicinal plants, suitable for that particular ecology.  The Ministry should 
ensure that plantations contribute meaningfully to carbon sinks and biodiversity 
restoration rather than short-term target fulfillment.

15. Forest land encroachment  
15.1 Forest land encroachment is a major environmental crisis in India.  There have been 
numerous reports of land grabbing of forest areas for non-forestry purposes.  Concerned over 
such reports, the Committee enquired from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change as to whether, in order to avoid illegal occupations, the Ministry / NGT intend to get 
drone survey of lands in forest areas done and place it in public domain to enable the concerned 
public / public authorities to verify the status of such lands before any commercial 
activity/sale/purchase relating to such land is undertaken. 
15.2 Responding in the matter, the Ministry informed the Committee as under: 
(i) As per the provisions of Section 2(1)(iii) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam 
Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 no forest land shall be leased or used for nonforestry 

21 
 
purposes, including for agricultural purposes, without the prior approval of the 
Central Government. The Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in W.P. (C) No. 
202/1995 in the matter of T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India has 
directed, from time to time, to ensure the strict compliance of the provisions of the 
Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980. 
 
(ii) Land being a State subject, the primary responsibility to monitor, prevent, detect, 
and remove illegal use of forest lands including encroachments, rests with the 
respective State Governments and UT Administrations.  
 
(iii) Further, as per the provisions of Rule 16(1) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam 
Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, all States and Union Territory Administrations should 
prepare and maintain consolidated records of all categories of forest land to which 
the provisions of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 are 
applicable. The objective of this provision is to enable all stakeholders including 
public and public authorities to have clarity on the status of forest lands. The 
Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, in Shri Ashok Kumar Sharma v. Union of India in 
W.P. (C) No. 1164 of 2023, in order dated 04.03.2025, had directed all States and 
Union Territory Administrations to ensure compliance of the provisions of Rule 
16(1) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Rules, 2023 in a time bound 
manner. 
 
15.3 The Committee expresses concern on forest land encroachment in the country.  
There are reports that over 13,000 sq km of forest area is occupied illegally across 25 
states.  The Committee is of the view that use of forest areas for non-forestry purposes 
reduces forested areas, driving biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and environmental 
degradation.  The Supreme Court of India has ruled that forest land recorded in all 
government records including the forest land as per dictionary meaning, shall be brought 
under the purview of Forest Conservation Act and prior approval of Central government 
shall be obtained for diversion of such forest lands for non-forestry purposes.  
15.4 The Committee notes that the Ministry needs to examine Committee’s query 
regarding getting the drone survey of lands in forest areas done. Although the Ministry 
has drawn attention to provisions of Rule 16(1) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam 
Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, whereby all States and Union Territory Administrations are 
required to prepare and maintain consolidated records of all categories of forest land to 
which the provisions of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 are 
applicable.  However, it is not clear whether such information is available in public 
domain or not or is easily accessible to the public at large.  There have been numerous 
instances of sale of forest land involving illegal conversion or unauthorized transfer, 
frequently involving nexus between private parties, developers and officials. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change should stress upon all State/UT Governments to get the drone survey of lands 
conducted in forest areas and place these reports in public domain to enable the 
concerned public / public authorities to verify the status of such lands before any 
commercial activity/sale/purchase relating to such land is undertaken.  Any instances of 
laxity in this regard by the public authorities should be severely dealt with. 

22 
 
15.5 The Committee further recommends that all eco-sensitive zones of the country 
should be mapped digitally and all necessary steps should be taken to protect the fragile 
ecosystems of the country.

more than 96% of the allocated funds. While the Ministry could utilize 72.35% of the 
allocated funds in 2024-25, the Ministry has been able to utilize only 67.87% (as on 
31.1.2026) of its RE allocation in 2025-26 of ₹3481.61 crore. The Committee takes note of 
steps being taken by the Ministry to ensure full utilization of allocation in remaining part 
of 2025-26 and recommends that the Ministry should take all necessary steps to ensure 
that the allocation made to it is utilized to the maximum possible extent.       (Para 2.4) 
 
The Committee further notes that the BE allocation of ₹3759.46 crore in 2026-27 is 
around 10 percent increase over the BE allocation of ₹3412.82 in the year 2025-26.  The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should make proactive efforts from the 
beginning of the next financial year and ensure that the funds allocated to it during the 
financial year are optimally utilised.                                   (Para 2.5) 
 
CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES  
The Committee notes that although the budget allocation for Central Sector 
Schemes was increased from ₹1060.56 crore in BE 2025-26 to ₹1451.52 crore at RE 2025-
26, the Ministry could utilize only ₹888.22 crore (as on 31.01.2026). There has been less 
utilization of funds in three out of the four components viz. ‘Environmental Knowledge 
and Capacity Building’, ‘National Coastal Management Programme’ and ‘Control of 
Pollution’.  The Committee also took note that the major contributor for less utilization is 
the ‘Control of Pollution’ Scheme.  The Committee recommends that all steps be taken to 
ensure utilization of funds allocated during 2025-26.                                                (Para 4.5) 
 
CONTROL OF POLLUTION  
The Committee observes the financial performance of the ‘Control of Pollution’ 
Scheme during the last three years.  The Committee noted that in 2025-26, the Ministry 
has been able to utilize ₹814.26 crore (upto 31.01.2026) out of the increased RE allocation 
of ₹1300 crore.  The Committee took note of the fact that for 2025-26, budget allocation 
for ‘Control of Pollution’ scheme has been increased from ₹853.9 core to ₹1300 crore. 
Environmental pollution in the country poses a significant, ongoing threat to public health 
and environmental stability and hence, the funds allocated for its control must be 
optimally utilized.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must take 
remedial measures, devise a robust monitoring system to monitor financial and physical 
progress of the works and ensure that the funds allocated under ‘Control of Pollution’ are 
thoroughly utilized in the next financial year, ensuring desired outcomes.             (Para 5.5) 
 
The Committee observed that the Air quality in Delhi NCR remained in the 
category of poor and below during most part of October-February period of current 
financial year.  The Committee feels that there is a need of a sturdy plan to mitigate the 
air pollution and recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change, in coordination with the Govt. of NCR of Delhi, should chalk out a long term plan 
to overcome this long standing problem.                       (Para 5.6) 
 

26 
 
ENVIRONMENT EDUCATION, AWARENESS, RESEARCH AND SKILL 
DEVELOPMENT  
The Committee notes the reasons advanced by the Ministry for underutilization of 
funds under ‘Environment Education, Awareness, Research and Skill Development’. The 
Committee is of the view that the reasons advanced by the Ministry for underutilization 
are mostly procedural and administrative in nature.  The Committee recommends the 
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change to further strengthen its 
administrative and monitoring mechanism for utilising the allocated resources and ensure 
that the fund for the schemes are not underutilized.                      (Para 6.4) 
 
The Committee recommends that environment education be made a national 
priority and all State Governments be made an integral part of it as a national 
programme.  The Ministry may also take up the matter with the Ministry of Education 
(Department of School Children and Literacy and Department of Higher Education) so 
that environment awareness and education is integrated into the syllabus of school 
children and environmental awareness and protection is imbibed into the minds of future 
generations from the very beginning and helps them become environmentally responsible 
citizens.                           (Para 6.6) 
 
CENTRALLY SPONSORED SCHEMES 
The Committee observes that the BE 2025-26 allocation of ₹720.00 crore under this 
Head was reduced to ₹391.75 crore at RE stage, which is merely 55 percent of the BE 
allocation.  Out of this reduced RE allocation, the Ministry has been able to spend only 
₹256.31 crore upto 31st January 2026 i.e. 65.40 percent of the allocated amount.  The 
Committee further observes that the reduced RE resulted in reduction in allocation in all 
sub-schemes under this scheme.  One of the major schemes namely, National Mission for a 
Green India, was also impacted adversely due to this.  The Committee is also concerned 
about only 60% expenditure i.e. ₹18.27 crore out of the RE allocation of ₹30.48 crore on 
Conservation of Natural Resources and Ecosystems.          (Para 7.2) 
 
NATIONAL MISSION FOR A GREEN INDIA 
The Committee observes that the BE 2025-26 allocation of ₹220.00 crore for 
National Mission for a Green India was reduced to ₹95.70 crore at RE stage, which is 
nearly 44 percent of the BE allocation.  Again, out of the reduced allocation of ₹95.70 
crore, the Ministry could utilise only ₹40.95 crore upto 31st January 2026 i.e. nearly 43 
percent of the RE allocation. The Ministry must work out a plan of action to expedite 
utilization of RE allocation. Full utilization of the available funds during the current 
financial year should be ensured. The Ministry has not provided any reason for the 
reduction in allocation at RE stage. The Committee is of the view that though the 
reduction at RE adversely affected the activities under the scheme, but the Ministry also, 
on its own part, has not able to utilize the available funds to the desired extent till January 
month. The Committee recommends the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change to examine the slow progress of funds utilization under this scheme and take 
measures to ensure that such funds are not underutilized.                     (Para 8.5) 
 
 

27 
 
FOREST FIRE PREVENTION AND MANAGEMENT 
The Committee notes that although the expenditure in this head had been 
satisfactory during 2023-24 and 2024-25, however, the pace of utilization has been slower 
during the current financial year so far, since only ₹15.52 crore have been spent out of the 
reduced RE allocation of ₹33.25 crore.           (Para 9.3) 
The Committee also observes that occurrence of forest fires has become more 
frequent in the country and have a devastating effect on environment, forest, biodiversity 
and wildlife. Forests in Uttarakhand invariably catch fire in summers every year.  In such 
a scenario, the Committee is of the view that there is need not only to minimize such 
incidents but also to devise a protocol for dousing of forest fires which may be followed in 
case of any forest fire in the Himalayan belt. The Committee also understands that 
modern advance technologies are now available for dousing of forest fires, including use 
of satellites and drones for early detection, alerts, cause and nature of forest fires, as well 
as dousing of the same. The Committee, therefore, further recommends that the Ministry 
should explore the latest technologies available to shift focus to a proactive, AI and data-
driven prevention and management to minimize the ecological damage due to forest fires 
and provide adequate budgetary support to State Governments in this regard.      
(Para 9.4) 
INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF WILDLIFE HABITATS  
The Committee finds that the performance of the Ministry under ‘Integrated 
Development of Wildlife Habitats’ has been extremely good during the last two financial 
years.  Since the Ministry has already utilized nearly 75% of the allocation upto 31st 
January 2026, the Committee hopes that the Ministry would be able to fully utilize the 
allocations under this head in the current financial year.       (Para 10.2) 
 
PROJECT TIGER & ELEPHANT 
Centrally-funded schemes are crucial for implementing national priorities, 
reducing inter-state inequalities, and ensuring uniform development.  The Committee 
finds the financial performance of the Ministry in ‘Project Tiger & Elephant’ satisfactory.  
The Committee is in agreement that the pace of expenditure had slowed down due to 
unavoidable administrative reasons.  The Committee also agrees that fund requirement 
under this scheme is significantly higher, as the number of Tiger Reserves, tiger 
population, landscape coverage, and human–wildlife conflict incidents have all increased 
in recent years.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should consider 
allocating additional funds to this head to address the rising demands of protection, 
relocation, and conflict mitigation.          (Para 11.7) 
 
NEED TO REDUCE CASES OF MAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT 
 The Committee observes that although the Ministry informed that they had been 
making efforts very assiduously to reduce the cases of man-animal conflict, such incidents 
were increasing day by day.  The Committee feels that the number of tigers and leopards 
has increased as compared to the forest area, and hence there is a shortage of habitat for 
them. The Committee recommends that all possible steps should be taken to prevent these 
animals from entering populated areas so that they remain restricted to forest areas only. 
Suitable funds may be allocated to build rescue centers for tigers and leopards in the 
forest areas so that they do not leave the forest area. The Ministry may also come up with 

28 
 
technological interventions to tackle this menace and to reduce the cases of man-animal 
conflicts.                                    (Para 12.2)  
 
PLANTATION OF MEDICINAL PLANTS FROM CAMPA FUNDS 
Medicinal plants have been an integral part of traditional and modern healthcare 
systems due to their therapeutic potential and bioactive compounds. Medicinal plants 
offer natural, cost-effective remedies with fewer side effects for a wide range of health 
conditions, including chronic diseases, infections, and metabolic disorders.  In order to 
reach maximum benefits of these traditional plants, the availability of such plants 
becomes essential.  In view of this, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
of Environment, Forest and Climate Change should make it mandatory that, in case of 
afforestation in degraded areas, at least 25 percent of the plantation from CAMPA funds 
should be of medicinal plants, suitable for that particular ecology.  The Ministry should 
ensure that plantations contribute meaningfully to carbon sinks and biodiversity 
restoration rather than short-term target fulfillment.      (Para 13.3) 
 
OTHER CENTRAL SECTOR EXPENDITURE 
The Statutory and Regulatory / Autonomous bodies play a crucial part by 
facilitating the Ministry in executing its mandate, acting as specialized arms for 
conservation, enforcement, and scientific assessment.  As brought out by the Ministry in 
the preceding paragraphs, the curtailment of allocation at RE in 2025-26 and a reduced 
BE 2026-27 would adversely impact almost all the Statutory and Regulatory / 
Autonomous bodies in carrying out their mandated functions, including slowing down 
some expansion activities and essential regulatory, research and wildlife conservation 
mandates.  The Committee supports the needs for improvement in the budgetary 
allocations for these institutions.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends that in 2026-
27, all the Statutory and Regulatory / Autonomous bodies under the Ministry should make 
proactive efforts to achieve the physical and financial targets in respect of their various 
activities at the earliest in the first half of the financial year to stake claim for enhanced 
allocations at RE stage.                        (Para 14.7) 
 
FOREST LAND ENCROACHMENT 
The Committee expresses concern on forest land encroachment in the country.  
There are reports that over 13,000 sq km of forest area is occupied illegally across 25 
states.  The Committee is of the view that use of forest areas for non-forestry purposes 
reduces forested areas, driving biodiversity loss, habitat destruction, and environmental 
degradation.  The Supreme Court of India has ruled that forest land recorded in all 
government records including the forest land as per dictionary meaning, shall be brought 
under the purview of Forest Conservation Act and prior approval of Central government 
shall be obtained for diversion of such forest lands for non-forestry purposes.   
(Para 15.3) 
The Committee notes that the Ministry needs to examine Committee’s query 
regarding getting the drone survey of lands in forest areas done. Although the Ministry 
has drawn attention to provisions of Rule 16(1) of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam 
Samvardhan) Rules, 2023, whereby all States and Union Territory Administrations are 
required to prepare and maintain consolidated records of all categories of forest land to 
which the provisions of the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980 are 

29 
 
applicable.  However, it is not clear whether such information is available in public 
domain or not or is easily accessible to the public at large.  There have been numerous 
instances of sale of forest land involving illegal conversion or unauthorized transfer, 
frequently involving nexus between private parties, developers and officials. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change should stress upon all State/UT Governments to get the drone survey of lands 
conducted in forest areas and place these reports in public domain to enable the 
concerned public / public authorities to verify the status of such lands before any 
commercial activity/sale/purchase relating to such land is undertaken.  Any instances of 
laxity in this regard by the public authorities should be severely dealt with.  
                   (Para 15.4) 
The Committee further recommends that all eco-sensitive zones of the country 
should be mapped digitally and all necessary steps should be taken to protect the fragile 
ecosystems of the country.                        (Para 15.5) 
 
ADDITIONAL BUDGETARY REQUIREMENTS FOR SUSTAINING KEY 
PROGRAMMES 
The Committee notes the constraints highlighted by the Ministry regarding budget 
allocations for key programmes, as well as the minimum financial requirements identified 
for sustaining these initiatives. The Committee concurs with the projections submitted by 
the Ministry. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Finance should positively 
consider the financial requirements of Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change.  It further recommends that, in 2026–27, the Ministry of Environment, Forest 
and Climate Change should strive to maximize the utilization of funds allocated at the BE 
stage, thereby placing itself in a strong position to seek additional allocations at the RE 
stage for the above stated schemes and programmes.                        (Para 16.2)

CHAPTER – 1 
INTRODUCTION 
  
The Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) was established on August 3, 1954, under the 
direct charge of the Prime Minister through a Presidential Order. It is responsible for the 
development and deployment of nuclear power technology and the application of radiation 
technologies in agriculture, healthcare, industry, and basic research. Over its 72 -year history, DAE 
has mastered numerous complex technologies, including those related to medical radiology, nuclear 
agriculture, desalination, food irradiation, radio astronomy, supercomputing, particle accelerators, 
plasma, and cryogenics. 
1.2 DAE's mandate includes the production of nuclear electricity, capacity building for the 
nuclear power cycle (including front -end and back -end fuel management), operation of research 
reactors and particle accelerators for radio -isotope production, and the application of radiation 
technology to address societal challenges in healthcare, food security, and water and waste 
management. The Department also contributes to national security. 
1.3 The atomic energy programme in India is executed by a diverse group of institutions unified 
under the aegis of DAE. These include: 
1. Six Research Centres: - 
 
i)   Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) – Mumbai 
ii)  Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) – Kalpakkam 
iii) Raja Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT) – Indore 
iv) Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC) – Kolkata 
v)  Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD) – Hyderabad 
       vi) Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership (GCNEP) 
 
2.  Three Industrial Organisations: 
 
i) Heavy Water Board (HWB) – Mumbai, 
ii) Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) – Hyderabad 
iii) Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT) – Mumbai 
             
            3.  Three Service Organisations 
            4. Five Public Sector Undertakings: 
    i) Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL) – Mumbai, 
    ii) Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Ltd. (BHAVINI), Kalpakkam, 
    iii) Uranium Corporation of India Ltd. (UCIL) – Jaduguda, 
    iv) Indian Rare Earths Ltd. (IREL) – Mumbai 
     v) Electronics Corporation of India Ltd. (ECIL) – Hyderabad

 i) Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR) – Mumbai

    iii) Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP) – Kolkata 
    iv) Institute of Physics (IOP) – Bhubaneswar 
     v) Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) – Gandhinagar

1.4 In addition, DAE oversees two boards for funding and promoting research: the Board of 
Research in Nuclear Sciences (BRNS) and the National Board for Higher Mathematics (NBHM). 
1.5 The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) functions as the independent regulatory 
authority. It is directly under the Atomic Energy Commission and operates independently of DAE.

Budget Estimate and actual utilization reflects a recurring pattern of over -estimation at the

extended to all secured DAE installations, so that procurement constraints unique to nuclear

2.19 The Committee is gravely concerned about the underfunding of uranium exploration 
activities. Uranium discovery and resource delineation are long -gestation activities with lead 
times of eight to twelve years between exploration and mine production. Any reduction in 
exploration investment today will tr anslate into a fuel supply bottleneck for India's nuclear 
programme a decade hence. The Committee strongly recommends that the full shortfall of 
Rs.118.18 crore in AMDER's capital allocation be restored at the Revised Estimate stage of 
2026-27. The Committ ee further recommends priority -based funding for AMDER for 
increased uranium and rare metal exploration to secure a stable domestic supply of nuclear 
fuel in alignment with India's long-term energy security objectives.

utilization in 2025 -26, with only Rs.12.43 crore utilized till December 2025 against a B.E. of

several high-value capital initiatives could not be met. The B.E. for BRIT's capital scheme has been 
set at Rs.76 crore for 2026-27.

projects occurs in a context of rapidly growing demand for radioisotope -based diagnostics 
and therapy in India. Radioisotopes play a critical role in the management of canc er, cardiac 
conditions, and other life -threatening diseases. The Committee recommends that BRIT 
should implement a quarter-wise, milestone-linked execution plan for its Rs.76 crore capital

Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), the implementing agency for the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor 
(PFBR) at Kalpakkam. The head -wise data reveals that BHAVINI utilized only Rs.  50 crore 
against an R.E. of Rs. 150 crore and B.E. of Rs. 374 crore for 2025-26 - a utilization of merely

Committee observes that BHAVINI's severe underutilization is particularly concerning given 
that approximately  70% of the PFBR core has been loaded as on February 2026. As 
commissioning activities accelerate towards First Approach to Criticality, BHAVINI's 
expenditure requirements will increase significantly. The Committee recommends that the 
Department should pre pare a quarter -wise cash flow plan for BHAVINI's Rs.  200 crore 
allocation for 2026-27, tied to specific commissioning milestones.

arrangements with the Russian Federation. Against a B.E. of Rs.  2,086 crore and R.E. of Rs.  
1,332.83 crore for 2025 -26, actual expenditure till December 2025 stands at only Rs.430.44 crore.

crore in anticipation of delivery milestones falling due during the year. 
 
2.24 The Committee notes that the wide year -to-year variation in utilization under this 
head - from 149.63% of R.E. in 2024 -25 to a significant shortfall in 2025 -26 - reflects India's 
considerable dependence on a single foreign supplier for an operationally cri tical input. The 
Committee recommends that the Department should prepare a comprehensive medium -term 
strategy for diversification of nuclear fuel supply for KKNPP, including assessment of the 
feasibility of indigenization of fuel fa brication for this react or type . The Committee also 
recommends that payment schedules under the inter -governmental arrangement be 
structured, to the extent feasible, to minimize large year-to-year fluctuations in expenditure.

inflection point, with the imminent first criticality of PFBR marking the transition to Stage 2. 
The Fast Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility (FRFCF) at Kalpakkam has utilized Rs.311.51 crore 
against an R.E. of Rs.450 crore for 2025-26, and has been allocated Rs.600 crore in B.E. 2026-

commissioning campaigns. India's contribution to ITER for fusion research has been 
maintained at Rs.745 crore in B.E. 2026 -27. The Committee commends the Department on 
these milestones, which represent decades of sustained scientific endeavour. The Committee 
recommends that the Department should prepare a consolidated roadmap for  transition to 
Stage 2 and eventual ly Stage 3 - including projected timelines for PFBR commercial 
operation, fleet-mode FBR deployment, and FRFCF full commissioning.

3.6 The Committee takes note of the significant increase in nuclear electricity generation 
from 47,971 MUs in 2023 –24 to 56,881 MUs in 2024 –25, representing a growth of 
approximately 18.6 per cent, and commends the Department for this achievement. The 
Committee notes, however, that nuclear energy’s share in the country’s total electricity 
generation remains at a modest 3.1 per cent. Given the ambitious national target of achieving 
100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047 as envisaged under the SHANTI Act and related policy 
frameworks, the Committee is of the view that the current pace of capacity addition falls 
significantly short of what would be required to realize this target. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the Government should establish a dedicated, ring -fenced funding 
mechanism for nuclear capacity addition, insulated from year -to-year budgetary variability, 
so as to provide long -term financial certainty to ongoing and planned projects. The 
Committee further recommends that the Department should undertake a comprehensive 
review of the legislative, regulatory, and institutional factors constraining the pace of nuclear 
capacity addition, and take appropriate remedial measures to accelerate project execution in 
line with national energy targets.

periods, contributing to avoidable generation gaps. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should introduce a performance -linked accountability framework for units that 
remain in project mode or extended shutdown for prolonged periods, so as to create 
institutional incentives for timely restoration of generation capacity.

however, achieved the following significant physical milestones in the recent past: core loading 
was commenced in March 2024; loading of eight Control Sub -Rod (CSR) sub -assemblies, three 
Diverse Safety Rod (DSR) sub -assemblies and 114 Blanket sub -assemblies was subsequently 
completed; regulatory clearance for loading of fuel sub -assemblies, first approach to criticality and 
low power physics experiments was obtained from the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB); 
and as on the date, 118 fuel sub-assemblies out of a total of 175 have been loaded with fuel loading 
towards the first approach to criticality continuing to progress. 
3.13 The Committee notes that while NPCIL’s revenue from operations grew from Rs. 
18,484 crore in 2023–24 to Rs. 19,880 crore in 2024 –25, its Profit Before Tax declined sharply 
from Rs. 6,486 crore to Rs. 4,343 crore — a reduction of approximately 33 per cent i n a year 
of record electricity generation. The Committee finds this divergence between revenue 

21 
 
growth and profit contraction to be a matter of serious concern. The Committee recommends 
that the Government cause an independent performance audit of NPCIL’s c ost structure to 
be undertaken, so as to identify the structural drivers of the divergence between revenue 
growth and profit contraction and to assess the efficiency of India’s nuclear generation 
operations against international benchmarks. The Committee f urther recommends that 
NPCIL be encouraged to develop a strategy for revenue diversification beyond electricity 
tariff income, so as to improve its long -term financial resilience and reduce cost -per-unit of 
generation over time. 
3.14 The Committee observes  that the PFBR, representing a national investment of Rs. 
8,181 crore, remains in the commissioning stage without having commenced power 
production, and that no operating revenue, profit or dividend has been generated by 
BHAVINI. The protracted delay in th e PFBR achieving commercial operation is a matter of 
deep concern, particularly in view of its strategic centrality to India’s three -stage nuclear 
power programme. The Committee recommends that Government  should introduce a 
milestone-linked budgetary relea se mechanism for BHAVINI, whereby future funding 
tranches are contingent upon regulatory certification of defined commissioning achievements, 
so as to align financial flows with actual technical progress. The Committee further 
recommends that BHAVINI should be encouraged to draw upon relevant international 
operational experience in fast breeder technology to reduce the risk of recurring technical 
delays.

3.31 The Committee observes tha t India possesses among the largest known reserves of 
thorium in the world, and the utilization of thorium as a nuclear fuel is central to the long -

thorium-based fuel cy cles remains at an early stage of development, with significant 
technological and infrastructural challenges yet to be resolved. The Committee is of the view
