if India is to realize its long-term energy security potential from this indigenous resource. The

development in thorium utilization, strengthen the institutional capacity and  resource 
allocation of relevant research establishments engaged in this work, and put in place a clear 
developmental roadmap with defined milestones for the progressive introduction of thorium -

4.24 The Department informed the Committee that the major challenges in advancing nuclear 
medicine in India include the lack o f dedicated radioisotope production facilities such as additional 
reactors and cyclotrons, ineffective supply chain management, non -availability of sufficient GMP -
compliant radiopharmaceutical research, production, and quality control laboratories, and a 
shortage of trained manpower. The Department stated that there is no hindrance from a regulatory 
or safety standpoint per se, but identified a critical structural gap: radiopharmaceutical production, 
research, and distribution are currently governed by mult iple overlapping agencies — the 
Radiopharmaceutical Committee (RPC) of DAE, CDSCO, DCGI, and State FDAs — creating grey 
areas in regulatory control. Products developed by G overnment agencies outside DAE and by 
private innovators do not fall within the RPC' s jurisdiction, while CDSCO monitors only imported 
radiopharmaceuticals. The Department suggested that integrating the RPC with the DCGI, or 
significantly strengthening the RPC to cover all radiopharmaceutical innovators with a clearly 
mapped approval pathway, would resolve this ambiguity. On infrastructure, the Department stated 

32 
 
that radiopharmaceutical production remains concentrated around Delhi and Mumbai, limiting 
access in other regions. Of the 30 cyclotrons in India — 20 in th e private sector and 10 in the 
Government sector — 90 per cent produce the same isotopes without coordination and without a 
minimum support price framework. The Department also highlighted the need for high -energy 
cyclotrons of 30 MeV and 70 MeV to enable production of next -generation isotopes such as 
64Copper, 89Zirconium, 211Astatine, and 225Actinium. The Department further stated that an 
additional reactor dedicated exclusively to radioisotope production for health and industry is 
urgently required. 
4.25 The Committee enquired regarding emerging trends in nuclear medicine research, the 
impact of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and big data analytics, and specific areas 
where nuclear medicine research in India is expected to make significant strides in the next five to  
ten years. 
4.26 The Department informed the Committee that India's nuclear medicine research landscape 
is being driven by AI, radiomics, and personalized medicine. TMC is pioneering AI research in 
radiomics, image reconstruction, internal dosimetry, and a utomated report generation for PET/CT

positioned for global export under the Local to Global initiative, given its potential to be sold at 20 
per cent of the cost of import ed alternatives. In the field of theranostics, the Department identified 
isotope pairs for near-term clinical development including 68Ga and 177Lu for neuroendocrine and 
prostate cancers, and 225Actinium and 211Astatine for alpha -particle therapy. Institut ions such as 
TMC, AIIMS, and PGI are developing foundation models using patient treatment, imaging, and 
radiomic data for AI -driven diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment planning. The Department 
expressed the view that theranostics — the integration of diagn ostics and therapy using 
radiopharmaceuticals — is expected to make significant growth in the next five to ten years and is 
likely to play an important role in the treatment of almost all cancer patients. 
4.27 The Committee enquired how nuclear medicine re search i s funded in India, the role of 
Government agencies, private sector, and international funding bodies, and what steps can be taken 
to attract more investment into nuclear medicine research to foster growth and innovation. 
4.28 The Department informed the Committee that nuclear medicine research is funded through 
intramural grants and extramural support from ICMR, DST, and DBT. Specific grants for nuclear 
medicine research, including for radiopharmaceutical development, are available from the B oard of

radiopharmaceutical and nuclear medicine research; r egulatory clarity through integration of the 
RPC with the DCGI or its strengthening as a comprehensive regulator; encouraging public -private

4.29 During its interaction with the Department, the Committee also expressed its displeasure 
over the fact that in the Action Taken Note submitted by the Department on the recommendations 

33 
 
made by the Committee in its 404 th Report in December 2025, the Department has merely 
acknowledged and appreciated the Committee‘s recommendation instead of taking any substantial

4.34 The Committee observes that the regul atory framework governing 
radiopharmaceuticals in the country  is fragmented across the Radiopharmaceutical 
Committee of DAE, CDSCO, DCGI, and State FDAs, with the RPC's jurisdiction confined

radioisotope production capacity in a planned and phased manner, explore all available 
funding mechanisms, and ensure that existing production infrastructure is adequately

therapy for neuroblastoma, and the TLC Scanner — represent breakthroughs with

4.39 The Committee observes that the Department has identified AI, radiomics, and 
personalized dosimetry as the most significant frontiers for nuclear medicine research in the

4.40 The Committee also observes that instead of merely acknowledging the 
recommendations made by the Committee regarding TMC  in its 404 th Report, the 
Department should have been more proactive in implementing those recommendations. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Department should formally approach the

concerned Central/State Government Ministries/Departments for implementation of the

4.41 During the course of the presentation , the Committee was apprised that TMC is planning to

CHAPTER – 5 
THE SHANTI ACT, 2025 
The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India 
(SHANTI) Act, 2025, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15th December 202 5, passed by the 
lower house on 17th December 2025, and subsequently approved by the Rajya Sabha on 18th 
December 2025, before receiving presidential assent on 20th December 20 25. This legislation 
repeals the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, to 
create a unifie d legal framework enabling private sector participation in building, owning, and 
operating nuclear power plants. Key provisions include granting statutory status to the Atomic 
Energy Regulatory Board (AERB), introducing graded operator liability caps rangi ng from ₹100 
crore to ₹3,000 crore based on reactor size, and removing the statutory right of recourse against 
suppliers—limiting it to contractual terms or proven intent to cause damage  . The Government 
retains exclusive control over sensitive activities such as uranium enrichment and spent fuel 
management, while expanding the definition of nuclear damage to include environmental harm. 
The Act forms part of India's strategy to achieve 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047, representing 
approximately 10% of the country's projected energy needs. 
5.2 The Committee enquired from the Department that after the enforcement of SHANTI Act, 
How the AERB will ensure functional autonomy given its composition and reporting structure and 
what mechanisms are in place to prev ent conflict of interest between the DAE‘s promotional and 
regulatory roles. The Committee also asked how will transparency in regulatory decisions b e 
maintained, especially under s ection 39 and what objective criteria will be used to determine if an 
entity is ―inimical to national security‖ under section 7(4) of the Act. 
5.3 The Department informed the Committee that the SHANTI Act while preserving the de 
facto independence of AERB provides for its institutionalization and de jure independence. The 
composition of the Board, appointment of Chairman and members, their terms, etc. has now been 
provided in the Act itself. The Board has been provided with complete functional autonomy to 
frame its own set of procedures for transaction of business. It is empowered  to frame regulations, 
issue safety codes and standards, grant safety authorization and exercise oversight through 
continued safety reviews and inspections. It has also been empowered to conduct investigation, 
carry out search and seizure and take appropri ate enforcement actions including imposition of 
monetary penalties. The Board is free to engage with any academic institutions, appoint experts and 
consultants and coordinate with national and international bodies to maintain its competency. The 
Board for all purposes remains accountable to the Parliament and its Annual Report shall be laid to 
the Parliament. As required by the Board, the Central Government shall provide the Board with 
financial and human resources. In view of opening up of the nuclear sect or, the information 
regarded as ‗restricted information‘ under Section 39 has been limited to only those which are 
detrimental to national security and public interest. In order to ensure transparency, the Regulatory 
Board is also entrusted with the respon sibility under section 24(3) (h) for planned public outreach 
and engagement with interested parties on matters related to nuclear safety without disclosing 
restricted information. Nevertheless, any person aggrieved by the decisions of appellate tribunal or  
awards for settlement of any claims can approach to court. The criteria for section 7(4) for 
determining an entity is inimical to the society may be based on certain aspects which includes: If 
any conduct of the licensee poses an intentional threat to hea lth of the public or environment, or if 
the Central Government has a reason to believe that the licensee is dominated by any entity which 
poses a security risk or if there are any inputs from intelligence or law enforcement agencies 
against the licensee.

5.4 The Committee then sought to know how DAE will ensure timely processing of license and 
safety authorization applications. The Committee was informed that the Rules and Regulations will

nuclear energy sector to private industry, an ecosystem will be dev eloped based on the requirement 
of the industry.

5.7 The Committee desired to know regarding how will the liability cap in the Second Schedule 
be determined and will it be periodically reviewed. The Committee was informed  that as per the 
section 13(2) the maximum amount of liability of an operator in respect of each nuclear incident for 
different categories of nuclear installation shall be as specified in the Second Schedule. The Central 
Government has the power to amend t he second schedule (if required) to provide for a higher or 
lower amount of liability having regard to deployment of nuclear installations with advanced 
technology and enhanced safety features and other relevant criteria. 
5.8 Regarding the right to recours e against suppliers and its impact on international 
collaboration and insurance costs, the Committee learnt that a s per the international convention, 
300 million SDR is the minimum limit to be a signatory of CSC. The SHANTI Act has kept the 
same limit as India being a signatory to CSC can claim compensation from international funds, if it 
exceeds compensation for nuclear liability exceeds 300 million SDR. The SHANTI Act is special 
law dealing with the subject on civil liability for nuclear damage and section 11 of the Act make the 
operator liable for the nuclear damage and it is only after payment of the compensation in case of a 
nuclear incident, the operator may seek recourse to the extent such right is expressly provided for in 
a contract in writing betwe en operator and supplier. There is no provision in the Act which makes 
supplier liable. Further, section 87 of the Act provides for overriding effect of the Act. Thus, the 
SHANTI Act is compliant to the provisions of CSC and is consistent with the principle of exclusive 
channeling of the liability to operator (who is a licensee under the Act). With increased safety 
features in modern reactors and stringent framework for ensuring quality control of the supplied 
components (section 24(3)(c)(ii)), section 32(1 )(d)), inspection of manufacturing site (section 28 
(1) (b)(ii)), the likelihood of supply of substandard equipment or material is minimal. Thus, doing 
away with supplier‘s liability does not affect the compensation amount to be paid to the victims. 
5.9 The Committee also enquired that how the SHANTI Act aligns with international best 
practices in nuclear safety and emergency response. The Department replied that India has a robust 
system of implementation of Nuclear Safety in Nuclear and radiation Faciliti es. The responsibility 
for ensuring the safety of civilian nuclear facilities in India lies solely with the Atomic Energy 
Regulatory Board (AERB). The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) implements the national 
plan for nuclear safety, radiation protecti on, and nuclear security through a comprehensive 
Integrated Management System (IMS). This system consolidates all regulatory and management 
processes into a unified framework, ensuring coherence, consistency, and effectiveness in 
regulatory decision-making. To streamline regulation and promote uniform standards, AERB has 

39 
 
developed a comprehensive set of safety codes, guide, and standards that all operators are required

verify compliance. In cases where non -compliance is iden tified, AERB provides corrective 
recommendations and technical guidance. In extreme situations of non -compliance, AERB holds 
the authority to suspend or revoke the operating license. Compliance with international nuclear and 
radiological safety conventions  across Indian nuclear facilities is systematically monitored and 
ensured by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) through a well -defined framework that 
integrates regulatory oversight, international cooperation, and alignment with globally accepted

5.21 The Committee observes that the current disclosure regime under Section 39 and 
Section 24(3)(h) places the burden of accessing safety information on citizens, making safety 
reports, inspection findings, and incident summaries available only "upon request" and 
subject to broad exceptions including commercial confidence and national security. This 
passive disclosure approach is inadequate for a sector that directly affects public health and 
environmental safety, particularly as private operators — who have stronger commercial 
incentives to suppress unfavourable findings — now enter the nuclear space. The Committee 
therefore recommends that AERB should be mandated through Rules framed under the 
SHANTI Act to proactively and periodically publish inspection findings, regulatory decisions, 
and incident summaries on a publicly accessible digital platform, with only a narrowly 
defined category of genuinely sensitive information withheld. This would bring India in line 
with international best practices followed by regulators such as the US Nuclear Regulatory 
Commission and France' s ASN, build public trust in the regulatory process, and act as a 
structural deterrent against both operator complacency and regulatory capture.

5.22 The Committee observes that while the Central Government retains the power to 
amend the liability caps sp ecified in the Second Schedule, this power is entirely discretionary 
with no mandatory timeline, triggering mechanism, or independent oversight requirement. 
The liability caps ranging from ₹100 crore to ₹3,000 crore risk becoming inadequate over 
time as re actor sizes increase, population densities around plant sites grow, inflation erodes 
the real value of compensation, and new reactor technologies introduce different risk profiles. 
The absence of a structured review cycle means caps could remain outdated f or extended 
periods without any institutional pressure for revision, leaving victims of a potential nuclear 
incident severely undercompensated. The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules 
framed under the SHANTI Act should mandate a statutory review of the Second Schedule 
liability caps at least once every five years, conducted by an independent expert committee 
comprising legal, technical, actuarial, and public interest representatives, whose 
recommendations should be placed before Parliament before any revision is notified. This 
would ensure that compensation limits remain meaningful, provide long -term planning 
certainty to private operators and insurers, and uphold the State's fundamental obligation to 
victims of the nuclear catastrophe. 
 
5.23 The C ommittee observes that the SHANTI Act's removal of the statutory right of 
recourse against suppliers — limiting it solely to contractual terms — eliminates a significant 
legal deterrent that previously incentivized suppliers to maintain rigorous component quality 
standards. While the Department has justified this change on the grounds of compliance with 
the Convention on Supplementary Compensation and the enhanced safety features of modern 
reactors, this reasoning presupposes the very quality control effect iveness that supplier 
liability was designed to enforce. As private operators begin procuring from a wider range of 
domestic and international suppliers, often under cost pressures, the risk of substandard 
components entering nuclear facilities without ade quate legal accountability is a genuine 
concern. The Committee therefore recommends that the removal of supplier liability must be 
compensated by making third -party independent auditing of supplier manufacturing sites a 
statutory requirement under Section 28, with audit findings reported directly to AERB 
rather than routed through the operator. This structural safeguard would preserve the 
quality assurance function previously served by the threat of legal liability, protect potential 
victims without burdening international nuclear commerce, and ensure that the channeling of 
liability exclusively to operators does not come at the cost of supply chain integrity. 
 

43 
 
5.24 The Committee observes that while the SHANTI Act opens the nuclear sector to 
private participation, the Act and the Department's responses do not specify any minimum 
financial, technical, or operational qualification thresholds that private entities must meet 
before receiving a licence  to operate in the sector . Unlike other infrastructure sectors opened 
to private investment, a failure in nuclear facility operation is not recoverable — it carries the 
risk of irreversible environmental contamination, transboundary harm, and long -term public 
health consequences. The experience of private sector participation in other sensitive 
infrastructure sectors in India has shown that without robust pre -qualification criteria, cost-
cutting and regulatory arbitrage can emerge, particularly in early years of a new framework. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must 
prescribe clear, publicly available and non -negotiable minimum qualification criteria for 
private nuclear operators, including minimum net worth requirements, mandatory insura nce 
coverage, demonstrated technical competency, and operational track records, before any 
private licence is granted. Further, a dedicated continuous monitoring mechanism should be 
established specifically for private operators during their initial years of operation to ensure 
that commercial pressures do not compromise nuclear safety. 
 
5.25 The Committee observes that the Department's response on public information during 
a nuclear incident focused primarily on the Claims Commissioner's role in publicisin g 
compensation procedures under Section 65, entirely conflating the immediate public safety 
alert function with the subsequent claims settlement process. These are two fundamentally 
distinct needs — the former requiring real-time, wide-area communication within hours of an 
incident, and the latter being a judicial process that unfolds over months or years. The 
Committee is of the opinion  that delayed and fragmented public communication during a 
nuclear emergency significantly compounds the humanitarian impa ct, regardless of the 
quality of subsequent compensation mechanisms. The Committee therefore recommends that 
the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must mandate a statutory real -time public alert 
protocol, specifying defined timelines for initial public not ification, designated responsible 
authorities at local, state, and national levels, and mandated communication channels — 
including digital, broadcast, and community -level systems — that are activated immediately 
upon a nuclear incident being declared, ent irely independent of the claims process. This 
protocol should be tested through mandatory periodic drills and reviewed annually by AERB 
in coordination with State Disaster Management Authorities. 
 

44 
 
5.26 The Committee observes that the SHANTI Act defers the framing of a radioactive 
waste management policy to a future Central Government notification under Section 32, 
without specifying any timeline or minimum standards that such a policy must meet before 
private operators are licensed to construct or operate n uclear facilities. This sequencing is a 
significant governance concern. Radioactive waste management is not an operational 
afterthought — it is a fundamental safety, environmental, and intergenerational 
responsibility that must be planned and regulated fro m the earliest stages of facility design. 
The original Atomic Energy Act, 1962, reserved spent fuel management exclusively for the 
Government precisely in recognition of its extreme sensitivity and long -term consequences. 
Allowing private operators to begi n construction or operation without a legally binding, 
comprehensive, and publicly available waste management framework in place risks the 
development of ad hoc, inconsistent, and potentially unsafe waste handling practices that 
could have irreversible env ironmental consequences. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Central Government should frame and publicly notify the radioactive waste 
management policy under Section 32 as a mandatory precondition before the first private 
nuclear licence is grante d under the SHANTI Act. This policy should specify standards for 
waste classification, storage, transportation, reprocessing, and long-term disposal, and should 
be subject to periodic review by AERB in consultation with the Central Pollution Control 
Board and relevant State authorities.

ATOMIC ENERGY REGULATORY BOARD 
 
The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) was established by the Government of India 
through a statutory order issued under Section 27 of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, with its primary

the Act. AERB carries out various regulatory and safety functions such as specifying regulatory 
requirements and providing guidance to meet these requirements, granting licenses to facilities and 
activities, carrying out regulat ory oversight through regular safety reviews & assessment and 
inspections, monitoring compliance, taking enforcement actions as necessary, and confirming 
satisfactory states of emergency preparedness and response. In addition, AERB carries out as well 
as p romotes safety and regulatory research and interacts with relevant agencies at national and 
international level, disseminates information to keep public informed on relevant safety issues and 
carries out safety promotion activities. 
6.2 The Committee enqui red the  role played by  AERB as a facilitator of Research and

facilitator of Research and Development of indigenous medical device used in the field of 
Radiology. However, AERB is open for providing guidance on safety and regulatory requirements 
to the developers (R&D institutions). AERB participates in professional forums & delivers 
technical talks, which are attended by the developers. Such approach of AERB is helpful to the 
developers for understanding the regulatory requirement and further submission to AERB for 
obtaining regulatory approvals. Moreover, user guide lines on regulatory processes are available on 
AERB's website.

6.7 The Committee also sought to know h ow does AERB's approval process for radiology 
machines com pare with that of the  U.S. FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health 
(CDRH) or Europe's CE marking process  under the EU's M edical Device Regulation (MDR). The 
Department replied that AERB regulates the suppliers/manufactures through type approval ra diology 
equipment. During type approval process AERB evaluates conformity of equipment performance 
with respect to radiation safety standards. AERB also regulates the user institutions by issuing

Department further informed that based on the information available in public domain on functioning 
of US-FDA and Europe's CE, the FDA primarily regulates manufacturers by evaluating the safety 
and effectiveness of devices. User institutions of radiology equipment are not directly licensed by the 
U.S.FDA for using radiology equipment.  In Europe, under the framework coordinated by the 
European Commission, CE marking emphasizes conformity assessment, technical documentation ,

6.8 The Committee also asked regarding steps taken by AERB in collaboration with customs and 
other agencies, to identify and prevent the installation of uncertified, counterfeit, or smuggled 
radiology equipment in the country. The Committee was informed that AERB coordinated with 
Director General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) in the past for revision of import policy conduction for 
Radiology X -ray equip ment. As per DGFT notification of 2018, one of the import conditions for 
Radiology X -ray equipment is its prior regulatory clearance from AERB. Accordingly, Customs 
verify the NOC for import issued by AERB to the user institution during import of radiology X -ray 
equipment in the country.

Organization (CDSCO)  to avoid dual regulato ry burdens while ensuring both radiation safety and 
medical device efficacy are addressed. The Committee was informed that AERB regulates radiation 
facilities under the Atomic Energy (Radiation Protection) Rules, 2004, while CDSCO regulates 
medical devices  under the Medical Device Rules, 2017. The two agencies coordinate and consult 
with each other, as and when required, to avoid dual regulatory burdens while ensuring both radiation 
safety and medical de vice efficacy are addressed. For example  AERB No -Objection Certificate 

47 
 
(NOC)/type approval from radiological safety considerations is a pre -requisite for issuance of license

6.10 The Committee enquired that h ow does the structure and autonomy of India's AERB 
compare with n uclear regulators in countries like the Unit ed States (NRC) or France (ASN). The 
Department replied that AERB is functionally autonomous and discharging its mandate effectively 
without any external influence in its regulatory decision making. The Integrated Regulatory Review 
Service (IRRS) mission of IAEA held in 2015 has acknowledged the functional independence of 
AERB as a regulator. The recently enacted SHANTI Act 2025 provides statutory status to AERB 
by embedding it in the law. This legal framework est ablishes an independent regulatory body for 
issuance of safety authorization, in line with other countries such as the US and France. 
 
6.11 The Committee also desired to know how AERB is preparing to regulate emerging 
technologies like nuclear fusion or ad vanced small modular reactors (SMRs). The Department 
informed that AERB safety and regulatory requirements for licensing of NPPs are mostly 
technology neutral. In light of the evolving developments in the field of SMRs, AERB has 
conducted review of its exi sting regulatory requirements and concluded that the same regulatory 
framework can generally be applied for safety regulation of advanced reactors such as SMRs, 
except a few technology specific aspects for which review may be required when details of 
proposed sites and design of specific SMR is submitted to AERB. AERB also participates in 
various international forums to keep itself abreast about the developments in regulation of SMRs 
and suitably adopt them when required. Commercial use for Fusion technolog y is not expected to 
be in the near future. 
 
6.12  The Committee sought to know that f or groundbreaking technologies (e.g., MR -LINAC 
systems, proton therapy machines), how does AERB's regulator y framework adapt. Does it engage in 
pre-submission dialogues with manufacturers to guide the development process against safety norms? 
The Department informed that i n the past, AERB has handled licensing for first -of-its-kind facilities 
such as Proton Therapy Facilities & MR-LINAC systems. The approach adopted is as follows: Based 
on the initial intent submitted by the user institute for establishing facilities incorporating new 
technologies (e.g., MR -LINAC systems, proton therapy machines), AERB engages with the 
manufacturer to discuss the relevant technical and regu latory aspects. Subsequently, AERB 
constitutes expert committees for specific areas (e.g., facility design approval, quality assurance 
aspects, etc.) and conducts further discussions with manufacturers and other relevant stakeholders, as 
required. AERB als o reviews international literature and regulatory practices for similar facilities in 
other countries to develop appropriate regulatory requirements. Using this approach, AERB has 
successfully licensed first -of-its-kind facilities such as Proton Therapy Fa cilities and MR -LINAC 
systems in the country. AERB remains open to a dialogue with manufacturers/suppliers to provide 
guidance on safety and regulatory requirements. 
6.13 The Committee also asked that in the context of public health needs, how does AERB manage 
the balance between ensuring rapid deployment of essential radiology machines (like in rural areas) 
and maintaining an uncompromising, often time -consuming, safety review process. The Department 
replied that AERB has implemented a digital regulatory p latform eLORA (e -Licensing of Radiation 
Application) covering all types of consenting processes, inventory management of sources & 
equipment, inspection activities and non -compliance management. Most of the consenting and safety 
review processes w ith respect to radiology equipment are processed faster using rules embedded in 
the eLORA system while ensuring that the safety aspects are duly covered. This in turns ensures 
effective regulatory oversight for rapidly expanding radiology facilities. 
6.14 The Commi ttee asked regarding AERB's policy on the import and installation of 
refurbished/used radiology machines and w hat additional safeguards and testing requirements are in 
place to ensure their safety and performa nce are comparable to new units. The Committee was 
informed that a s per AERB policy, only refurbished or used radiology equipment that is not more 

48 
 
than seven years old is permitted for import. However, if manufacturer support for refurbishment is 
available, equipment up to ten years old may also be imp orted. AERB issues an operational license 
for such refurbished or used equipment only after verifying that its performance (i.e.QA test) is 
satisfactory. The QA requirements are same irrespective of nature of machine i.e. new/refurbished. 
 
6.15 The Committ ee enquired regarding AERB's mechanism for monitoring the long -term 
performance and safety of radiology machi nes in the field. The department replied that AERB 
monitors the long -term performance and safety of radiology machines in the field through 
verification of periodic quality assurance (QA) reports, periodic safety status report and regulatory 
inspections. Also, the type approval of such machines is  renewed based on user feedback on the 
performance of equipment from radiological safety view point. 
6.16 The Committee also sought to know that w hat AERB has done to align its guidelines with 
globally accepted best practices to ensure that it is not a bottleneck but a facilitator in the 
development of indigenous ―Make in India‖ R adiology devices in the count ry. The Committee was 
informed that AERB's role is to carry out safety reviews and approvals based on compliance with the 
safety requirements, which are in line with globally accepted practices and standards. Moreover, 
AERB is open for providing guidance o n safety and regulatory requirements to manufacturers. 
AERB's regulatory approvals for Radiology equipment are issued through AERB's eLORA (e -
Licensing of Radiation Application) system. eLORA system provides convenience of submission and 
faster regulatory approvals, thereby promoting ease of doing business. 
6.17 The Committee also enquired regarding AERB‘s role  in promoting ―Make in India‖ in the 
field of medical devices in the country. The Department informed the Committee that AERB‘s role is 
that of the r egulator for radiation safety and it has no direct role as a promoter. However, AERB is 
open for providing guidance on safety and regulatory requirements to manufacturers. AERB 
participates in professional forums, delivers technical talks and conduct NCRI (National Conference 
on Regulatory Interface), which are attended by the equipment manufacturer. Such openness 
approach of AERB is helpful to the manufacturer for understanding the regulatory requirement and 
further submission to AERB for obtaining regulat ory approvals. Also, as elaborated earlier, AERB's 
eLORA system provides convenience of submission and faster regulatory approvals, thereby 
promoting ease of doing business. 
6.18 The Committee observes that providing guidance and participating in professional 
forums is a passive approach. The development of indigenous medical devices requires 
proactive and structured support. The Committee therefore recommends that AERB should 
establish a formal "Innovation Facilitation Cell" or a "Regulatory Sandb ox" framework. 
This would allow developers of indigenous radiology and radiotherapy devices to engage in 
early, confidential, and structured pre -submission dialogues with AERB experts. This 
formalizes the ad -hoc expert committee approach used for Proton Th erapy and makes it 
accessible for domestic R&D, helping them navigate safety norms from the design stage itself, 
thus reducing time-to-market. 
6.19 The Committee also recommends that to build greater trust and identify process 
bottlenecks, AERB should publ ish more granular performance data on its public dashboard. 
This could include: (a) TAT broken down by type of application (import vs. license vs. type 
approval), (b) TAT for "first -of-its-kind" technologies vs. standard equipment, and (c) the 

49 
 
number of applications that went through multiple review cycles. This aligns with the global 
best practice of regulatory transparency and helps stakeholders manage their own planning. 
6.20 The Committee further recommends that AERB should move towards a more 
dynamic, risk-based post-market surveillance system. This could involve u tilizing data from 
the eLORA system to identify trends in equipment performance, recurring non -compliances, 
or specific manufacturers/models that may require more frequent oversight.  AERB should 
establishing a clear, mandatory, and simple mechanism for users (radiologists, technicians) to 
report any safety -related malfunctions or "near misses" directly to AERB, creating a 
national database for learning and preventative action. 
6.21 The Committee no tes that the current coordination of AERB with CDSCO needs a 
more proactive approach. To provide clarity to the industry and avoid duplication, the two 
agencies should formalize their coordination through a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) 
or a Memorandu m of Understanding (MoU). This document should clearly map the 
regulatory pathway for a medical device and establish a joint review mechanism for 
technologies that blur the lines between radiation safety and medical efficacy. This "single -
window" clarity would greatly benefit the "Make in India" initiative.

7.28 The Committee acknowledges the extensive and multifaceted efforts undertaken by

HRI, TIFR, and IMSc run excellent programmes, the overall effort appears fragmented. A 
student or teacher in a sma ll city may not be aware of opportunities available at different 
DAE institutions. To maximize impact, optimize resource utilization, and create a more 
cohesive national strategy, the Committee  recommends that the DAE should develop a 
centralized, user -friendly web portal that aggregates all mathematics outreach activities 
across its institutes (NISER, HRI, IMSc, TIFR, CEBS, etc.). This portal should feature a 
common calendar of events (workshops, camps, lectures), a repository of learning resources 
(including Vigyan Pratibha modules in multiple languages), and information on internships 
and fellowships. This would act as a single window for students and educators nationwide, 
significantly increasing the visibility and accessibility of DAE's programmes.

deep mathematical thinking and a sense of community among pre -university students. The 
Committee recommends that DAE should consider providing dedicated funding and 
administrative support to scale this programme. This could involve  establishing new Maths 
Circles in different regions, anchored by other DAE institutes like IMSc in the South, HRI in

the Central regio n, and NISER in the East. The Department could also come up with a 
"Maths Circle in a Box" toolkit (with curated problem sets, activity guides, and training

own circles, supported remotely by the DAE Institutes.

Pratibha, Maths Circle, Talent Search) or undergraduate/postgraduate students (SPIM, 
Summer Research Fellowships). There is an opportunity to create a more seamless pipeline.

Vigyan Pratibha to identify motivated students.  The Department could i nvite the top

advanced programmes like SPIM or the Maths Circle, or create dedicated "bridge camps" to

explicitly connect the summer research programmes (at HRI, IMSc, TIFR) to the PhD

that the Department should develop dedicated training modules for school teache rs of 
Mathematics in the country. The module should focus on training teachers to kindle interest

BUDGET ANALYSIS 
 
The Committee urges the Ministry of Finance to sympathetically consider the 
Department's requirements at the R.E. stage, particularly for time -sensitive nuclear

allocations. This pattern, which recurs across multiple financial years, suggests systematic 
over-estimation at the budget preparation stage. To enhance financial discipline and project 
execution, the Committee recommends that the Department should adopt the following 
corrective measures: firstl y, Budget Estimates for capital schemes should be prepared based 
exclusively on projects that have received formal sanction, while proposals pending approval

 The Committee takes note of the significant increase in nuclear electricity generation 
from 47,971 MUs in 2023 –24 to 56,881 MUs in 2024 –25, representing a growth of

Committee notes, however, that nuclear energy’s share in the country’s total electricity 
generation remains at a modest 3.1 per cent. Given the ambitious national target of achieving 
100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047 as envisaged under the SHANTI Act and related policy 
frameworks, the Committee is of the view that the current pace of capacity addition falls 
significantly short of what would be required to realize this target. The Committee therefore 
recommends that the  Government should establish a dedicated, ring -fenced funding 
mechanism for nuclear capacity addition, insulated from year -to-year budgetary variability, 
so as to provide long -term financial certainty to ongoing and planned projects. The 
Committee further recommends that the Department should undertake a comprehensive 
review of the legislative, regulatory, and institutional factors constraining the pace of nuclear

capacity addition, and take appropriate remedial measures to accelerate project execution in 
line with national energy targets.

 The Committee observes that several units across multiple stations, including TAPS -1, 
TAPS-2, MAPS -1 and KGS -1, remain under project mode or maintenance for extended 
periods, contributing to avoidable generatio n gaps. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should introduce a performance -linked accountability framework for units that 
remain in project mode or extended shutdown for prolonged periods, so as to create 
institutional incentives for timely restoration of generation capacity.

milestone-linked budgetary release mechanism for BHAVINI, whereby future funding 
tranches are contingent upon regulatory certification of defined commissioning achievements,

The Committee observes that while the SHANTI Act provides statutory and de jure 
independence to AERB, the structural relationship between DAE — which actively promotes 
nuclear energy expansion — and AERB remains a source of potential conflict of interest. The 
Department's response does not adequately address the concern that the same Ministry 
driving India's 100 GW nuclear ambitions may influence the composition and leadership of 
the body meant to regulate it. The Committee therefore recommends that the Central 
Government should establish an independent Appointments Committee for the selection of 
AERB's Chairman and Board members, comprising members drawn substantially from 
outside DAE. This would create a structural firewall between the promotional and regulatory 
arms of nuclear governance. 
(Para 5.20) 
 
The Committee observes that the current disclosure regime under Section 39 and 
Section 24(3)(h) places the burden of accessing safety information on citizens, making safety 
reports, inspection findings, and incident summaries available only "upon request" and 
subject to broad exceptions including commercial confidence and national security. This 
passive disclosure approach is inadequate for a sector that directly affects public health and 
environmental safety, particularly as private operators — who have stronger commercial 
incentives to suppress unfavourable findings — now enter the nuclear space. The Committee 
therefore recommends that AERB should be mandated through Rules framed under the 
SHANTI Act to proactively and periodically publish inspection findings, regulatory decisions, 
and incident summaries on a publicly accessible digital platform, with only a narrowly 
defined category of genuinely sensitive information withheld. This would bring India in line 
with international best practices followed by regulators such as the US Nuclear Regulatory 
Commission and France's ASN, build public trust in the regulatory process, and act as a 
structural deterrent against both operator complacency and regulatory capture. 
(Para 5.21) 

65 
 
 
The Committee observes that while the Central Government retains the power to 
amend the liability caps specified in the Second Schedule, this power is entirely discreti onary 
with no mandatory timeline, triggering mechanism, or independent oversight requirement. 
The liability caps ranging from ₹100 crore to ₹3,000 crore risk becoming inadequate over 
time as reactor sizes increase, population densities around plant sites g row, inflation erodes 
the real value of compensation, and new reactor technologies introduce different risk profiles. 
The absence of a structured review cycle means caps could remain outdated for extended 
periods without any institutional pressure for revi sion, leaving victims of a potential nuclear 
incident severely undercompensated. The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules 
framed under the SHANTI Act should mandate a statutory review of the Second Schedule 
liability caps at least once every five years, conducted by an independent expert committee 
comprising legal, technical, actuarial, and public interest representatives, whose 
recommendations should be placed before Parliament before any revision is notified. This 
would ensure that compensation l imits remain meaningful, provide long -term planning 
certainty to private operators and insurers, and uphold the State's fundamental obligation to 
victims of the nuclear catastrophe. 
(Para 5.22) 
 
The Committee observes that the SHANTI Act's removal of the statutory right of 
recourse against suppliers — limiting it solely to contractual terms — eliminates a significant 
legal deterrent that previously incentivized suppliers to maintain rigorous component quality 
standards. While the Department has justified t his change on the grounds of compliance with 
the Convention on Supplementary Compensation and the enhanced safety features of modern 
reactors, this reasoning presupposes the very quality control effectiveness that supplier 
liability was designed to enforce . As private operators begin procuring from a wider range of 
domestic and international suppliers, often under cost pressures, the risk of substandard 
components entering nuclear facilities without adequate legal accountability is a genuine 
concern. The Committee therefore recommends that the removal of supplier liability must be 
compensated by making third -party independent auditing of supplier manufacturing sites a 
statutory requirement under Section 28, with audit findings reported directly to AERB 
rather than routed through the operator. This structural safeguard would preserve the 
quality assurance function previously served by the threat of legal liability, protect potential 
victims without burdening international nuclear commerce, and ensure that the channeling of 
liability exclusively to operators does not come at the cost of supply chain integrity. 
(Para 5.23) 
 
The Committee observes that while the SHANTI Act opens the nuclear sector to 
private participation, the Act and the Department's responses do  not specify any minimum 
financial, technical, or operational qualification thresholds that private entities must meet 
before receiving a licence to operate in the sector. Unlike other infrastructure sectors opened 
to private investment, a failure in nuclear facility operation is not recoverable — it carries the 
risk of irreversible environmental contamination, transboundary harm, and long -term public 
health consequences. The experience of private sector participation in other sensitive 
infrastructure sectors in India has shown that without robust pre -qualification criteria, cost-
cutting and regulatory arbitrage can emerge, particularly in early years of a new framework. 
The Committee therefore recommends that the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must 
prescribe clear, publicly available and non -negotiable minimum qualification criteria for 
private nuclear operators, including minimum net worth requirements, mandatory insurance 
coverage, demonstrated technical competency, and operational track records, before  any 
private licence is granted. Further, a dedicated continuous monitoring mechanism should be 
established specifically for private operators during their initial years of operation to ensure 
that commercial pressures do not compromise nuclear safety. 

66 
 
(Para 5.24) 
 
The Committee observes that the Department's response on public information during 
a nuclear incident focused primarily on the Claims Commissioner's role in publicising 
compensation procedures under Section 65, entirely conflating the immediate public safety 
alert function with the subsequent claims settlement process. These are two fundamentally 
distinct needs — the former requiring real-time, wide-area communication within hours of an 
incident, and the latter being a judicial process that unfol ds over months or years. The 
Committee is of the opinion that delayed and fragmented public communication during a 
nuclear emergency significantly compounds the humanitarian impact, regardless of the 
quality of subsequent compensation mechanisms. The Commi ttee therefore recommends that 
the Rules framed under the SHANTI Act must mandate a statutory real -time public alert 
protocol, specifying defined timelines for initial public notification, designated responsible 
authorities at local, state, and national le vels, and mandated communication channels — 
including digital, broadcast, and community -level systems — that are activated immediately 
upon a nuclear incident being declared, entirely independent of the claims process. This 
protocol should be tested through mandatory periodic drills and reviewed annually by AERB 
in coordination with State Disaster Management Authorities. 
(Para 5.25) 
The Committee observes that the SHANTI Act defers the framing of a radioactive 
waste management policy to a future Central Gov ernment notification under Section 32, 
without specifying any timeline or minimum standards that such a policy must meet before 
private operators are licensed to construct or operate nuclear facilities. This sequencing is a 
significant governance concern. Radioactive waste management is not an operational 
afterthought — it is a fundamental safety, environmental, and intergenerational 
responsibility that must be planned and regulated from the earliest stages of facility design. 
The original Atomic Energy Act , 1962, reserved spent fuel management exclusively for the 
Government precisely in recognition of its extreme sensitivity and long -term consequences. 
Allowing private operators to begin construction or operation without a legally binding, 
comprehensive, an d publicly available waste management framework in place risks the 
development of ad hoc, inconsistent, and potentially unsafe waste handling practices that 
could have irreversible environmental consequences. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Cen tral Government should frame and publicly notify the radioactive waste 
management policy under Section 32 as a mandatory precondition before the first private 
nuclear licence is granted under the SHANTI Act. This policy should specify standards for 
waste classification, storage, transportation, reprocessing, and long-term disposal, and should 
be subject to periodic review by AERB in consultation with the Central Pollution Control 
Board and relevant State authorities. 
(Para 5.26) 
 
ATOMIC ENERGY REGULATORY BOARD 
 
The Committee observes that providing guidance and participating in professional 
forums is a passive approach. The development of indigenous medical devices requires 
proactive and structured support. The Committee therefore recommends that AERB should  
establish a formal "Innovation Facilitation Cell" or a "Regulatory Sandbox" framework. 
This would allow developers of indigenous radiology and radiotherapy devices to engage in 
early, confidential, and structured pre -submission dialogues with AERB experts . This 
formalizes the ad -hoc expert committee approach used for Proton Therapy and makes it 
accessible for domestic R&D, helping them navigate safety norms from the design stage itself, 
thus reducing time-to-market. 

67 
 
(Para 6.18) 
 
The Committee also recommends that to build greater trust and identify process 
bottlenecks, AERB should publish more granular performance data on its public dashboard. 
This could include: (a) TAT broken down by type of application (import vs. license vs. type 
approval), (b) TAT for "first -of-its-kind" technologies vs. standard equipment, and (c) the 
number of applications that went through multiple review cycles. This aligns with the global 
best practice of regulatory transparency and helps stakeholders manage their own planning. 
(Para 6.19) 
The Committee further recommends that AERB should move towards a more dynamic, 
risk-based post -market surveillance system. This could involve utilizing data from the 
eLORA system to identify trends in equipment performance, recurring non -compliances, or 
specific manufacturers/models that may require more frequent oversight. AERB should 
establishing a clear, mandatory, and simple mechanism for users (radiologists, technicians) to 
report any safety -related malfunctions or "near misses" direct ly to AERB, creating a 
national database for learning and preventative action. 
(Para 6.20) 
 
The Committee notes that the current coordination of AERB with CDSCO needs a more 
proactive approach. To provide clarity to the industry and avoid duplication, the two 
agencies should formalize their coordination through a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP ) 
or a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This document should clearly map the 
regulatory pathway for a medical device and establish a joint review mechanism for 
technologies that blur the lines between radiation safety and medical efficacy. This "single -
window" clarity would greatly benefit the "Make in India" initiative. 
(Para 6.21) 
 
 
 
PROMOTION OF HIGHER MATHEMATICS IN THE COUNTRY 
The Committee acknowledges the extensive and multifaceted efforts undertaken by 
the DAE and its aided institutions to promote  advanced mathematics. The programmes like 
SPIM, the Maths Circle, and the Vigyan Pratibha initiative are particularly noteworthy for 
their depth and reach. However, the Committee notes that while individual institutes like 
HRI, TIFR, and IMSc run excellen t programmes, the overall effort appears fragmented. A 
student or teacher in a small city may not be aware of opportunities available at different 
DAE institutions. To maximize impact, optimize resource utilization, and create a more 
cohesive national stra tegy, the Committee  recommends that the DAE should develop a 
centralized, user -friendly web portal that aggregates all mathematics outreach activities 
across its institutes (NISER, HRI, IMSc, TIFR, CEBS, etc.). This portal should feature a 
common calendar of events (workshops, camps, lectures), a repository of learning resources 
(including Vigyan Pratibha modules in multiple languages), and information on internships 
and fellowships. This would act as a single window for students and educators nationwide, 
significantly increasing the visibility and accessibility of DAE's programmes. 
(Para 7.28) 
The "Maths Circle India" initiative led by TIFR is a powerful model for nurturing 
deep mathematical thinking and a sense of community among pre -university students. The 
Committee recommends that DAE should consider providing dedicated funding and 
administrative support to scale this programme. This could involve establishing new Maths 
Circles in different regions, anchored by other DAE institutes like IMSc in the Sout h, HRI in 

68 
 
the Central region, and NISER in the East. The Department could also come up with a 
"Maths Circle in a Box" toolkit (with curated problem sets, activity guides, and training 
manuals) to enable motivated teachers or college clubs anywhere in the c ountry to start their 
own circles, supported remotely by the DAE Institutes. 
(Para 7.29) 
The Committee observes that many programmes target either school students (Vigyan 
Pratibha, Maths Circle, Talent Search) or undergraduate/postgraduate students (SPIM, 
Summer Research Fellowships). There is an opportunity to create a more seamless pipeline. 
The Committee recommends that DAE should develop a formal Mathematical Talent 
Nurturing Pipeline. The Department should leverage the Talent Search Examinations and 
Vigyan Pratibha to identify motivated students. The Department could invite the top 
performers from these school -level programmes to special introductory tracks within 
advanced programmes like SPIM or the Maths Circle, or create dedicated "bridge camps" to 
ease the transition from school -level problem-solving to university -level conceptual thinking. 
The Department should ensure that students who excel in these programmes are actively 
mentored and guided towards opportunities like the NISER undergraduate progr amme, 
summer internships, and the NBHM Olympiad training camps. The Department should 
explicitly connect the summer research programmes (at HRI, IMSc, TIFR) to the PhD 
programmes within the DAE system, potentially creating a fast -track channel for the most  
promising students. 
(Para 7.30) 
The Committee also feels that the curriculum of Mathematics in the schools is outdated 
and inadequate in generating curiosity towards the subject amongst the students. Moreover, 
the curriculum is heavily skewed towards the theoretical aspects and lacks application of the 
subject in daily life. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should 
approach CBSE, NCERT, State Boards and SCERTs for a complete overhauling of the 
Mathematics curriculum in the country. The  Committee also recommends that the 
Department should develop dedicated training modules for school teachers of Mathematics in 
the country. The module should focus on training teachers to kindle interest in the subject 
amongst the young children, highlight ing achievements of the country’s ancient and modern 
geniuses of the country in the subject and the vast applications of the subject in not only our 
day to day life but in modern technologies like AI/ML, cybersecurity, genetics, etc. 
(Para 7.31)

CHAPTER – 1 
INTRODUCTION 
 The Department of Biotechnology (DBT) was initially set up as an independent board in 
1982 and was later elevated to a full-fledged Department under the Ministry of Science & 
Technology in 1986. Its core mandate includes policy formulation, promoting research, and 
overseeing biotechnology-related manufacturing activities across the country. DBT designs and 
implements integrated biotechnology programs, ensuring they are effectively executed and aligned 
with national priorities. It identifies and supports research and development efforts, especially in 
biologicals and biotech manufacturing, and establishes Centres of Excellence to drive progress in 
key scientific areas. In addition, the department acts as a regulatory and advisory body for the 
import, transfer, and approval of new biotechnological products and technologies. It also formulates 
safety protocols for biotech research and production and serves as the central authority for the 
import of genetically modified materials, while simultaneously encouraging domestic production. 
1.2 A major responsibility of DBT is fostering inter-ministerial and international partnerships, 
managing technology transfers, and promoting the development of recombinant DNA products, 
cell-based vaccines, and biotech diagnostics. Human resource development is another critical focus 
area, carried out through various agencies, commissions, and research boards established by the 
Government of India. Furthermore, DBT leads national efforts in bioinformatics by facilitating 
training programs, building infrastructure, enabling data collection, and promoting knowledge 
sharing in the field of biotechnology research. 
1.3 The Department oversees a network of autonomous institutions engaged in advanced 
research fields such as genomics, immunology, neuroscience, regenerative medicine, and 
bioresource management. It also manages the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and 
Biotechnology (ICGEB) based in New Delhi. In addition, DBT supervises public sector 
undertakings that contribute to biotech innovation, vaccine development, and industrial research 
support. Together, these organizations play a vital role in strengthening and advancing India’s 
biotechnology landscape.

Environment, Forests and Climate Change considered the Demands for Grants (2026-27), Demand 
No. 90 of the Department of Biotechnology in its meeting held on 25th February, 2026.

CHAPTER – 3 
 BIO-RIDE: PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION AND KEY ACHIEVEMENTS 
 
In September 2024, the Union Cabinet approved the merger of the Department of 
Biotechnology's (DBT) two umbrella schemes—'Biotechnology Research & Development' and 
'Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development'—into a single, integrated scheme 
named "Biotechnology Research Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development (Bio-RIDE)." 
 
3.2 Approved for the 15th Finance Commission cycle (2021-22 to 2025-26) with a total outlay 
of ₹9,197 crore, Bio-RIDE introduces a third new component: 'Biomanufacturing & Biofoundry', 
which has a dedicated allocation of ₹1,500 crore. This merger aims to create a unified framework to 
foster research, innovation, and entrepreneurship across the biotechnology sector. 
 
3.3 The scheme's three key components are: 
A. Biotechnology Research and Development: This component focuses on building the 
foundational scientific capacity of the nation through human resource development, 
research infrastructure, competitive grants, international collaboration, and programs for 
societal and regional development, particularly in the North East. 
B. Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development: This component is designed to stimulate 
innovation within the Indian biotech industry. It supports public-private partnerships 
(PPP), the 'Make in India' initiative, and the establishment of biotech parks to help 
startups and SMEs create affordable, impactful products. 
C. Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry: This new, strategic component aims to propel India 
into a leadership position in the global bioeconomy. It will focus on high-performance 
biomanufacturing in areas like bio-based chemicals, smart proteins, and precision 
therapeutics, supported by cross-cutting national platforms such as Biofoundries and Bio-
AI Hubs. 
 
3.4 Bio-RIDE scheme is the only central sector scheme under the Department. The scheme was 
allocated Rs. 2300 crore in B.E. 2025-26 which was substantially reduced to Rs. 1717 crore at R.E. 
stage. Out of this reduced R.E., the Department spent Rs. 1629.11 crore which comes to around 
94% of its R.E. The Department has again been allocated the same amount as last year i.e. Rs. 2300 
crore.  
 
3.5 The scheme was allocated Rs. 1680 crore in 2022-23 which was marginally reduced to Rs. 
1645 crore in 2023-24. In the next fiscal year, this was substantially reduced to Rs. 1174 crore. 
However, in FY 2025-26, the budget allocation under the head was almost doubled to Rs. 2300 
crore which has maintained in the FY 2026-27 also.  
 
3.6 The budgetary trends for the Bio-RIDE scheme reveal a persistent pattern of volatility 
between initial allocation and final expenditure, coupled with a recent substantial increase 
that has been sustained. To enhance the effectiveness and predictability of this central sector 
scheme, the Committee recommends that the Department should prioritize improving the 
accuracy of its budget estimates to mitigate the sharp reductions witnessed at the Revised 
Estimate stage, thereby ensuring that the enhanced allocation of Rs. 2300 crore translates 

10 
 
into actual spending rather than a notional figure. Furthermore, given the Department's 
demonstrated efficiency in utilizing 94% of the reduced RE, it is well-positioned to absorb 
and effectively deploy this increased allocation, but this requires a strategic shift towards 
multi-year financial planning and robust implementation framework that can safeguard the 
scheme from future cyclical cuts. 
 
3.7 The Committee enquired regarding significant achievements made under the scheme in 
recent years. The Department informed that the Biotechnology Research and Development 
component has yielded remarkable achievements across multiple sectors. In healthcare, the 
Department completed the GenomeIndia project sequencing over 10,000 genomes from healthy 
individuals across 83 populations. Indigenous vaccines were developed including the quadrivalent 
Human Papillomavirus (qHPV) vaccine Cervavac against cervical cancer which received market 
authorization. The low-cost Rotavac vaccine became part of the Universal Immunization 
Programme (UIP). India's first gene therapy clinical trial for Hemophilia A was approved and five 
patients were infused with the therapy. The Interdisciplinary Group for Advanced Research on 
Birth Outcomes and Maternal and Infant Health (GARBH-INI) pregnancy cohort enrolled 12,000 
women and established a national biorepository with 15 lakh aliquots. Artificial Intelligence (AI)-
driven tools were developed for accurate assessment of gestational age and prediction of birth 
outcomes. 
 
3.8 In agriculture biotechnology, the Department developed numerous climate-resilient and 
disease-resistant crop varieties. Five climate-resilient rice varieties were developed with tolerance 
to drought, submergence, and salinity. Two chickpea varieties, ADVIKA and SAATVIK, were 
released with 11-15% higher yield under drought stress. Three Indian mustard varieties with white 
rust resistance were developed and provided to seed companies for commercialization. A sesame 
variety VRI-5 suitable for high-density sowing and resistant to multiple pests was developed. 
Genome editing through Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats 
(CRISPR)/Cas9 produced six mustard lines with reduced anti-nutrients. The AccelBreed speed 
breeding facility was established at Punjab Agricultural University (PAU) spanning 540 square 
metres with eight controlled chambers capable of cultivating over 40,000 plantlets. The National 
Certification System for Tissue Culture Plants (NCS-TCP) certified over 1.5 billion hardened plants 
since inception, with more than 227 million plants certified in the current year alone. Over 35 lakh 
virus-infected plants were identified and destroyed preventing potential viral epidemics. 
 
3.9 In animal biotechnology, the Translational Research Platform for Veterinary Biologicals 
(TRPVB) successfully transferred two technologies to industry including a Lumpy Skin Disease 
Virus vaccine candidate strain. Over 4,422 biological products were manufactured and distributed. 
An immersion vaccine for warm water lactococcosis in rainbow trout was developed with a 
confidentiality disclosure agreement signed for marketing. Diagnostic protocols for anthrax were 
standardized and field-usable diagnostic kits developed. 
 
3.10 In environmental biotechnology, bioremediation technology was developed for ecological 
restoration of degraded mangrove ecosystems demonstrated over 150 acres in Indian Sunderbans. 
Nearly forty institutions are engaged in developing biobased and biodegradable solutions including 
corn-derived biopolymers and algae-based plastics. A rapid test-tube enzymatic biodegradation 
model was developed for polycaprolactone (PCL) and polylactic acid (PLA) plastics showing up to 
49% molecular weight loss in seven days. Lignocellulose-based scalable luminous photonic 
biopolymers were developed from wheat and rice biomass waste with processing capabilities of 
200 kilograms. 

11 
 
3.11 In microbial biotechnology, researchers developed silk-fibroin carriers for corneal-
endothelial cell culture achieving cell density of approximately 500 cells per square millimetre. 
Four plant extracts showed over 80% inhibition against theileriosis including Calotropis procera 
and Withania somnifera. New virus-indexing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) were 
developed for black pepper, citrus, and strawberry strengthening disease-detection capabilities. 
3.12 The Department further informed that the Industrial and Entrepreneurship Development 
component implemented through BIRAC has catalyzed remarkable growth in the start-up 
ecosystem. More than 10,000 biotech startups now exist in the country. The incubation centre 
network supported by BIRAC has expanded to 95 facilities across 24 States. India's bioeconomy 
reached $165.7 billion in 2024, growing 9.7% from the previous year and contributing 4.25% to 
national Gross Domestic Product (GDP). The sector has maintained a Compound Annual Growth 
Rate (CAGR) of 17.9% over four years driven primarily by BioIndustrial at 47.2% followed by 
BioPharma at 35.2%. Over 800 products and technologies have been launched in the market. The 
Fund of Funds Accelerating Entrepreneurs (AcE) initiative with 16 daughter funds has supported 
88 biotech startups with total funding support of ₹1,200 Crore. Follow-on funding raised by these 
startups amounts to over ₹4,300 Crore, putting together about ₹5,500 crore investment infused in 
biotech startups. The Biotechnology Ignition Grant (BIG) scheme has supported approximately 
1000 innovations with total commitment of ₹500 Crore. The SEED Fund has empowered 149 high-
potential biotech startups through strategic investment of ₹45 Crore. The Small Business 
Innovation Research Initiative (SBIRI) has supported 341 projects with commitment of ₹306.38 
crore leading to development of over 90 products. The Biotechnology Industry Partnership 
Programme (BIPP) has supported 249 projects with commitment of ₹577.7 crore resulting in 
development of over 90 products.  
 
3.13 The Department also apprised the Committee that the Biomanufacturing and Biofoundry 
component launched under the BioE3 Policy has made rapid progress since August 2024. The first 
DBT-BIRAC joint call for proposals received over 2000 proposals with more than 200 projects 
recommended for funding. India's first National Biofoundry Network comprising six Biofoundries 
was launched. Twenty-one proposals were recommended for setting up Biofoundries and 
Biomanufacturing Hubs including six from academia and fifteen from industry. A MoU was signed 
between DBT and ISRO for cooperation in space biotechnology and biomanufacturing with a joint 
working group constituted and call for proposals announced. The first MoU for Centre-State 
partnership was signed with the Government of Assam in March 2025 to formalize strategic 
collaboration. BioE3 Cells have been notified in the State of Sikkim. Operational Guidelines for 
Establishment of BioE3 Cells in States have been approved. The first BioE3 Strain Resource was 
setup at iBRIC National Centre for Cell Science (NCCS), Pune for sharing production strains with 
freedom-to-operate for high-performance biomanufacturing. A stakeholder consultation on 
emerging regulatory pathways for Cell and Gene Therapy Products was organized in February 
2025. A memorandum of understanding was signed between DBT and MeitY for mutually enabling 
AI-driven biological research ecosystem. 
 
3.14 The Committee enquired with the Department regarding mechanisms to ensure continuity 
between lab scale innovation and commercial deployment within BioE3. The Department replied 
that the BioE3 policy is designed to strengthen bio-innovation and biomanufacturing in India by 
creating a seamless pathway from laboratory research to commercial deployment. To enable this 
transition, advanced infrastructure with pilot-scale facilities are being established in close proximity 
to research institutions, allowing innovators to validate and scale technologies before market entry. 
In parallel, programs led by BRIC and BIRAC such as the Entrepreneur-in-Residence (EIR) 
initiative, focus on equipping research scholars with industry-relevant skills, entrepreneurial 
exposure, and translational training. Together, these mechanisms ensure continuity between lab-
scale innovation and commercialization while strengthening the national biomanufacturing 
ecosystem. The Department along with BIRAC is setting up BioEnablers i.e. Biofoundries and 

12 
 
Biomanufacturing Hubs across the country. These are shared infrastructure for scaling-up of bio-
based products. The Biofoundries are facilities for early scale up of proof-of-concept, while the 
Biomanufacturing Hubs are shared pilot-scale and pre-commercial-scale facilities designed to 
bridge the gap between laboratory research and full-scale manufacturing. India’s 1st National 
Biofoundry Network of 6 Biofoundries and ‘High-Performance Biomanufacturing Platform under 
the BioE3 Policy’ comprising 15 Biomanufacturing Hubs, have been launched to augment 
Biomanufacturing of Bio-based products. Setting up of next round of biofoundries and hubs is in 
the pipeline. Additionally under the BioE3 Policy, the "Bridging the Gap" category funds projects 
across the key sectors of bio-based chemicals and enzymes, functional food and smart proteins, 
precision biotherapeutics, climate-resilient agriculture, biofuels and carbon capture utilisation, and 
futuristic marine and space research to develop pilot-scale projects with potential commercial 
deployment to ensure continuity between lab scale innovation and commercial deployment.

Biomedical Engineering and Biodesign programmes aim to promote multi-disciplinary research

b) 3D-Bioprinted Contact Lens Embedding Host-Defense Peptide S100A12 as Precision

c) At IIT-Guwahati DBT Biodesign Centre, a group of fellows are working towards

3.16 The Committee further enquired that whether there are any collaboration with private sector 
companies to accelerate the development and commercialization of these devices. The Department 
replied that BIRAC fosters collaboration with private sector companies through its various 
programmes to accelerate the development and commercialization of biomedical devices and 
advanced healthcare technologies. 
a) Under the Biotechnology Ignition Grant (BIG) scheme, early-stage innovators and startups 
receive proof-of-concept funding to validate novel technologies and develop initial 
prototypes. This enables high-risk ideas in medical devices and diagnostics to progress

b) Further, under SEED and LEAP Funds, equity investments are made in eligible startups

stakeholders to advance product validation, obtain regulatory approvals, and facilitate

c) Through these programme frameworks, BIRAC enables co-development models, 
technology transfer arrangements, regulatory facilitation, and industry linkages, thereby 

13 
 
fostering effective public–private collaboration and accelerating the translation of

d) BIRAC provides financial support to Start-ups/Companies/LLPs and academic institutions,

3.17 The Committee recommends that the Department should establish a robust, real-time 
monitoring and evaluation framework for the newly integrated Bio-RIDE scheme. Given the 
merger of two major schemes and the addition of a significant new component, it is crucial to 
track not just financial expenditure but also tangible scientific and industrial outcomes. This 
framework should set specific, time-bound milestones for each of the three components—
Research & Development, Industrial & Entrepreneurship Development, and 
Biomanufacturing & Biofoundry. Under the R&D component, the Committee recommends 
tracking the number of patents filed and technologies licensed, not just the number of 
fellowships awarded. For the IED component, the focus should be on the survival and growth 
rate of incubated startups beyond the initial funding stages. For the new Biofoundry 
component, the focus should be on the number of industry partners utilizing the national 
platforms and the successful scaling of bio-manufacturing processes. This data should be 
publicly accessible to ensure transparency and accountability. 
 
3.18 To build on the impressive start-up ecosystem supported by BIRAC, the Committee 
recommends creating a dedicated mentorship and industry-linking program for startups 
graduating from the BioNEST incubators. While seed funding and grants are vital, many 
promising ventures falter during the transition from proof-of-concept to commercial-scale 
manufacturing and market entry. The Committee recommends that BIRAC, in partnership 
with successful bio-pharma and bio-industrial companies, should establish a "Venture 
Development Program." This program would pair select startups with experienced industry 
mentors who can provide guidance on regulatory approvals, quality control, supply chain 
management, and market access strategies. This would increase the success rate of startups in 
attracting larger follow-on funding and ultimately launching their products, thereby 
converting innovative ideas into economic assets. 
3.19 To accelerate the development of affordable healthcare devices, such as the 
intraocular lenses and cardiovascular stents, the Committee recommends creating a focused, 
mission-mode programme. Instead of supporting isolated projects, this programme should 
bring together clinicians, engineers, and entrepreneurs to solve specific, high-priority needs 
identified by the healthcare system. The Committee recommends that this mission mode 
programme be structured with clear, end-to-end milestones: from prototype development 

14 
 
and clinical validation to regulatory approval and finally, volume manufacturing. Funding 
should be released in tranches tied to achieving these milestones, and a dedicated unit within 
BIRAC should be assigned to help these projects navigate the approval process with the 
Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) from an early stage, thereby 
reducing the time to market.

production from grain, reducing external glucoamylase needs by ~50%.

effective alternative to imported yeast, with commercialization discussions underway. 
C. Space Biotechnology:  
The following two experiments, designed by ICGEB scientists have been successfully 
conducted on board the International Space Station by Group Commander Subhanshu 
Shukla as part of the Axiom-4 mission.   
 In one experiment, the potential of microalgae for space-based applications has been 
successfully validated. Two edible microalgal species, Chlorella sorokiniana-I and

growth in microgravity compared to ground controls.

cyanobacteria on urea. This opens the possibility for developing methods to utilise
