ANALYSIS OF THE BUDGETARY TRENDS OF THE MINISTRY OF EARTH SCIENCES  
 
         The Committee notes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES ) had projected an 
outlay of ₹4371.54 crore to the Ministry of Finance under Demand No. 24 for the financial 
year 2026–27. However, the Ministry of Finance approved an outlay of ₹3789.23 crore, which 
is about 86.67 % of the projected amount. The Committee is of the view that the pattern and 
extent of fund utilization during the current financial year significantly influence the 
allocation made in the subsequent year. A careful examination of the Ministry‟s expenditure 
pattern over the years indicates that i t has not been able to fully utilize the outlays sanctioned 
to it. For instance, the Ministry was allocated an outlay of ₹3658.08 crore at the BE stage in 
2025–26, which was subsequently revised downward to ₹3388.27 crore at the RE stage. 
Further, the Ministry has been able to incur an expenditure of only ₹2826.83 crore up to 31 st 
January, 2026. This relatively slow pace of expenditure appears to have contributed to the 
reduction in allocation made to the Ministry in BE 2026 –27 vis-à-vis the projected outlay. The 
Committee also observes that the gap between the outlay projected by MoES to the Ministry 
of Finance and the allocation approved has widened over the years. The outlay allocated to 
the Ministry in BE 2023–24 constituted 99.43% of the projected outla y. In BE 2024–25, the 
allocation was 107.90% of the projected outlay , while in BE 2025–26 it accounted for 97.69% 
of the projected outlay . However, the allocation for the forthcoming financial year represents 
only 86.67% of the projected outlay , indicating  a comparatively lower level of budgetary 
provision against the projected requirement.  In view of the above, the Committee urges the 
Ministry of Earth Sciences to take necessary measures to improve the rate of budget 
utilization and strive to achieve full utilization of the allocated funds in the coming financial 
year, so as to avoid any reduction in future budgetary allocations.                                                                                                                                 
(Para 2.7) 
 
ASSESSMENT OF THE PATTERN OF BUDGET UTILIZATION BY THE MINISTRY OF 
EARTH SCIENCES 
The Committee notes with concern  the persistent underutilization of budgetary 
allocations by the Ministry of Earth Sciences over the past few years. An analysis o f the 
pattern of expenditure indicates that the utilization of funds has ranged between 83% and 
93% in recent years , and the Ministry has not been able to utilize the full budgetary 
allocation in any of the recent years. The Committee is of the view that such a pattern reflects 
a slow pace of expenditure and limited capacity to absorb the funds allocated , particularly 
under the Capital Head.  The Committee further observes that the reduction in allocation at 
the Revised Estimates stage , as seen in 2025 –26, h as been attributed by the Ministry to 
procurement delays, implementation challenges, site finalization issues, and other technical or 
operational constraints . While acknowledging that certain scientific and technological 
projects may involve complex proced ures, the Committee is of the firm opinion that it is the 
responsibility of the Ministry to anticipate such challenges and establish effective mechanisms 
to overcome them in a timely manner . The Committee also notes that the capital allocation 
has shown a declining trend in recent years, partly due to lower utilisation and the completion 
of certain major capital procurements. In the Committee‟s view, the persistent shortfall in 

73 
 
utilisation has also contributed to a comparatively lower allocation in BE 2026 –27. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry strengthen its planning, project 
management and financial monitoring mechanisms so as to ensure timely and efficient 
utilisation of allocated funds . The Ministry should institute periodic reviews of expenditure, 
particularly under capital-intensive projects, and take proactive steps to address procedural, 
technical and operational bottlenecks that delay implementation.                            ( Para 2.14)   
CHAPTER III 
ASSESSMENT OF THE SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY 
PRITHVI VIGYAN (PRITHVI) 
 
The Committee recommends developing advanced indigenous technologies for desalination 
plants that run on non -renewable energy. Deployed in coastal areas and cities, these plants 
would augment fresh water supplies to help address existing shortages.                                    
(para 3.17)  
The Committee acknowledges the significant role played by the PRITHVI (Prithvi 
Vigyan) Scheme  in strengthening India‟s capabilities in Earth System S ciences through its 
integrated focus on atmosphere, oceans, cryosphere, geosciences and societal applications. 
The Committee notes that several Low-Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD) plants  
have been established in the Lakshadweep islands under the PRITHVI-OSMART initiative to 
address the critical issue of potable water availability for island communities. While the 
Committee recognizes the importance of these plants in ensuring sustainable drinking water 
supply, it also notes that the desalination pla nts currently operate using electricity generated 
through diesel generator sets, which power the island systems. Considering the environmental 
sensitivity of island ecosystems and the broader national commitment towards clean and 
renewable energy, the Comm ittee is of the view that reliance on diesel -based power sources 
should be progressively reduced. The Committee therefore recommends the Ministry to 
explore the feasibility of making these desalination plants eco -friendly by using sustainable 
power sources  such as solar energy, Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), or other 
suitable renewable energy technologies.              (Para 3.18)
  
The Committee also examined the proposal for establishing Maitri-II, a new research 
station in Antarctica to replace t he existing Maitri station, which was commissioned in 1989 
and has now exceeded its designed operational life. The Committee notes the Ministry‟s 
submission that the present station is facing structural deterioration and limitations in waste -
management and environmental compliance systems, making the establishment of a modern 
replacement station necessary to ensure safety, operational sustainability, and India‟s 
continued year -round scientific presence in Antarctica in accordance with evolving 
environmental norms under the Antarctic Treaty System. However, the Committee notes that 
the architectural and design consultant for the Maitri -II project has been selected through a 
global design competition and that the winning consortium comprises Ramboll Deutschlan d 
GmbH and bofArchitekten, Germany. In this regard, the Committee recalls that India‟s first 
Antarctic research station, Dakshin Gangotri, was constructed with the involvement of the 
Indian Army, demonstrating indigenous capability in undertaking complex o perations in 
extreme polar conditions. The Committee is therefore of the view that greater consideration 
could have been given to Indian firms with relevant engineering and infrastructure expertise 
in cold-weather construction technologies. Such an approac h could have contributed to cost 
savings while also providing impetus to the objectives of Make in India and promoting greater 
self-reliance in specialized polar infrastructure development. The Committee recommends 
that, in future projects of this nature, the Ministry explore ways to ensure greater 

74 
 
participation of Indian companies, either independently or through collaborations, so that 
domestic capabilities in polar infrastructure and extreme -environment engineering are 
further strengthened.                                                           (Para 3.19) 
 
DEEP OCEAN MISSION 
The Committee notes that the Deep Ocean Mission , launched in 2021, with an 
approved outlay of ₹4,077 crore , for a period of five years, is a flagship initiative aimed at 
strengthening India‟s capabilities in deep -sea exploration, resource assessment, marine 
biodiversity research and development of advanced ocean technologies. While the Committee 
acknowledges the efforts made by the Ministry and its institutions in progressing with certain 
components of the Mission, it observes with concern that the overall progress achieved so far 
does not appear commensurate with the objectives and timelines originally envisag ed. The 
Committee further notes that key components of the Mission, including the Samudrayaan 
programme and the development of an integrated deep -sea mining system for polymetallic 
nodules, are still incomplete. It is also observed that against the approve d project cost of 
₹4,077 crore, only about ₹1,445 crore has been utilised so far, which constitutes roughly 35 
per cent of the total project outlay. In the Committee‟s view, the pace of progress under 
certain critical verticals of the Mission needs to be s ignificantly accelerated to ensure that the 
intended outcomes are achieved within a reasonable timeframe. In this regard, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry establish clearly defined and measurable milestones under 
each of the six verticals of the Deep Ocean Mission. The Committee further recommends that 
specific timelines be fixed for the achievement of these targets, along with a structured 
monitoring mechanism to periodically review progress and address implementation 
bottlenecks.                                                                                                (para 3.30) 
MISSION MAUSAM 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by the Ministry under Mission Mausam, 
which aims to transform India into a “Weather-ready and Climate-smart” nation through the 
deployment of advanced observational systems, next -generation modelling, and improved 
weather forecasting and early warning mechanisms. The Committee notes the progress made 
in strengthening Doppler Weather Radar networks, operationa lizing advanced forecasting 
systems, developing AI -based weather interpretation tools, and establishing platforms for 
hyper-local weather information dissemination.  At the same time, the Committee expresses 
concern over the increasing incidence of extreme weather events, particularly cloudbursts, 
which in recent years have caused significant loss of life, damage to infrastructure, and 
disruption of livelihoods in several parts of the country, especially in mountainous and 
ecologically fragile regions. The C ommittee notes the Ministry‟s initiative to establish a state-
of-the-art cloud microphysics laboratory  at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology 
(IITM), Pune, and to deploy specialised observing systems in cloudburst -prone regions such 
as the North-Eastern States, the Western Ghats, and the Western Himalayas. The Committee 
recommends that these research efforts should be strongly oriented towards developing 
reliable forecasting capabilities and an effective early warning system for cloudburst events so 
that timely alerts can be issued to vulnerable communities and disaster management 
authorities.                                                    (para 3.41)
  
           The Committee further notes that ocean –atmosphere interactions play a crucial role in 
influencing weather and climate patterns, including the formation and intensification of 
cyclones and extreme rainfall events. In this regard, the Committee takes note of the proposal 
under consideration for the development of floating radar systems mou nted on buoys  to 

75 
 
enhance meteorological observations over oceanic regions where land -based radar coverage is 
limited. The Committee believes that such systems could significantly improve monitoring of 
cloud formation and rainfall dynamics over the seas and  strengthen cyclone detection and 
tracking capabilities.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Ministry to accord due 
priority to the development and deployment of floating radar observation systems and 
provide adequate financial and institutional suppo rt for this initiative under Mission 
Mausam.                                   (para 3.42) 
 
The Committee recommends that the Ministry should coordinate with bodies like 
Central Water Commission and Survey of India to develop scientific models for analyzing 
riverine water flow. This initiative would enable accurate flood forecasting, thereby 
mitigating damage, particularly in the nation's flood-prone regions.                         ( para 3.43)
  
CHAPTER IV  
ASSESSMENT OF THE FUNCTIONING OF THE INSTITUTIONS OF THE MINISTRY 
OF EARTH SCIENCES 
V ACANCIES 
The Committee observes that the Ministry of Earth Sciences is currently implementing 
three major national missions, namely Deep Ocean Mission, Prithvi Vigyan and Mission 
Mausam, which are of critical importance for advancing the country‟s capabilities in ocean 
exploration, weather and climate services,  and earth system science. The successful 
implementation of these missions depends significantly on the availability of adequate and 
skilled human resources across the Ministry and its affiliated institutions. However, a 
substantial number of vacancies exi st across different categories of posts in the Ministry and 
its institutions. The Committee has been informed that the Recruitment Rules for the entry -
level posts of the scientific cadre in the Ministry and its affiliated offices are under finalization 
in consultation with the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) . Further, the finalization 
of the sanctioned strength of the scientific cadre  is under consideration with the Department 
of Expenditure . The Ministry has also submitted that the Department of Per sonnel and 
Training (DoPT) is the cadre -controlling authority for administrative posts of the Ministry, 
except in the case of Multi-Tasking Staff (MTS) . The Committee is of the view that such a 
large number of vacancies, particularly in scientific and technical posts, could adversely affect 
the effective implementation of these critical national missions. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that the Ministry pursue the matter vigorously with the concerned authorities, 
including UPSC, the Department of Expe nditure and DoPT, to expedite the finalization of 
recruitment rules, sanctioned strength and recruitment processes.                             (Para 4.4) 
INDIAN METEOROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT (IMD), NEW DELHI 
           The Committee notes that numerous advan ced technologies, including Artificial 
Intelligence, are being utilized globally to enhance the accuracy and affordability of weather 
forecasting. In this context, the Committee recommends that the Ministry should conduct a 
detailed outcome analysis of the  budgetary allocations made to the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD).                                                                                                         (Para 4.12)
  
         The Committee is of the opinion that accurate and timely weather prediction is critically 
important for a country like India , where a large segment of the population depends on 

76 
 
weather-reliant economic activities . The Committee has been informed that 48 Doppler 
Weather Radars (DWRs) are currently operational ac ross the country . However, the 
Committee observes that the existing network does not provide adequate coverage across 
several parts of the country , which may affect the accuracy and timeliness of short -range and 
nowcasting services, particularly for locali zed severe weather events. The Committee is of the 
view that DWRs are critical components of a modern weather observation system , as they 
provide high -resolution, real -time information on rainfall intensity, wind patterns, 
thunderstorms and severe weather systems. Expanding the DWR network across the country 
would significantly enhance forecasting capabilities, strengthen early warning systems, and 
support more effective disaster preparedness and response mechanisms. The Committee notes 
that under Mission M ausam, the Government has proposed the installation of an additional 
84 DWRs across the country to address the existing coverage gaps. The Committee further 
notes that the estimated expenditure for this expansion is approximately ₹942.57 crore . In 
view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry may take necessary steps to 
ensure that the proposed additional Doppler Weather Radars are installed at the earliest  so 
that most parts of the country are adequately covered by the radar network. The Co mmittee 
further recommends that the required financial resources may be provided to IMD in a 
phased manner to facilitate timely implementation of the proposed expansion.   
(Para 4.13) 
         The Committee also notes that a large section of the public is unaware of the existence of 
Mausam app developed by IMD. Moreover, the user interface of the app is not very user 
friendly and pales in comparison to other popular apps in this domain. The Comm ittee 
therefore recommends that IMD  should take steps for populariz ation of the app. The 
Committee also recommends that IMD should improve the overall U ser Interface of the app 
to make it more appealing to the general public.                                                        (Para 4.14 ) 
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF TROPICAL METEOROLOGY (IITM), PUNE 
        The Committee recognizes the significant role played by the Indian Institute of Tropical 
Meteorology (IITM), Pune, as a premier national research institutio n engaged in advanced 
studies on the atmosphere, ocean and climate systems, particularly in improving weather and 
climate forecasts for the tropics and understanding the dynamics of the monsoon over India. 
The Committee notes the research undertaken by IIT M under Mission Mausam to examine 
the meteorological factors contributing to severe air pollution in Delhi during the winter 
months. In view of the continuing severity of air pollution in Delhi and the National Capital 
Region, the Committee is of the opini on that scientific research findings such as those 
generated by IITM are extremely valuable for informed policy -making and mitigation 
planning. The Committee therefore recommends that the research findings and analytical 
insights generated by IITM should b e shared regularly with relevant regulatory and policy -
making bodies , including the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Delhi Pollution 
Control Committee (DPCC), and the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM), as 
well as other concerned agencies.                 (Para 4.18) 
 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM RANGE WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF), 
NOIDA 
            The Committee notes the important role played by the National Centre for Medium 
Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF), Noida , in developing and oper ating advanced 
numerical weather prediction models for short -range, medium -range, extended -range and 
seasonal forecasts, which are widely used by various user agencies including the India 

77 
 
Meteorological Department. The Committee appreciates the development  of the High-
Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) forecasting system , which is designed for short -range 
prediction of rapidly evolving weather systems, particularly in complex terrains such as the 
Himalayan region. Considering the increasing occurrence of extre me rainfall and cloudburst 
events in the Himalayan region and the serious damage caused by such incidents in recent 
years, the Committee is of the view that strengthening scientific capabilities for their 
prediction and early warning is of critical importa nce. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Ministry to provide sustained support to NCMRWF for further development 
and operationalization of high -resolution modelling systems such as HRRR, including 
enhanced assimilation of radar and satellite observati ons over mountainous regions. The 
Committee further recommends that efforts be made to integrate the outputs of these 
advanced models with early warning dissemination systems so that actionable and timely 
alerts can be provided to disaster management authorities and vulnerable communities.  
(Para 4.25) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR SEISMOLOGY (NCS), DELHI 
 The Committee notes that the National Centre for Seismology (NCS), Delhi , 
established in 2015, plays a critical role in monitoring seismic activity across the coun try, 
maintaining the National Seismological Network, conducting earthquake hazard assessments, 
and supporting research in seismology, earthquake precursor studies, and deep borehole 
investigations. However, the Committee is constrained to note that even af ter nearly a decade 
of its establishment, the NCS does not have any sanctioned posts of its own and continues to 
function with personnel drawn on a loan basis from the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES) 
and the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The Com mittee finds it difficu lt to 
understand why a specializ ed national institution entrusted with such crucial responsibilities 
is still operating without a dedicated cadre of scientific, technical, and administrative staff.  
While noting the Ministry‟s submiss ion that proposals for the creation of dedicated posts for 
NCS have been submitted under the PRITHVI scheme, the Committee strongly recommends 
that the matter be pursued on priority and that the approval process be expedited.                                      
(Para 4.29) 
INDIAN NATIONAL CENTRE FOR OCEAN INFORMATION SYSTEM (INCOIS), 
HYDERABAD 
           The Committee recognizes the critical role played by the Indian National Centre for 
Ocean Information Services (INCOIS)  in providing ocean information and advisory services 
that support fisheries, maritime operations, coastal management and disaster preparedness. 
The Committee is of the view that a robust and comprehensive ocean observation network is 
essential for improving the accuracy and reliability of ocean forecasts, early warning systems 
and long -term marine research.  The Committee notes that there remain long -standing 
observational gaps in near  shore wave measurements along several parts of the Indian 
coastline. In this regard, the Wave Monitoring Along Near shore (WAMAN)  project has 
played an important role in generating real -time coastal wave observations that support 
operational wave forecasting, early warning services, maritime safety and scientific research. 
However, the Committee observes that the present WAMAN network covers only selected 
segments of the coastline. The Committee therefore recommends that the network of wave 
buoys under WAMAN be progressively expanded to cover the entire Indian coastline so that a 
more comprehensive and reliable near shore observation system can be established.                                                                        
(Para 4.38) 

78 
 
        The Committee also notes that coastal regions in the country remain relatively u nder-
observed, with limited availability of physico -chemical, biological and fisheries -related data. 
The absence of observations for several parameters constrains the accuracy of ocean 
information and advisory services and limits the effectiveness of forec asting systems. In this 
context, the Committee emphasizes the importance of establishing regional shore stations 
equipped with appropriate laboratory and monitoring facilities to support long -term coastal 
observations, data analysis, model validation and c apacity building. The Committee is of the 
view that strengthening coastal observation infrastructure through an expanded WAMAN 
network and the establishment of shore stations will significantly improve ocean forecasting 
capabilities and generate valuable l ong-term datasets. The Committee therefore recommends 
that the Ministry provide adequate financial support to INCOIS for strengthening the 
WAMAN network and for establishing the proposed regional shore stations in a time -bound 
manner.                                     (Para 4.39) 
CENTRE FOR MARINE LIVING RESOURCES AND ECOLOGY (CMLRE), KOCHI 
        The Committee notes that the Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel  (FORV) 
Sagar Sampada, which serves as the backbone of the Marine Living Resources programme 
implemented by the Centre for Marine Living Resources and Ecology (CMLRE), was 
commissioned in 1984 and has been in service for more than four decades. The Committee is 
concerned that the ageing of the vessel has resulted in several operational limitations and that, 
in its current condition, the vessel may remain operational for deep-sea surveys for only about 
seven more years. In view of these limitations and considering the growing requirements of 
deep-sea research under programmes such as the D eep Ocean Mission and the PRITHVI 
Scheme, the Committee strongly feels that the country requires a modern and advanced 
Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel capable of supporting expanded scientific 
observations in deep and distant waters. Given that F ORV Sagar Sampada is already nearing 
the end of its operational life, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
necessary procedural formalities and take time -bound steps for the acquisition and 
construction of the new vessel. The Committee i s of the view that the new Fishery and 
Oceanographic Research Vessel should be built and commissioned at the earliest, preferably 
within the next two to three years, so that India‟s marine research programmes are not 
adversely affected due to the declining operational capability of the existing vessel.                                                                                              
(Para 4.44) 
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR POLAR AND OCEAN RESEARCH (NCPOR), GOA 
        The Committee takes note of India‟s growing engagement in the Arctic through scientific 
expeditions, international collaborations, and the operation of the Himadri research station in 
Svalbard. The Committee observes that polar research has acquired increasing significance in 
recent years due to its direct relevance to global climate systems, ocean circulation, sea -level 
rise and their impact on weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon. The absence of a 
dedicated ice-class Polar Research Vessel has be en a major constraint in expanding India‟s 
polar research activities, particularly in the wider Arctic Ocean. The Committee notes with 
satisfaction that in -principle approval has already been accorded by the Department of 
Expenditure for the acquisition of a Polar Research Vessel with ice-breaking capabilities at an 
estimated cost of ₹2,329.40 crore. In view of the strategic and scientific importance of this 
project, the Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the remaining procedural 
formalities an d ensure that adequate financial resources are made available so that the 
project progresses in a time -bound manner. The Committee further recommends that, 
wherever feasible, Indian shipbuilding firms should be actively involved in the construction of 

79 
 
the Polar Research Vessel. Such an approach would not only strengthen domestic 
shipbuilding capabilities but also contribute to the objectives of promoting indigenous 
manufacturing and technological self-reliance in specialized marine infrastructure.                                                                                                                          
(Para 4.50) 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT), CHENNAI 
         The Committee notes that the National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) has 
transferred around 40 technologies between 2020 –26, generating a total revenue of ₹1.64 
crore. The Committee expresses concern that these technologies are being transferred at 
relatively low prices compared to their commercial potential. It is o bserved that private 
partners often earn significant profits from these technologies, while the originating public 
institutes receive only a marginal share of the value created. The Committee understands that 
there is no robust mechanism to verify whether the benefits of these low -cost technology 
transfers reach the intended target users, and that the fees for renewal of licenses after expiry 
remain undefined. In view of this, the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Earth 
Sciences should adopt a more competitive, market-aligned pricing framework for technology 
transfer. Licensing fees should reflect the true commercial value, uniqueness, and societal 
impact of publicly funded technologies. The Committee further recommends the 
establishment of clear pro cedures and norms for technology valuation and licensing, with the 
National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and the technology developer jointly 
determining fees. To ensure transparency, accountability, and proper utilization of publicly 
funded technologies, all technology transfer agreements should be subjected to periodic third -
party audits, and the outcomes of such audits should govern future licensing and renewal 
terms.                                      (Para 4.58)

R E P O R T
 
 
      Biotechnology is a fascinating field of science.  Mankind has used biotechnology since ancient times for wine making
 and baking.  The modern science has uncovered the scientific truth behind these processes.  It has also multiplied the
 applications of biotechnology manifold in several areas of human welfare.      Biotechnology has emerged as the
 technology, which is set to shape the future by promising food security for the world, disease resistance and control,
 sustainable environmental options and thus a more healthier world scenario and ensure optimum utilisation of the scarce
 resources such as land.  The term “Biotechnology” was first described in 1920, although the origin of biotechnology could
 be traced beyond 6000 B.C. Biotechnology involves methods employed to living systems to produce/design or modify
 certain products for selective applications.  It has since made significant advances  and has come out with products that are
 of immense use in the most important areas of health, agriculture and industry. 
2.   The challenges in the modern biology and biotechnology in the next millenium are enormous in terms of research,
 product and process development and commercial exploitation thereof.  Adequate skilled human resources are also crucial. 
 The field of biotechnology in India has already opened opportunities for commercial exploitation in high value Biologicals,
 new generation vaccines, diagnostics in human and animal health care, value addition to agricultural crops through
 nutritional improvements, pests and disease resistance. Water and salinity stress resistance are the agenda for the coming
 years towards food and nutritional security.  Solutions for environmental protection through phytoremediation,
 bioremediation and microbial technologies may be available for treatment of degraded soils, enhanced oil recovery and
 pollution remediation and monitoring.  Therefore, Biotechnology provides a tremendous scope in the form of modern tools
 and techniques for improvement of human life through poverty alleviation, upgradation of skills and self-employment to
 large sections of society  in the rural areas to provide hem sense of social security.
3.   The Committee was informed that during the year 2000-2001 a consolidated effort would be made for application of
 biotechnology for the uplift through skill development of rural population especially women and weaker sections of the
 society and that, these  initiatives would be  pursued.  The efforts made in the first three years of 9
th plan have culminated
 into transfer of about 27 applications of biotechnology, filing of 41 Indian patents and granting of 7 Indian patents and 6
 U.S. patents.
4.   The Department   envisages consolidation of many activities during the third year of the current five year plan,
 operationalisation and speedy implementation of various programmes and supporting new initiatives.  The department is
 consciously moving towards product development in addition to basic research, as is evident from  technology transfers that
 have taken place in  the previous year.  A few  more diagnostics are expected to be taken up by the industry next year.

 tremendous potential of biodiversity, scientific and technical manpower and existing infrastructure it is likely to become an
 important global player in biotechnology in the next 10 years or so.  Keeping the mandate of the Department in view the
 Committee feels that sufficient funds need to be provided to the Department so that it can carry out its  mission effectively.
AGRICULTURAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
8.   The Committee was informed that drought and salinity are two major problems  which tend to limit plant growth and
 make soils unproductive.  A novel gene p5cs (phyroline-5-carboxylate synthase) has been reported to be a functional gene
 and over expression of this gene in transgenic tobacco results in an increased production of proline. Consequently, the
 transgenic plants produced were found to be tolerant to drought and salinity. A programme to develop transgenic indica rice
 (cv.Rasi) with p5cs gene was initiated two years ago at Madurai Kamaraj University (MKU), Madurai.
9.   A protocol for high frequency plant regeneration from embyogenic calli has been confirmed by PCR analysis.  The
 transgenic plants with desired traits would be generated in coming two years and  subjected to field evaluation.
10.The concept of organic farming is capable of  ensuring good soil health, food security and  reduce  environmental 
 pollution.  The  Committee  was  informed  that  the  department  had  started
 
national network programme on integrated nutrient management for sustainable maintenance of soil health through organic
 farming.  The efforts were being made to consolidate use of various biofertilisers and biopesticide technologies in the
 farmers’ field or specific cropping system.  This would ensure optimum use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides.  The
 technologies would help in maintenance of soil health as well as ensure environmental protection.  Various programmes on
 organic farming, specially using vermi compost have also been started in farmers’ field, demonstration to SC/ST, weaker
 sections, rural and women population.
11.The Committee feels that with the rising  costs of chemical fertilisers and the accompanying  risks of degradation of soil
 fertility because of increasing resource of the fertilisers, the role of biofertilisers and biopesticides is becoming significant. 
 The Committee recommends that the Department should encourage  the use of biofertilisers and biopesticides by educating
 the farmers though print & electronic media and field demonstrations, so as to achieve higher consumption levels of the
 bioproducts and with a view to increase their yields.  
PLANT TISSUE CULTURE TECHNOLOGIES FOR LARGE SCALE PRODUCTION AND COMMERCIALISATION
12.Tissue culture is an important tool of biotechnology which can be used to improve the productivity of planting material

 through enhanced availability of identified planting stock with desired traits.  The Committee was informed that the Task
 Force on Plant Material provided by Department of Biotechnology on plant tissue culture (Introduction plant) Tissue
 Culture set up by the Department of Biotechnology considered the need for initiating specific programmes for different
 plant species.  Thus, a number of research and development projects were supported for perfecting complete protocols of
 important plant species – Forest Trees, Horticulture Crops and Plantation Crops.  The  objective behind these  projects was
 to develop a package of technology for production of large quantities of planting material of improved varieties.  Two
 Tissue Culture Pilot Plant facilities were also set up for large-scale production of elite planting material with the main
 objective of demonstrating the field performance of tissue culture raised plants forest trees. 
13.The Committee was informed that plant tissue culture technology has been commercialised and many companies in India
 were producing large quantities of planting materials.  Commercialisation of technology requires scaling up and field
 evaluation before transfer to the industry.  The Department of Biotechnology supported projects have successfully
 standardised complete protocols and processes for a number of economically viable  plant species.  These protocols have
 been scaled up at the Hardening Units and tissue Culture Pilot Plants.  The Tissue Culture Pilot Plants were converted to
 Micropropagation Technology Parks (MTP) to provide an effective platform for transfer of the proven technologies to the
 entrepreneurs.  The MTP’s at National Chemical Laboratory, Pune & Tata Energy Research Institute, New Delhi have
 optimised a large number of technologies and also transferred to the industry.
14.The Committee feels that with a view to replenish  the depleting forest cover and improve the environment  the role of
 tissue culture technique  has assumpted importance.  The committee observes that the techniques if proved successful in
 case of ongoing projects, may be replicated in  case of value based forest trees, horticultural crops and plantation crops.
MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY
15.In the area of medical biotechnology, the Department proposes to lay  emphasis on the development of diagnostics,
 vaccines for prophylactic and therapeutic use, drug delivery systems, production of important biological/biomolecules and
 creation of infrastructures in hitech biomedical areas in order to undertake further research.  During the year 1999-2000 the
 Department  has considered 42 new projects besides monitoring 55 ongoing projects and the National Jai Vigyan
 
Science and Technology Mission on development of New Generation technologies for Vaccines were initiated..
16.The department has been funding research for the development of indigenous diagnostics for major communicable and
 non-communicable diseases.  The basic purpose has been to develop easy to use, affordable and accurate test systems for
 Indian strains which could be converted into appropriate kits with the help of industries for large scale use.  The Committee
 was informed that after reaching  the level of prototype systems, the department is endeavouring  to upscale these
 technologies. The Committee was apprised of the achievements made in the area of major communicable and non-
communicable diseases which include HIV/AIDS, Japanese Encepalitis, Hepatitis, Tuberculosis, Cholera, Shipella, 
 Rotavirus,  Helicobacter pylori, Leishmaniasis Malaria etc
17.The Committee recommends that besides supporting and developing indigenous diagnostics for major communicable and
 non-communicable diseases, the department should simultaneously endeavour to find market for indigenous products, and
 strive for better qualities to ensure priority for indigenous products over the imported ones.
HUMAN GENETICS AND GENOME ANALYSIS
18.The “Human Genetics & Genome Analysis” programme was initiated during 1994 with the objective to identify, map
 and characterise genes related to genetic disorders prevalent in India for diagnosis, prevention and management of genetic
 disorders and to develop new methods of the analysis and interpretations of genomic DNA sequences. Genetic diagnosis-
cum-counselling units established by the department have been providing molecular diagnosis and counselling for the
 common genetic disorders such as betathalassemia, Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD), haemoglobinopathies and
 neurogenetic disorders prevalent in the country, to the affected families.
19.The Committee was informed that since the inception of 14 genetic diagnosis cum counselling units, about 11,000
 affected families have benefitted from prenatal diagnosis and counselling for major genetic disorders an a population of
 1,700 tribals screened for these disorders.
20.While the Committee commends the efforts made by the Department in providing counselling and diagnostics services
 for the common genetic disorders prevalent in the country to the affected families, the question remains how many people
 are aware of such facilities.  Such programmes and facilities should be named in a language which people can understand. 
 The symptoms of such disorders should be publicised as also the programmes and facilities.   The Committee therefore
 recommends that the Department may provide wide publicity to the programme by involving print as well as electronic
 media so that the benefits of these activities of the Department could percolate to the underprivileged and weaker sections
 of the society.
FOOD BIOTECHNOLOGY
21.The  Committee  has  been  given  to  understand  that  efforts  are  underway   for commissioning of pilot plants for

BIOTECHNOLOGY BASED PROGRAMMES FOR SOCIETY
23.DBT has started a new scheme, for the  last two years, for the empowerment and skill development of women and rural
 poor for their economic upliftment.  The Department is extending support in the areas of food technology, sericulture,
 floriculture, organic farming, waste management, medicinal plants, biodiversity conservation, aquaculture, environment
 protection and awareness building.  This programme has benefitted more than 6000 women including rural poor.
24.The  Committee  notes  with satisfaction the efforts made by the Department for upliftment of SC/ST population of
 country, women and rural poor. The Department has launched Biotechnology based programme  for the welfare of SC/ST
 population through proven technologies.  It facilitates SC/ST population to upgrade their skills and create additional job
 avenues or help in improving their health status.  The main activities are cultivation and distillation of medicinal and
 aromatic plants, vermicomposting, spirulina production, fish and poultry farming, production and application of various
 biofertilisers for better soil health, biological control agents for plant pests and survey of genetic disorders and counseling. 
 Forty-three projects have been pursued in 19 states and union territories, which benefited about 15,000 families.  The
 Committee observes that benefits of such programmes should be equally distributed among all the intended sections of the
 society.
NATIONAL JAI VIGYAN MISSION ON DEVELOPMENT OF NEW GENERATION VACCINES
25.The Committee was informed that the Department has initiated the programme based on several leads obtained from the
 R&D projects funded by the department earlier.  The objectives of the programme include generating candidate vaccine(s)
 for diseases like cholera, rabies, Japanese encephalitis, tuberculosis, malaria and HIV.  The programme has been grouped
 under three categories.  Category (A) includes those ‘candidate vaccines’ where potential research leads are available and
 which now require clinical trials or generating pre-clinical data.  Under this category, vaccines for cholera and rabies are
 being attempted.  The programmes under category (B) are related to available leads on candidate vaccines where efficacy
 and immunogenicity need to be worked out.  The target vaccines are tissue culture-based Japanese encephalitis, DNA
 vaccines, epitope vaccinogenes of Japanese encephalitis and synthetic candidate malaria vaccine.  Under category (C),
 programmes requiring sustained R&D efforts with the possibility for development of candidate vaccine(s).  Under this
 category, efforts would be made to produce candidate prophylactic anti-HIV and DNA vaccines for tuberculosis.  It is
 expected that at the end of the programme at least 2-3 vaccines will be available for upscaling and use to control/contain the
 infections while others would reach the stage of the clinical trials.
26.As regards the activities of the vaccine production unit, namely, Bharat Immunologicals & Biologicals Coprn. Ltd.
 (BIBCOL) set up by the Department for the production of viral vaccines, the Committee was informed that BIBCOL is
 formulating Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) from imported bulk since January 1996 and is supplying it to the National
 Immunisation Programme.  During the year, the company has formulated 175 million doses of OPV, a part of which was
 supplied to UNICEF.  When enquired about the proposed diversification plan for production of BCG, Measles and Tetanus
 toxoid vaccines as submitted by BIBCOL, the Committee was informed that the proposed plan has been finalised from
 BIBCOL side and the same is being submitted to the operating agency namely BIFR.
 
 
BIOTECHNOLOGY INFORMATION SYSTEM
27.The Secretary, Department of Biotechnology informed the Committee that recognising the importance of the information
 technology for pursuing advanced research in modern biology and biotechnology, a bioinformatics programme, envisaged
 as a distributed database and network organisation, was launched during 1986-87.  The programme has become  very
 successful vehicle for transfer and exchange of knowledge, information, technology packages and references in the country
 involving 8-10 thousand scientists.  Ten Distributed Information Centres and 38 Sub-Distributed Information Centres
 located in universities and research institutions are fully engaged in this task, five national facilities have been set up for
 interactive graphics based molecular modeling and other biocomputational needs.  The entire network has emerged as a
 very sophisticated scientific infrastructure for bioinformatics involving state-of-the art computational and communication
 facilities.  The computer communication network, linking all the bioinformatics centres, is playing a vital role in the success
 of the bioinformatics programme.  Database development, R&D activities in bioinformatics, human resource development

 useful to the scientific community.
28.The Committee was apprised of the broad functions and services rendered by the Bioinformatics Centre which are as
 follows;-
(i)         the principal objectives of a Bioinformatics Centre is to function as an information base in each speciality so
 that the scientists have ready access to the computer-based information on resources, databases in subject
 fields, and to build up expertise in bioinformatics in keeping with the rapid development in this area;
(ii)        to provide a computer-based information storage and retrieval system of database that collects structured
 information generated by research and industrial institutions in the identified fields of biotechnology,
 continually update the databank and make the information available to the users;
(iii)       an active network mode, in which the scientists get access to the biotechnology community in the identified
 areas, answer requests for information in an interactive and discussive  mode and actively initiate dialogue
 among groups with common interest;
(iv)       to provide  retrieval service either online or offline in their specialised areas and to give overall information
 support even in areas other than those assigned to them;
(v)        to provide communication link with international databases for selective bibliographic information for the
 user scientists;
(vi)            to develop software packages and databases specific to user needs; and
(vii)      to conduct training courses in the specialised areas, periodically to meet the special requirements of
 manpower development in the area and to promote awareness about the computerised storage and retrieval
 facility among bio-scientists and information scientists.
29.The Committee commends the efforts made by the Department of Biotechnology in the field of bioinformatics, which are
 expected to yield multidimensional results in variety of areas.  The Committee, however, recommends that the Department
 should make all out efforts to ensure that biological data created in agricultural and other sectors be disseminated in a way
 
that it also reaches the persons working at grassroots levels and desiring to make use of it, so as to ensure optimum use of
 the data created
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS
30.Department of Biotechnology supports research activities in the autonomous institutions; viz; National Brain Research
 Centre, National Centre for Plant Genome Research, National Institute of Immunology, National Centre for Cell Science
 and Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF IMMUNOLOGY
31.The Committee was informed that the Institute has excelled in the pursuit of rigorous fundamental research and emerged
 as a centre of excellence in basic immunology, infectious diseases and molecular design.  As regards the most recent
 achievements of the Institute, the Committee was informed that a major fundamental discovery concerning pathogenesis,
 which concerns survival of bacteria in phagocytes, has been reported in the Journal of Cell Biology. The complete genome
 of an Indian isolate of JEV(GP78) has been sequenced revealing its evolutionary closeness to the Chinese SA14 isolate.  A
 novel immunomodulatory use of an Indian medicinal plant product (NII-60) to prevent septic shock received a US patent
 and was transferred to an Indian Pharmaceutical industry for commercialisation.  A transgenic mice expressing the hepatitis
 B virus X  gene has been generated.  In a novel strategy, genes for different stages of plasmodium falciparum have been
 stitched and expressed in baculovirus system.  The resultant proteins elicit good immune response in experimental animals.
32.The allocation for the National Institute of Immunology has been kept at Rs.14.00 crores for the year 2000-2001 as
 against Rs.13.00 crores as was in B.E. and R.E. for the  1999-2000.  The Committee wanted to know whether the increase
 of Rs.1 crore would be sufficient to carry on the initiatives the Department  propose to take up during the year under
 review.  In response the Department has  informed that the allocation for the Institute has been increased by Rs. 1 crore,
 which is essential to augment the infrastructure of P-3 laboratory which is  to handle infectious materials as well as
 pathogenic microbes and would be sufficient to augment P-3 laboratory facilities.
33.In reply to a question as to how many of the technologies related to diagnosis of AIDS virus, anti leprosy vaccine etc.
 which were under trial, have yielded desired results and have been transferred to industry for pilot level production, the
 Committee was informed that three diagnostic technologies developed under DBT supported programme on HIV/AIDS
 have been transferred to three industries for further refinement/pilot level production.  The technology of anti-leprosy
 vaccine has been transferred to M/s Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd. after obtaining regulatory clearances.  The anti-leprosy
 vaccine as immunomodulator is being marketed by this concern as Leprovac.  The contraceptive candidate vaccine,  Beta

 formulation so as to obtain predictable and sustainable immune responses in vaccinated women.  The improvement of the

34.The Committee is satisfied with the work being done by the National institute of Immunology.  However it observes that
 there are  certain unexplored areas in the field of  Immunodiagnostics and other diseases, where the institute can focus its

NATIONAL BRAIN RESEARCH CENTRE (NBRC)
35.A budgetary allocation of Rs.5.00 crores has been sought for NBRC.  Asked about the priorities which have necessitated
 the enhanced allocation, the Committee has been  informed that the basic theme of the Centre is to understand brain, to
 protect brain and to create  brain.  During the financial year 1999-2000 various activities in generation of manpower were
 initiated under Medical Biotechnology.  The Department proposes to undertake research  in the identified priority areas
 during the financial year 2000-2001.  This would be on computational neurosciences, developmental neurosciences, and
 cognitive neurosciences.  The centre has currently initiated research work at the ICGEB campus.  The NRBC would utilise
 some of the unfinished building structures after appropriate re-modelling at IVCOL site.  At the same time hitech
 laboratories are also proposed to be constructed at Manesar, Gurgaon.
NATIONAL CENTRE FOR PLANT GENOME RESEARCH (NCPGR)
36.The Committee was informed that NCPGR, an autonomous research institution is presently carrying out its research
 activities from the  Centre of Plant Molecular Biology of Jawaharlal Nehru University.  The Centre has initiated the work
 for analysing chickpea genome, identifying genes, develop suitable regeneration protocols for improving the nutritional
 quality and resistance against various diseases and a biotic stresses.  More than 100 ESTs have been sequenced from
 chickpea.  
37.The Committee is of the view that Agriculture is not really sustainable anywhere on account of loss of top soil and
 excessive use of pesticides and fertilizers besides growth of population at a rapid pace.  Hence the need for higher
 productivity and for nutritious food. The object can be achieved by changing the plant characteristics by genetic
 modification.  The Committee impresses upon the Department to work with full vigour in this area and efforts should be
 made to cover  value based crops under its ambit which may solve the problem of under nourishment  at the glassroot levels
 of the society.
38.After making a detailed scrutiny of the Demands for Grants of the Department of Biotechnology and assessing the
 progress of various important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands
 for Grants of Rs.136.08 crores as sought by the Department of Biotechnology for the current financial year, under Demand
 No.75 may be approved.

R E P O R T
           
      Information Technology (IT) has tremendous potential to become an engine of growth and productivity improvement for
 all sectors of the economy and for the country.  With the continued thrust on liberalization, in order to make IT products
 cost effective and  price competitive, the  use and penetration of computers in the society is fast expanding with special
 emphasis on multi-lingual technologies.
2.   Ministry of Information Technology was set up on 15 th October, 1999 to be the nodal institutional mechanism for
 facilitating all the initiative in the Central Government, the State Government, Academia, the Indian private sector and
 successful Indian IT professionals abroad.  With a view to accelerate the Internet revolution in India, emphasizing the
 creation of useful contents in Indian languages, IT-enabled services, IT education, electronics and computer hardware
 manufacturing and exports, silicon facility, e-Commerce and Internet based enterprises, the Ministry has been entrusted the
 task of implementation of a comprehensive action plan to make India an IT Superpower in the early part of the next century
 and achieve a target of $ 50 billion in software exports by 2008.
      The Ministry has been entrusted with the following responsibilities:-
(i)            Policy matters relating to IT;
(ii)        Promotion of knowledge based enterprises, Internet, e-commerce, IT education and IT based education;
(iii)            Development of Electronics;
(iv)            Development of Microelectronics and Silicon facility;
(v)            Promotion of Information Technology and Standardization;
(vi)            National Informatics Centre (NIC); and
(vii)            Electronics and Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC)
In order to make India an IT Super Power by the Year 2008, the vision translates into a mission-‘Move works to India’. 
 The Vision objective are:
(i)            Creation of Wealth
(ii)            Employment Generation
(iii)            IT led Economic Growth
The role of the Ministry of IT will be of a
(i)            Pro-active facilitator
(ii)            Pro-active motivator
(iii)            Pro-active promoter
(iv)            Spread of IT to masses speedily and

3.   Investment in knowledge based industries will determine a country’s dominance in the next century.  The software
 industry  has  emerged  as  one of  the fastest  growing  sectors  in  the economy with Cumulative Annual Growth Rate
 (CAGR) exceeding 50% over the last five years and with a likely turnover of US$ 6 billion and exports of US$ 4 billion
 during 1999-2000.  The Government has targeted an export of US$ 50 billion by the year 2008 for the Indian software
 industry.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.   The Ministry has been provided budgetary support of Rs.392.20 crores (Rs.365.20 crores plan and Rs.27.00 crores Non-
Plan) for the financial year 2000-2001 against the revised estimate of Rs.195.00 crores (Rs.170.00 crores Plan and Rs.25.00
 crores Non-Plan) for 1999-2000.  The allocation for the year 2000-2001 is thus Rs.197.20 crores more than R.E. of 1999-
2000.
4.1As regards the justification for enhanced allocation, the Committee was informed that in the 2000-01 B.E., an enhanced
 outlay of Rs.2.25 crores and Rs.10.00 crores has been provided for initiating Information Technology Certification and
 Information Technology Brand Equity Fund (IBEF) respectively.  IBEF is proposed to be set up with the objective to make
 ‘Made in India’ label a symbol of quality, competitive price, reliability and service to the customers.  In addition, a
 provision of Rs.142.17 crores and Rs.2.00 crores has been made for National Informatics Centre (NIC) and Electronics and
 Computer Software Export Promotion Council (ESC) respectively.  These organizations have now been brought under the
 administrative control of the Ministry since October, 1999.

NATIONAL INFORMATICS CENTRE (NIC)
5.   National Informatics Centre (NIC) which was set up in 1977, is a premier S&T organization of the Government of India
 in the field of Informatics Services and Information Technology (IT) applications in India. NIC was a constituent unit under
 the erstwhile Department of Electronics and then brought under the Planning Commission in 1988. It is now a part of the
 Ministry of Information Technology.  Its main objective is to provide computer support to Central Government
 Departments, State Government Departments, District Administration and new districts being created by the State
 Governments.  NIC has set up a satellite based computer communication network for providing E-mail, INTERNET, File
 Transfer access to  National & International databases etc.  NIC has set up a Local Area Networks(LAN) in Central
 Government Departments and State Government Secretariats.  NIC has been training the Government employees on a
 regular basis to enable them to use MIS databases.  Training is provided upto district level.  It is the only Government
 Organization in India, at present, offering network services over C-band and Ku-band VSATs, Wireless Metropolitan Area
 Networks and Local Area Networks (LANs) with NICNET gateway for Internet resources, so as to promote  social,
 economic, scientific and technological activities, and also for “macro-economic adjustment programme” of the
 Government.
5.1Since its inception, NIC has been propagating “IT-led Development” facilitating rapid economic growth and social
 transformation in India, by setting up a countrywide satellite based VSAT network (NICNET), first of its kind among the
 developing countries, linking about 540 District Administrations, 25 State Secretariats, and 7 NCT/UT Administrations. 
 NICNET links extend to Andaman Islands, Lakshadweep & Minicoy Island , Ladhakh Region, Indian High  Commission
 (Mauritius), and B.P. Koirala Institute of Medical Sciences in Kathmandu (Nepal).  NIC provides the state-of-the-art IT
 solutions to information management, information dissemination, and decision support requirements of the Central as well

5.3In some of the offices there is a large accumulation of hardware such as computer terminals, keyboards and related
 material such as transformers etc. which contained software, which is not in use now because of the upgradation of
 technology.  This material is now lying as junk for so many years with no action for its removal in sight.   Unless urgent
 steps are taken for the disposal of the hardware, which appears to have been rendered obsolete, it may pose an
 environmental hazard, more so because of the rapid advances being made in this field.  When asked about removal of this
 material lying in the Government offices, the Committee was informed that the NIC has set up a Obsolete Declaration
 Committee to identify obsolete equipments and outdated software and recommend their disposal.  It has also set up an
 Auction Committee to expedite the auction of the items recommended as obsolete by the Obsolete Declaration Committee.
5.4The Committee notes the reply of the Ministry that the provision of Rs.142.17 crores for the NIC for the year 2000-01 is
 sought to be utilized mainly towards its on-going activities.  If it be so, the Committee fails to understand as to how NIC
 will catch up with rapid advances being made in this field as a result of technical innovations.  The Committee therefore
 observes that the Ministry should review its priorities and, if necessary, come out with additional financial projections at
 R.E. stage.  The Committee feels that financial constraints should not be allowed to stay in the way of IT culture being
 spread in the country or in the matter of gaining supremacy in the field.
5.5       The attention of the Secretary, Ministry of Information Technology was drawn to the following recommendation of
 the Committee contained in its Sixty-seventh Report:
“The Committee finds that the Planning Commission has sanctioned a budget support of Rs.300 crores for Information
 Technology to be spent during the Ninth Five Year (1997-2002) period.  The allocation has not been earmarked against any
 of the Ministry/Department of Government of India.  The Department is working on so many programmes/projects
 concerning Information Technology such as ERNET, NII, TDIL, Electronic Commerce, Electronic Governance, Venture
 Capital for Software etc. and the Planning Commission have not allocated sufficient funds for the said
 programmes/projects.  As DOE is responsible for promotion of Information Technology in the country, the Committee is
 strongly of the view that the amount of Rs.300 crores provided by the Planning Commission to be spent during the Ninth
 Plan may be allocated under the administrative control of Department of Electronics and the Department may be designated
 as a nodal agency in the field of Information Technology.”
In the Action Taken Report, the Ministry has informed as follows:
      “…… the matter was taken up with the Planning Commission in June’99 to allocate funds for IT in the IX Plan under the
 administrative control of the Department of Electronics.  The Planning Commission has constituted a group to work out
 modalities to be adopted for allocation of funds under the new Plan Scheme for development of IT.  Ministry of Information
 Technology has since been set up to addresses all policy matters and promotion of IT in the country.  In view of this
 development, Planning Commission has been approached again to place funds under the Ministry of Information
 Technology”. 
 5.6      Asked about whether the allocation of Rs.300 crores was placed under the administrative control of the Ministry, the

 adopted for allocation of funds under the new Plan Scheme for development of IT.  Ministry of Information Technology has
 since been set up to address all policy matters and promotion of IT in the country.  In view of this development, Planning
 Commission has been approached again to place funds under the Ministry of IT.

 Planning Commission expressed the view that during the current year and in the subsequent years, the Ministry must spend
 for the promotion of Information Technology  from their own Budget provision.
5.9The Committee is not happy with the reply given by the Secretary on the allocation of Rs.300 crores being placed under
 its administrative control. The Ministry had informed the Committee through the Action Taken Report “that the Planning
 Commission has been approached again to place funds under the Ministry of IT”.  It is not clear from the Secretary’s reply
 whether the Ministry received any formal reply on the subject from the Planning Commission.  The Committee would
 therefore like the Ministry to look into the matter again, obtain a suitable reply from the Planning Commission and
 appearing the Committee on its part, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation (67
th Report) that the amount of
 Rs.300 crores has been sanctioned by the Planning Commission for IT to be spent during the Ninth Five Year (1997-2002)
 period.  The allocation has not been earmarked against any of the Ministry/Department of Government of India.  The
 Department is working on so many programmes/projects concerning Information Technology such as ERNET,NII, TDIL,
 Electronic Commerce, Electronic Governance, Venture Capital for Software etc. and the Planning Commission have not
 allocated sufficient funds for the said programmes/projects.  As DOE is responsible for promotion of Information
 Technology in the country, the Committee is strongly of the view that the amount of Rs.300 crores provided by the
 Planning Commission to be spent during the Ninth Plan may be allocated under the administrative control of Department of
 Electronics and the Department may be designated as a  nodal agency in the field of Information Technology.
 TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL PROGRAMME
6.   The Technology Development Council (TDC) programme  seeks to support the new initiatives responding to changing
 developmental needs of the electronics sector keeping in line with the liberalized industry policy framework.  The
 programme aims to promote and support research, design, development and engineering in the areas of computer and
 computer communications, control and instrumentation, consumer electronics telecommunications and broadcasting.
6.1When asked about the disproportionate variations in respect of TDC programme, the committee was informed that the
 original provision during 1999-2000 for TDC programme was Rs.8.00 crores (6.80 crores as grants-in-aid and Rs.1.20
 crores as loan), which was reduced to Rs.4.00 crores in R.E. (Rs.3.30 crores as grants-in-aid and Rs.0.70 crores as loan). 
 The reduction in provision has been in view of new project proposals from some of the implementing organisations having
 not materialized and delay in release of funds from some of the ongoing projects owing to funds already available with
 some of the institutes against the earlier releases.  The provision for 2000-01 has been proposed at Rs.5.00 crores (Rs.3.00
 crores as grants-in-aid and Rs.2.00 crores as loan)  which would be utilized mainly towards the ongoing projects and  new
 projects.
 
6.2The Committee observes that it is necessary to ensure perfect co-ordination among the    project implementing agencies 
 supported under TDC programme.  This could be reflected only when allocation made during the period under review is
 utilized fully.
INDUSTRIAL ELECTRONIC PROMOTION PROGRAMME
7.   The Industrial Electronics Promotion Programme (IEPP) aims at development and application of Electronics &
 Information Technology based products and systems to improve productivity, quality and safety in the industrial sector. 
 Under the programme, generic technologies applicable to all industry in general as well as industry specific technologies for
 example meant for paper, textile and steel industries are developed and implemented.  System engineering projects are also
 taken up to enhance productivity, conserve energy and improve quality.
7.1The Committee was informed that the allocation for IEPP was reduced from Rs.3 crores in B.E. of 1999-2000 to Rs.2
 crores in R.E. of that year due to some of the new projects having  not materialised   for want of some clarifications.  The
 Committee was apprised that the B.E. for 2000-2001 has again been increased to Rs.3 crores as seven ongoing projects
 would be completed in the current year and six other projects would be nearing completion by 2000-2001.   New project
 initiatives have been taken in the area of Coal Mining and Food Industry.
7.2The Committee was also informed that with emphasis on Information Technology implementation, IEPP programme

NATIONAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE(NII)
8.   Information Infrastructure is vital for the country and has a tremendous potential for bringing rapid transformation in our
 work culture and thus  the development of the country.   Therefore,  the Ministry  has initiated a focused attention on
 National Information Infrastructure (NII) with the aim of promoting use and proliferation of  Information Technology. 
 Thus, the objective of  the programme is to demonstrate the use of contemporary tools in Information Technology,
 enhancing overall efficiency in work, reduce delays in decision making, promote optimal utilization of manpower resources
 by improving access to information and Information Technology tools and  demonstrate the concept in action to other
 users.  Some of the sectors proposed to be covered under the programme include, literacy, education and life-long learning
 leading to increase in employment opportunities, better health care, environment friendliness, opportunities for rural
 populace to acquire new skills etc.  A number of initiatives have also been taken in the area of multi-media promotion,
 electronic governance and ATM test bed.
8.1The allocation for NII during 2000-2001 has been kept at Rs.11.00 crores as against Rs.10.00 crores in B.E. and Rs.6.00
 crores in the R.E. of the year 1999-2000.  The Committee was informed that the enhanced allocation for the NII programme
 during 2000-2001 is because of the requirement of the network security and also towards new test-beds/applications
 projects and promotional measures  towards e-commerce implementation, online learning amongst others.  Three new 
 projects are also in progress for development of e-commerce technology, tourism information system and creation of
 information infrastructure for Sikkim Government.  Certain new projects in the field of telephony overy internet, networks
 security, e-commerce applications and web enabled database management are being initiated. 
8.2The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs.10 crores was made for NII at B. E. stage of the year 1999-2000 which was
 reduced to Rs.6 crores at the R.E. of that year and it has again been increased to Rs.11 crores in 2000-01.  In view of  the
 variations in the allocation, it appears that either the Ministry is not following realistic approach towards the programme or
 there has been   utilization of funds due to  other reasons.  The Committee therefore reiterates its earlier observation made in
 its 67
th Report and would like to emphasize that having once drawn up the programmes, the Ministry should aim at full
 utilization of the budgetary provisions.    
8.3  The Committee observes that logging into the Internet in Delhi through telephone numbers announced by NIC and in
 the North-eastern region is next to impossible in view of poor telecom infrastructure.  A decision was taken by VSNL to set
 up an International gateway at Guwahati and it was to be commissioned in 1999.  Till date, the element of uncertainly hangs
 about the project and there appears no physical progress.  The Committee therefore recommends that the International
 gateway should be commissioned within a definite time frame.   Efforts should also be made to improve accessibility to the
 internet through telephone network as an individual subscriber may not have the advantage of LAN.
PUBLIC SECTOR ENTERPRISES
9.   There are three public sector enterprises, namely, Computer Maintenance Corporation Ltd. (CMC), Semiconductor
 Complex Ltd. (SCL) and Electronics Trade and Technology Development Corporation Ltd. (ET&T) under the Ministry of
 Information Technology.

 networking facilities management and hardware support.  In the first half-year of 1999-2000, CMC has made the best ever
 performance with a revenue of Rs.183 crores with a growth rate of 23%.  In 1999-2000 CMC’s MoU rating with
 Government of India has been “Very Good”.  CMC stocks are also performing well and recently ICRA, the leading credit
 rating agency has awarded “A1+ “ rating to CMC for its commercial programmes.  Besides, the Government has also given
 clearance to CMC for the enhancement of its equity.  This would provide CMC the required funds to meet its further
 expansion plans.
9.2SCL has been set up for developing and sustaining indigenous capability in the hardware sector for strategic reasons
 keeping in view the larger   national considerations of self reliance. SCL’s broad programmes, inter-alia, are to design,
 develop and manufacture new VLSLs to meet the requirements of Telecom sector, Watch & clock industry and other
 industrial electronic market; and to cater the requirements of strategic sector viz. Space and Defence by development of
 Applications Specific Integrated Circuits.  The Company has also just completed the development of 0.8 micron CMOS

 day expenses and it was not proving to be a profitable company but the situation has  improved  now and the Corporation is
 in a position  to meet its expenses cent percent .  The only problem is that of some past loans and once it is sorted out,

 consolidated its position.

 Circuits.  The Committee feels that this national asset should not be allowed to   whither away.   It is therefore necessary
 that SCL is made a nucleus of growth for the future technology in India.
9.7The Committee further observes that SCL is placed in a unique position to be the supplier of indigenous Smart Cards
 considering the infrastructure and the technical background and experience of the company and the potential the chip holds
 in the present culture of the country.  The Committee therefore recommends that, if necessary, with little orientation the
 Government should consider designating SCL as a sole Smart Cards manufacturer to the Nation.

 be helped to play a major role in the manufacture and supply of  Electronics Energy Meters to  various State  Electricity

 Corporation (PFC), for the purchase of Electronic Energy Meters from SCL at predetermined price which shall be
 competitive vis-à-vis the market price.

 there is need to have a fresh look on the viability of the Company taking into account that it has partly turned the corner and

 is that ET&T is now engaged, as a premier institution, in the spread of computer education and training to the youth who
 constitute a potential work force for the future.  Given the fresh lease of life, it may be in a position to compete with high-
tech premier institutions in the field.
SOCIETY FOR APPLIED MICROWAVE ELECTRONICS ENGINEERING AND RESEARCH (SAMEER)
10.SAMEER , with three Centres at Mumbai, Chennai and Calcutta, is engaged in focused R&D in specific areas of
 microwave engineering, millimeter waves  and applied electromagnetics.  It also undertakes development of components
 subsystem/system and integrated large systems for meeting specific requirements in Defence, Space and Meteorology. It
 has been working in the thrust areas such as, microwave and RF applications in industry, instrumentation and health, linear

 meteorology, antennas, thermal and industrial design of electronic products, etc.  At SAMEER the activities are prioritized
 towards resource generation and special attention to the core R&D areas.  So, SAMEER has maintained its lead in the area
 of EMI/EMC and RF/Microwave technology.  SAMEER has also got a contract for consultancy and electromagnetic
 ambient survey at Jordan.

SOFTWARE/HARDWARE EXPORT PROMOTION
11.The programme aims at the creation of basic facilities for development and export of software to data links and promote
 integrated development of software/hardware in the country for domestic as well as export market.  Computer software
 remains a thrust area and the fastest growing sector both in export and domestic sector.  Software Export has risen to
 Rs.17,000 crores during 1999-2000 from Rs.10,940 crores during 1998-99, registering a growth rate of over 55%. Domestic
 Software industry is likely to go up to Rs.7,300 crores during 1999-2000 from Rs.4,900 crores  during  1998-99.  The 
 schemes  broadly  covered by  the  programme are : -  a)  Software Infrastructure (STPs); b) Quality Assurance,
 Certification and Information Security Management; c) Development support for software (R&D); and Export Promotion
 Campaigns and Markets Intelligence studies.
11.1Asked about the reasons for enhanced allocation for the said programme during the year 2000-01, the Committee has
 been informed that the increase in allocation for Software/Hardware Export Promotion (SEPP) from Rs.5.0 crores in B.E.
 and R.E. of 1999-2000 to Rs.7.0 crores in B.E. of 2000-01 is due to expansion of Software Technology Parks of India
 (STPI) infrastructure and setting up of some of the new Software Technology Parks  (STPs) as well as towards launching of
 some new projects.
11.2The Committee has been given to understand that very low investment is coming forward in Hardware industry and
 foreign investment is going to Taiwan, China, Brazil, Malaysia, etc.  The Committee notes that during the year 1999-2000,
 computer software industry has witnessed a growth of 53% whereas it is abysmally low at 10% in hardware industry. 
 While software industry is doing well in the country, there is need to focus attention at hardware production and analyse the
 reasons that tend to block its growth and take remedial steps.  The Committee observes that hardware sector is showing
 reverse trends and as such has made little progress.  The Committee, therefore recommends, the Ministry should endeavour
 to bridge the gap between two sectors by chalking out concrete plans for speedy promotion and development of hardware
 export in the country.

 required to support growing software export industry and to achieve targeted export.  Under the programme, expansion
 activities of the Bangalore Unit of the National Centre for Software Technology (NCST) have been undertaken to
 strengthen R&D and higher end software education and training.  Other project included in the programme is expansion of
 NCST activities in Navi Mumbai to promote research and development and Advanced Software Education.  This center
 would specialize in the area of Network and Internet Technology, Visual and Artificial Computing.  An advanced one year
 programme in Software Technology has already been initiated.  The budget allocation for the programme during the year
 2000-2001 has been kept at Rs.6.50 crores.
