 project of NCST, Bangalore and first phase of main building for Navi Mumbai.  R&D activity in the identified areas of
 excellence in both centers is also proposed to be initiated.  New programmes relating to ‘Enterprenuers Development Centre
 of IT-Enabled Services’, support to finishing schools, specialized training in Web Designing Software Tools etc. would be
 initiated.
12.2The Committee notes the position with satisfaction.  However, it feels that there is still a scope for publicity for different
 projects under the programme so to educate maximum number of people.  This would help the programme to achieve
 desired results.

EDUCATION AND RESEARCH NETWORK (ERNET)
14.The ERNET Project was initiated in 1986 to strengthen national capabilities in the area of a computer networking and
 data communication, to make it competitive by world standards and to carry the benefits to nationwide academic and
 research community, industry and variety of users.  Today ERNET has about 750 institutions connected to its network.  In
 order to facilitate network access to its users, ERNET Points of Presence (PoPs) are being established in all major cities in
 the country.  Considering the special communication requirement for student community in North East  region of  the
 country, ERNET has taken a special  initiative and established a dedicated satellite Network in the region.  With this,
 isolated Universities and Colleges in this region would be able to reap benefits of Internet revolution round the globe.
14.1     Asked about the constant reduction in the allocation for the programme, the Committee was informed that the
 reduction in financial allocation for Education and Research Network (ERNET) India in R.E. for 1999-2000 to Rs.16.00
 crores from Rs.25.00 crores in B.E. for that year is due to delay in getting 8.2 M bp backbone lines with state-of-art network
 equipment from Department of Telecom.  The outlay from Ministry of Information Technology for ERNET India was
 recommended by Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) at Rs.60.00 crores, based on which the draft CCEA note was
 prepared and circulated to concerned Ministries.  Ministry of  Finance however, desired that the outlay from Government of
 India need to be further reviewed and suitably reduced.  Hence, the revised CCEA through Ministry of Finance.  Against the
 proposed Government support of Rs.19.85 crores, the amounts already been released to  the Society during 1997-98
 (Rs.5.30 crores) and 1998-99 (Rs.14.55 crores) and the likely releases to be made during 1999-2000 were Rs.16.00 crores
 as per R.E.  Thus, the remaining balance to be paid to ERNET India during 2000-2001 and 2001-02 works out to Rs.19.15
 crores only, against which the allocation made in Demands for Grants for MIT for 2000-01 is Rs.15.00 crores and the
 balance of Rs.4.01 crores will be made in 2001-02.
14.2 The Committee feels that initiation of ERNET project is a praiseworthy step as this would facilitate commercial
 exploitation of the technologies by the industries and other users.

 Integrated Circuits.  The Committee feels that this national asset should not be allowed to   whither away.   It is therefore
 necessary that SCL is made a nucleus of growth for the future technology in India.
(Para 9.6)
9          The Committee further observes that SCL is placed in a unique position to be the supplier of indigenous Smart Cards
 considering the infrastructure and the technical background and experience of the company and the potential the chip holds
 in the present culture of the country.  The Committee therefore recommends that, if necessary, with little orientation the
 Government should consider designating SCL as a sole Smart Cards manufacturer to the Nation.
(Para 9.7)
10.       The Committee also feels that in order to promote comprehensively indigenous Electronics Energy Meters, SCL
 should be helped to play a major role in the manufacture and supply of Electronics Energy Meters to various State
 Electricity Boards (SEBs) by the Government possibly by tying-up the Loans for the purpose to SEBs from Power Finance
 Corporation (PFC), for the purchase of Electronic Energy Meters from SCL at predetermined price which shall be
 competitive vis-à-vis the market price. 
(Para 9.8)

 that there is need to have a fresh look on the viability of the Company taking into account that it has partly turned the corner
 and is in a position to meet its expenses in full. Another important consideration that necessitates reconsideration of its
 existence is that ET&T is now engaged, as a premier institution, in the spread of computer education and training to the
 youth who constitute a potential work force for the future.  Given the fresh lease of life, it may be in a position to compete
 with high-tech premier institutions in the field.
(Para 9.9)
12.       The Committee is happy at the performance of SAMEER and hopes that its officers and staff will continue to work

R E P O R T
      The Department of Ocean Development was created in July, 1981 within the Cabinet Secretariat directly under the
 charge of the Prime Minister. In March, 1982 it became a separate Department and has since been functioning as a nodal
 Department for organising, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country, in line with the Ocean
 Policy Statement of 1982. The programmes pursued by the Department over the years have also kept pace with
 developments World over and addressed National needs and issues.
      The programmes of the Department are directed towards:
(i)         Technology Development Programmes for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic
 significance.
(ii)        Societal Programmes with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot
 project demonstration with the participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for
 coastal area development.
(iii)       Marine Resources Programmes for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic
 studies to evolve strategies for sustainable exploration and utilisation, and resource enhancement.
(iv)       Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with
 scientific and geo-political significance.
(v)        Capacity Building Programme towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human
 resource development and establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
(vi)
              Creation of public awareness on the potential and uses of ocean.

 crores for the other Plan schemes.

th Scientific Expedition to Antarctica, carrying out scientific experiments, maintenance of the permanent research

 outer limits of our continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles Exclusive Economic Zone has to be made before 2005. The
 time frame for carrying out the bathymetric and seismic surveys and preparing necessary documents to submit to the
 Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf is  5 years. Considering this, the Government approved the scheme with an

POLAR SCIENCES
Antarctic Expedition:
15.The Secretary informed the Committee that the 19
th Indian Scientific expedition to Antarctica was launched from Cape
 Town, South Africa, on 9 th December 1999, keeping in view the likely scientific and economic benefits and future
 international cooperation in the field of polar science between India and other countries. The 19 th Expedition to Antarctica
 consisted of a 47 member team including 30 scientists and 17 logistic personnel, under the leadership of Mr. Arun
 Chaturvedi a scientist of Geological Survey of India, including a two member lady team – one medical Doctor from India
 and a Geologist from Peru.  This included a contingent of 25 members who would winter-over in Antarctica for 16 months
 duration in pursuit of science.  The logistic support for the Expedition had been provided by a contingent of Army
 personnel, which is headed by Maj. Ravi Sangwan.
16.In addition to the ongoing programmes several new experiments have been initiated during the course of this expedition,
 which includes:
(i)                 Study of earth-air current systems to give an insight to the deep space processes.
(ii)        Experiments on crack propagation of the ice-shelf in order to understand the dynamics and processes of
 Iceberg generation.
(iii)       Installation of a number of automatic weather stations to measure energy balance and albedo factors of the
 ice, as a part of global change studies.
(iv)       Reconstruction of the past climatic and vegetative history through the study of organo-debris present in the
 fresh water lake sediments of Antarctica.
(v)        Establishment of an environment monitoring laboratory for the first time at Maitri in order to carry out an 
 assessment of the status of air, noise, water biological and land environment of Antarctica, throughout the
 year.
17.The summer team of the XIX expedition returned to India via Cape Town on 6 th March, 2000 along with the winter team
 members of the XVIII expedition.
18  The Committee observes that this heralds another scientific feat in the realms of polar science at the end of this
 millennium and demonstrates the capabilities and interest of the country to pursue a well-focussed scientific campaign from
 a pristine scientific platform provided by Antarctica.
18.1  The Committee recommends that  the National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research(NCAOR) Goa, should be
 designated as the nodal  agency of the Department in planning, coordinating and executing the XX Indian Scientific
 Expedition to Antarctica for continuation of the scientific/research programmes initiated during the XIX expedition. The
 Committee hopes that the scientific and logistics co-operation gained  with the  launching of the XIX Expedition from Cape
 Town would lead to the initiation of state-of-the-art research programmes in Polar Sciences and should be carried forward in
 initiating and executing Southern Ocean Oceanography & Paleoclimatology, and Antarctic Global Change.

ISLAND DEVELOPMENT
54.NIOT has taken up new initiatives towards helping island communities in their needs relating to Ocan Science and
 Technology as well as marine resource enhancement. The first activity taken up by NIOT is a programme on lobster resource
 enhancement for islands under the DOD project on Living Marine Resources Enhancement (LMRE).
55.In a study conducted on lobster fattening using gray clam as live feed, a remarkable increment in body weight (i.e. around 35
 g/month) has been achieved. Another experiment was conducted using green mussel as a feed source in place of clam. The
 various biochemical analysis such as protein, free amino acids, carbohydrates, free & bound sugars, protease, a-amylase and
 chitinase indicate the suitability of mussel meat as a better alternative to the clam as feed source for lobsters.
56.During the fattening of lobsters, various hydrobiological parameters such as temperature, pH, salinity, dissolved oxygen,
 nitrite, nitrate, silicate, ammonia and phosphate in the source water as well as the experimental tanks were estimated. The
 phytoplankton species present in the source water were also identified in order to utilize them as feed for larvae. The occurrence
 of various protozoans, total heterotrophic bacterial population and Vibrios load was observed in the body surface of lobster, live
 feeds and water (both from tanks and source). The animals with tail rot syndrome were successfully treated with appropriate
 concentration of malachite green and 100% recovery was observed in 20-22 days.
57.At the new campus of NIOT,  R&D laboratories, which will cater to all the analytical requirements of the LMRE project,
 have been organised. All major and minor equipment were commissioned and the laboratory is fully operational.
58.A survey on landing of lobsters at various sites in Gulf of Mannar and Andaman islands has been completed by December
 1999. It indicates a decline in landings at various sites, a trend which was in evidence from previous surveys of lobster
 resources during the last few years.

 Development has been integrated with NIOT as Andaman and Nicobar Centre for Ocean Science and Technology (ANCOST)
 in order to implement the various core activities previously initiated under the LMRE programme. For this purpose, already
 existing facilities like boats and sea water pumps have been repaired and commissioned. A layout of new laboratory building
 has been finalised and the building is expected to be functional very soon. Using the farm facility in Minnie Bay, the problems

60.The Committee  shares the perception that the genetic and biotic equilibrium should be maintained in the Indian
 environment.  However, it  is of the view that the Department should carry out further research on formulation of appropriate
 feeds for maximum growth of lobsters and also develop the  larval rearing technology in Indian spiny lobster. At the same time
 the Department should also implement  projects on development of technology for sustainable shrimp farming, lobster and
 seaweed culture and polyculture of marine organisms at ANCOST.
DELINEATION OF OUTER LIMITS OF CONTINENTAL SHELF
61.Traditionally the Coastal States had been claiming few nautical miles into the sea.  In accordance with the UN Convention on
 Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), now the States can establish 12 nautical miles of territorial sea and 200 nautical miles of Exclusive
 Economic Zone (EEZ) from baselines and there are no major technical difficulties in establishing the limits.  The States are also
 entitled for the
rights over the continental shelf, slope and rise extending beyond the EEZ.  The continental shelf comprises the seabed and
 subsoil of the submarine areas that extend beyond the territorial sea throughout the natural prolongation of the land territory. 
 The continental shelf is rich in non-living resources and the minerals, including hydrocarbon resources.
62.The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea stipulates that where the coastal state intends to establish the outer limits of the
 continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles, it shall submit particulars of such limits to the Commission on the Limits of
 Continental Shelf (CLCS), along with the supporting scientific and technical data as soon as possible, but in any case within 10
 years of entry into force of the Convention for that State.  The Convention came into force on 16.11.1994 and India ratified the
 same in June 1995.  India thus must submit all the necessary data to the CLCS by June 2005.  If delineation is done properly
 India would be in a position to claim more than 1 million sq.km beyond the EEZ.  India is represented as an elected member on
 the Commission on the Limits of Continental Shelf (CLCS).
63.The Committee observes that with the ratification of the UN Convention on Law of the Sea, a new international order has
 been established for the oceans and  India being represented in almost all the important bodies on oceans will stand to benefit
 enormously by provisions of the convention, only if we can build an integrated approach for scientific planning, formulation,
 implementation and overall management of the programmes with a comprehensive organisational and institutional back up.
64.After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress of
 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 158.00
 Crores as sought by the Department of Ocean Development for the year 2000-2001, under Demand No.92  may be
 approved.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS AT GLANCE
 
1.   The Committee recommends that in order to ensure continuity of the programmes an addition allocation may be allotted 
 to the Department at the time of R.E. stage so that rescheduled programmes can be completed in the current year itself. 
(Para 11)
2.   The Committee observes that this heralds another scientific feat in the realms of polar science at the end of this
 millennium and demonstrates the capabilities and interest of the country to pursue a well-focussed scientific campaign from
 a pristine scientific platform provided by Antarctica.
(Para 18)
3.   The Committee recommends that  the National Centre for Antarctic and Ocean Research(NCAOR) Goa, should be
 designated as the nodal  agency of the Department in planning, coordinating and executing the XX Indian Scientific
 Expedition to Antarctica for continuation of the scientific/research programmes initiated during the XIX expedition. The
 Committee hopes that the scientific and logistics co-operation gained  with the  launching of the XIX Expedition from Cape
 Town would lead to the initiation of state-of-the-art research programmes in Polar Sciences and should be carried forward in
 initiating and executing specific and specialized programmes in the scientific disciplines of Polar Remote Sensing, Southern
 Ocean Oceanography & Paleoclimatology, and Antarctic Global Change.
(Para 18.1)
4.   The Committee observes that under Marine Living Resources programme the Department would  continue its research
 towards studies to establish techniques for estimation of fish, zooplankton and Deep Scattering Layer(DSL) of the  biomass;
 large marine ecosystem  studies of the Arabian Sea; assessment of mesopelagic resources of the high seas and studies on the
 benthic productivity/biodiversity and the fish biodiversity of the continental slope area.

R E P O R T
 
 
The Indian Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, is geared to achieve the goal of self-reliant use
 of Space Technology to ensure rapid progress in diversified fields of the country including social, economic, cultural and
 scientific for finding solutions to the problems of man and society. Even as India entered the new millennium, the space
 programme in the country has matured to a status where space has become an important element of the national
 infrastructure, especially in the areas of communication, broadcasting, meteorology, disaster management and resources
 monitoring. India is recognized the world over for its unique application driven space programme. Further, industry
 participation in the space programme  has been expanding, bringing economic benefits. The plan to further enhance and
 improve the space services by launching follow-on satellites in the INSAT and IRS series in coming years and to enhance
 the launch capability to place INSAT class of satellites in orbit through GSLV, the Indian Space Programme is well poised
 to play a stronger role in the country's march towards progress in the new millennium.
2.     Whereas the efforts of the Indian Space Programme in the early sixties were confined to getting familiar with space
 technologies and developing technical and organisational infrastructure in order to develop satellite launch vehicles, during
 the eighties, the space programme moved closer to realising the goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national
 development. The country entered the nineties with the launch of more ASLVs and PSLVs. With the launch of IRS-IB and
 INSAT 2A and 2B, the Indian Space Programme becomes fully operational through its own communication and remote
 sensing satellites. The Indian Space Programme is broad-based and it has an impressive array of achievements in putting to
 use space technology for vital applications - for telecommunications, TV broadcasting, weather watching, forecasting
 agricultural crop and forests wealth assessment, water resources management, flood mapping, drought forecasting,
 identification of marine resources, protection of the environment and rural literacy campaign etc.
3.     Self-reliance in space technology has been an important target of the programme from the very beginning.  Long-range
 plans have been drawn up, from the very beginning, for each decade, to steer the programme effectively, ensuring
 appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development. Over the last three-and-half decades, significant achievements have been made in country in the area of space
 technology (i) for building world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing, (ii) for launching the remote
 sensing satellites from India with our own launch vehicle and (iii) in reaching  the benefits of space technology to improve
 the quality of life at the grass root level, thus contributing to several areas of national development.  Necessary
 organizational and institutional mechanisms with users, industries and academia have also been established. In tune with the
 goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian Space Programme are:-
(a)    Satellite-based communication for various applications;
(b)    Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental monitoring;
(c)    Meteorological applications; and
(d)   Development and operationalisation of indigenous satellites and launch vehicles for
         providing these space services.

4.     The Department of Space, which was set up in 1972 to promote unified development and application of Space Science
 Technology for identified national objectives, is entrusted with the task of implementing the policies framed by the Space
 Commission.   The policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant-in-
aid institutions viz., the National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the
 National Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar facility (NMRF).
5.     Today, the space  sector world over, is poised for a transformation towards a matured, scientific and industrial sector,
 with multiple players and changing roles. Besides, it needs to adapt itself to the implications of a market driven economy
 and the formidable challenges arising out of increased societal needs, technological limitations, resource constraints and
 geo-political scenarios.   In India, while integrating the programmes with the international scenario, the national needs are to
 be addressed; the gains achieved so far have to be consolidated; new and potential areas of space technology utilization are
 to be identified and developed; organisational as well as managerial support have to be ensured to surge forward, harnessing
 national capability and capacity, ensuring synergy amongst the partners as well as space systems.
6.    The Committee observes India is one of the six countries with homemade satellites in orbit. Despite being a new entrant
 to the competitive global space club, which hitherto was an exclusive preserve of a handful of countries, India's overall
 track record both in the field of rocketry and satellites has been impressive. This, of course, does not overlook the fact that it
 had its share of failures too, which needless to say can be expected in any hi-tech project. To cite a few, one can recall the
 failure of the ASLV and of the PSLV.   But these failed missions only proved to be another step on the ladder to success.
 The subsequent flights were a resounding success. This endorsed India's claim to be growing space power. The Committee,
 however, would like the Department to keep the analysis of each failed mission in view so that corrective measures can be
 taken while executing future programmes.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
7.     The Committee was informed that the total expenditure on Space research till the end of Eight Plan Period i.e. from the
 inception in 1962-63 to 1996-97 was Rs.7431.67 crores. During the Eight Plan Period most of the programmatic targets and
 missions have been achieved and the total expenditure incurred on these programmes was Rs.3928.53 crores (Plan
 Rs.3155.74 crores and non-plan Rs.772.79 crores).
8.     It has been stated that the Department of Space had asked for an allocation of Rs.11,000 crores for the Ninth Plan
 period to meet the programmatic requirements of the Department, but the allocation was restricted to Rs.6511.72 crores for
 the entire plan period from 1997 to 2002. This is however subject to review on annual basis by the Planning Commission. In
 the first three years of the 9
th plan, the Department has expended Rs.4,164 crores which is 54% of the total plan outlay.
9.     Analysing the performance of the Department on the basis of the information made available, the Committee found that
 during 1997-98, the Department had utilised the funds to the extent of 99.13 percent. In 1998-99, the fund utilization level
 was about 99.9 per cent. The provisional expenditure for 1999-2000 indicates utilization of funds by the Department. The
 Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has made optimum utilization of the funds allocated to it during
 1997-98, 1998-99 and 1999-2000.
10.    The programme directions and proposals for Ninth Plan (1997-2002) have been formulated after extensive interactions
 and consultations with user Ministries. The guidelines provided by the Space Commission have been adopted in the process
 of formulation. The Committee was informed that consistent with the programme directions and targets envisaged for the
 Ninth Plan period, the specific activities/projects to be undertaken during the year 2000-2001 have been carefully prioritised
 while working out the B.E. for 2000-2001 which are in pursuance of the Zero Base Budgeting Methodology of the
 Department in formulating the process of annual budgets. The financial allocation for 2000-2001 works out to Rs.2019.22
 crores as against Rs.l725.86crores in the R.E. of 1999-2000 and Rs.1755.00 crores in the B.E. of 1999-2000, which is
 higher by Rs.293.36 crores over the revised estimates and Rs.264.22 crores over the B.E. of 1999-2000 (Annexure).
11.    The major landmark achieved by the Department during the year 1999-2000 is the successful launch of the Indian
 Remote Sensing Satellite, IRS-P4 (Oceansat) alongwith two foreign satellites, one belonging to South Korea and other to
 Germany. The successful mission has not only given the ISRO enough confidence to market its launchers abroad but also
 enhanced the space services to the nation in the areas of telecommunication, television broadcasting, meteorology, disaster
 management and resources survey.
11.1  The Committee observes that these achievements are a feather in the cap of the Department as the launch of three
 satellites in a single flight is a technological achievement and it marks India's entry in the commercial launch market.

 the largest domestic communication satellite systems in the world today which is entrusted with the task of providing
 services in the areas of telecommunications, television broadcasting, radio networking and meteorology including disaster

SATELLITE NAVIGATION
13.    Satellite navigation equipment has been made mandatory by the International Civil Aviation Organization on all
 civilian aircraft. It is expected to become operational in many advanced countries in the next few years. In India, the Airport
 Authority of India (AAI) is planning to make them adaptable to the Future Air Navigation System through the introduction
 of Indian Wide Area Differential GPS system. In its endeavour to conform to the standards set out by the International Civil
 Aviation Organisation, the AAI is planning to replace the existing navigational aids with satellite navigation equipment by
 the year 2010.
13.1   Department of Space is playing a vital role in establishing the satellite navigation infrastructure in the country. It has
 sent a preliminary project report on satellite based navigation system to the AAI and is working in close coordination with
 the National Steering Committee on Communications, Navigation and Surveillance Air Traffic Management for giving
 shape to the plan of action.
13.2  The Committee feels that in order to fall in line with international standards, the Department should consider
 establishing a satellite based navigation system as that would facilitate modern air navigation system. The Committee is of
 the view that the Airport Authority of India and the Department of Space should work in close coordination to achieve the
 objective.
INDIAN REMOTE SENSING SATELLITE (IRS)
14.    The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) system, which was commissioned in 1988, constitutes an important element of
 National Resources Management System (NNRMS) providing continuously space based data related to land, water and
 ocean resources as well as atmospheric observations. The IRS system now comprising five satellites IRS-1B, IRC-1C, IRS-
ID, IRS-P3 and IRS-P4 (Oceansat), forms the largest constellation of remote sensing satellites in the world to undertake
 space based remote sensing. The recent launch of IRS-P4 has opened up new vistas for ocean remote sensing, while the
 next in the series IRS-P5 is exclusively devoted to cartographic applications and IRS-P6 targeted for resources survey.
 These are scheduled for launch in the next couple of years. The application of remote sensing data is being extended to
 more areas in agriculture, forestry, surface and ground water harnessing, geology, urban planning, land use and land cover
 mapping and ocean resources survey flood mapping etc.
14.1   The remote sensing applications in the entire country are carried out under the broad umbrella of National Natural
 Resources Management System (NNRMS). As the effective utilization of IRS database on an operational basis is possible
 with the involvement of the states in setting up appropriate mechanism to integrate the database for effective management
 of natural resources in the states, the idea of State Natural Resources Management System (SNRMS) was conceptualized,
 on the pattern of existing NNRMS. The Government of Uttar Pradesh took the pride of being first in establishing SNRMS.
 States like Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal and Maharashtra are expected to finalise the process of establishing SNRMS in
 their respective states, in the near future.
14.2  While the Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in augmenting its remote sensing
 capability, what is important is not only the effective management and utilization of natural resources but locating more of
 such resources considering that such resources are on the verge of depletion in the times ahead. The Committee  therefore 
 observes  that  the  efforts  should  be  so  oriented  with emphasis  on mapping more of natural resources as also the
 optimum utilization of the resources already tapped.

INTEGRATED MISSION FOR SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT (IMSD)
15.    Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development (IMSD) was initiated in 1992 to generate action plan for sustainable
 development of natural resources in rural areas. The mission is an extension of the pilot studies taken up by the Department
 during 1988-90 in predominantly drought prone/desert districts. Under IMSD, local-specific plans for development of land
 and water resources are generated through integrated analysis of thematic maps generated using remote sensing,
 conventional and socio-economic data and also R&D inputs provided by research institutions.   These locale-specific
 developmental/action plans are generated on watershed/blocks basis, thus covering a geographical area of 84 million
 hectares.
15.1   Asked about the implementation of IMSD programme in problem districts of the country, the Committee was
 informed that the IMSD is extended to 247 areas in 175 districts, out of which 34 districts are covered in full.
15.2  IMSD is mainly carried out in the problem districts of the country and the scope of IMSD is expected to be enlarged in
 a phased manner after detailed review of the progress made so far. Recently, IMSD has been extended to 8 districts of
 Orissa. Plans are also being worked out, in consultation with users to extend IMSD for critical areas (IMSD Phase - III).
 The financial allocation ofRs.1.00 crores in B.E. of 2000-2001 is towards monitoring the implementation of action plans in
 selected watershed and for IMSD Phase - III.
15.3  The Secretary, Department of Space, informed the Committee that the Department was planning to start Development
 Programme under the IMSD scheme in some districts of Jammu & Kashmir.
15.4 The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation (68
th Report) that even though the programme was heading
 towards a right direction, the pace of the programme appeared slow. The Committee feels that the tempo of the programme
 needs to be geared up and it should have time bound targets.
 DISASTER MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
16.    The Disaster Management System (DMS) is visualised to provide the backbone support for management of disasters in
 near-real time and also for disaster zonation studies and effective initiation strategies. Space-based disaster management
 system provides valuable inputs when appropriately integrated with the conventional ground-based systems. In the Ninth
 plan period, the efforts are on to complete a system definition study of the DMS and also conduct pilot experiments for
 establishing a prototype DMS. Plot project on DMS has been initiated in some flood-prone districts of Assam.
16.1   With a view to ensure timely dissemination of weather warnings of impending disaster from approaching cyclones,
 specially designed receivers i.e. Cyclone Warning Dissemination Systems (CWDS) have been installed in the cyclone-
prone coastal areas to disseminate cyclone warning messages directly to the affected areas. . At present 250 CWDS have
 been deployed in various coastal states of India.
16.2  The Secretary, Department of Space, informed the Committee that the Department was reviewing its Disaster
 Management System. In this direction, the Department in cooperation with IMD, was planning to install New Generation
 receiver with Global  Positioning  System  to  track
early movements of cyclones.
16.3  The Secretary, further informed the Committee that after Orissa cyclone, the Department was assisting the relief
 agencies by providing them satellite maps of the area indicating the degree of damage. For flood management the
 Department is embarking on geographical information base. The Department, besides Orissa and Andhra Pradesh, is
 working with the Brahmaputra Flood Control Mission and creating geographical maps in Assam in order to identified flood
 prone areas.
16.4  The Committee is constrained to observe that the perfection in the functioning of the Cyclone Warning Dissemination
 Systems (CWDS) for predicting the contours of the cyclone is yet to be achieved. The country has witnessed the fury of
 weather Gods in the form of cyclones and other weather extremes resulting in tremendous loss of life and property in some
 states. There is thus an imperative need to perfect the system. The projects therefore need to be taken up with sense of
 urgency and, if necessary, in cooperation with other Departments and agencies. The Committee feels that the constraint of
 funds should not be allowed to stand in the totality of these projects.
GEO-SYNCHRONOUS LAUNCH VEHICLE (GSLV) PROJECT
17.   The Geo-Synchronous Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is designed and developed to achieve capability   for     placing    
 INSAT     class     communication     satellites   in   Geo-Synchronous transfer orbit. With the launch of GSLV the country
 is expected to bid in the multibillion  dollar commercial satellite launch market. The GSLV contains three stages - solid
 propellant, liquid propellant and cryogenic engine. The first GSLV flight scheduled for launch from Sriharikota  this year
 would use the Russian-built engine and stages.  The second cryogenic engine has also been developed and was awaiting

CRYO-UPPER STAGE (CUS) PROJECT
18.   The Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS) Project, approved in 1994, was intended to achieve a stage carrying 12.5 tonnes of
 propellant and produce a thrust of 7.5 tonnes. It is expected that GSLV will put INSAT Class of satellites into geostationary
 transfer orbit. The objective of the CUS Project is to develop and qualify a restartable cryogenic stage for the upper stage of
 GSLV. A cryogenic engine which provides one and half times more specific impulse  than conventional space engines, is
 necessary for launching GSLV. Apart from being far more efficient, and enabling heavier payloads to be injected into
 farther orbits, cryogenic engines are cost effective  and are also environment friendly.
18.1   The Committee was informed mat the allocation for the project during the year 2000-01 has been reduced because
 certain materials required for the cryo stage development to be procured from foreign sources could not be realized because
 the tendering action did not result in acceptable quotations and hence had to be retendered. In view of the above, the cash-
flow requirement for the project for RE 1999-20000 had been reduced.
18.2   The Secretary, DOS, informed the Committee that out of approved project cost of Rs.335.89 crores, during the last six
 years i.e. from 1994 to 2000, Rs.251.65 crores have been spent on the development of the project and the Department is
 expected to achieve the first cryogenic stage by the year 2003.
18.3   The first indigenously fabricated cryogenic engine was put on test on 16 February, 2000 at Mahendragiri. While the
 engine was successfully ignited after meticulous preparation, the test was aborted at 11 seconds due to a leak in hydrogen.
 This is the first of  the series of qualification tests for Cryogenic engine. The recorded results will enable suitable corrective
 action to be identified.
18.4  The Committee observes that there is imperative need for the country to perfect its cryogenic capabilities. Sustained
 effort and perseverance should help in that direction. Added to this the analysis of past experiments would act as a guidance
 to the future.
DIRECT - TO- HOME (DTH) TV MISSION
19.    The basic concept of a Direct-to-Home Television Broadcasting Satellite System is a high power satellite operating in
 the KU-Band for direct broadcasting of TV programmes to homes. Responding to the Indian broadcasting industry's
 demand. Government permitted import of KU-Band equipment in 1996 but banned the import in the subsequent year. Since
 then the mission has not made any remarkable progress. The imperative for such a decision is stated to be the need to have a
 comprehensive broadcasting law on the subject. Further, due to decision of the Government not to fund the programme, its
 success depends on the participation of private investors, but this can be achieved only after the law in this regard has been
 enacted.
19.1   The Committee feels that the Government should clear the fog on the issue as early as possible or else its credibility to
 spread information technology is bound to suffer. DTH is a part of information technology and Government should clear the
 hurdles on the subject keeping the interest of the viewers uppermost while enacting any taw on the subject.

SPACE-INDUSTRY INTERFACE

SPONSORED  RESEARCH  PROGRAMME (RESPOND)
24.   Sponsored   Research   Programme   (RESPOND)   of     the     Department    is    aimed   at  ensuring a close academic
 interaction. The prime objectives of the programme is to strengthen the ISRO academic institution interaction for generation
 of a wider infrastructural and manpower training base for space research in the country. ISRO supports the research
 activities in space science, space applications and space technology in various national academic/research institutions
 through grants-in-aid, besides supporting conferences, symposia and publications. The budgetary allocation for this
 programme has been kept at Rs.5.50 crores during the year 2000-2001.
24.1   Currently, apart from IISC and IIT, ISRO supported 31 ongoing projects and 30 new projects at various academic

24.2 The Committee recommends that apart from initiating the research projects in the academic institutions, the Department
 should constantly monitor the performance of these projects so that country could be benefited by the completion of these
 projects. It should be the endeavour of the Department to complete the projects within the stipulated time frame.
SPACE PROGRAMME PUBLICTY
25.   The Committee was informed that ISRO information required to be in the public domain is already available on
 INTERNET. Various other publicity measures like brochures on space programme, exhibitions, media visit, live telecast of
 PSLV and INSAT launches, etc. are also undertaken. All the centres of the Department of Space also conduct workshops
 and symposia at various place to familiarize teachers and student community on space science, technology and applications.
 In order to encourage the young talents, Department of Space supported the International Astronomy Olympiad training
 camp and in turn, Indian students performed exceedingly well at the Olympiad held at Ukraine in 1999. The Department has
 also organised mobile exhibitions to educate people about its activities.
25.1  The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department of Space for rendering services to farmers,
 fishermen, for urban area town planning, etc. and for publicising its activities, particularly in the developmental and socio-
economic sectors.
ANTRIX CORPORATION
26.    M/s Antrix Corporation Ltd, the commercial wing of ISRO, is marketing India’s space products and services. The
 objective is to gain entry into the highly competitive international market.   Some important achievements of the
 Corporation include marketing of IRS data, satellite launch contracts with Germany, Korea and Belgium, sale of a sounding
 rocket to Norway and supply of satellite hardware to major space companies in the world. Antrix Corporation and
 Arianspace have companies in the world and have also signed an agreement to enlarge the launch opportunities for small

77th Report of Committee on Science & Technology
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/77threport.htm[29-08-2018 16:14:18]
 satellites. The company is also engaged in providing commercial aspects for transfer of ISRO's spin-off technologies to
 Indian industries.
26.1   The Secretary, DOS, informed the Committee that the Indian industries are only utilising the services provided by the
 space programme and are not eager to purchase  space products The Secretary, however, added that the Antrix Corporation
 has proved its commercial viability and its commercial operations for this year amount to Rs.33 crores.
26.2  The Secretary, further informed the Committee that Antrix Corporation have given 9 transponders on contract. The
 Department is getting 20% as acquisition fee and 10% as royalty for IRS data, thus earning a total of two to three million
 dollars.
26.3  The Committee is happy to note that Antrix Corporation is progressing well in commercialising Indian space product
 and services in the highly competitive international space market and that will set a stage for further boost to the India's
 multi faceted space programme. Effort should be made to secure the wider involvement of the industry in marketing and
 other areas of its activities.
27.   After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Space and assessing the progress of various important
 programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.2019.22 crores,
 as sought by the Department of Space for the year 2000-2001, under Demand No. 93, may be approved.
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS AT GLANCE
1.    The Committee observes India is one of the six countries with homemade satellites in orbit. Despite being a new entrant
 to the competitive global space club, which hitherto was an exclusive preserve of a handful of countries, India's overall
 track record both in the field of rocketry and satellites has been impressive. This, of course, does not overlook the fact that it
 had its share of failures too, which needless to say can be expected in any hi-tech project. To cite a few, one can recall the
 failure of the ASLV and of the PSLV.   But these failed missions only proved to be another step on the ladder to success.
 The subsequent flights were a resounding success. This endorsed India's claim to be growing space power. The Committee,
 however, would like the Department to keep the analysis of each failed mission in view so that corrective measures can be
 taken while executing future programmes. 
(Para 6)
2.  The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has made optimum utilization  of the funds allocated to it
 during 1997-98, 1998-99 and 1999-2000.
(Para 9)
3.  The Committee observes that these achievements are a feather in the cap of the Department as the launch of three
 satellites in a single flight is a technological achievement and it marks India's entry in the commercial launch market.
(Para 11.1)
4.  The Committee feels that in order to fall in line with international standards, the Department should consider establishing
 a satellite based navigation system as that would facilitate modern air navigation system. The Committee is of the view that
 the Airport Authority of India and the Department of Space should work in close coordination to achieve the objective.
(Para 13.2)
5.  While the Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department in augmenting its remote sensing capability,
 what is important is not only the effective management and utilization of natural resources but locating more of such
 resources considering that such resources are on the verge of depletion in the times ahead. The Committee therefore
 observes that the efforts should be so oriented with emphasis on mapping more of natural resources as also the optimum
 utilization of the resources already tapped.
(Para 14.2)
6. The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation (68
th Report) that even though the programme was heading towards
 a right direction, the pace of the programme appeared slow. The Committee feels that the tempo of the programme needs to
 be geared up and it should have time bound targets.
 (Para 15.4)
7.  The Committee is constrained to observe that the perfection in the functioning of the Cyclone Warning Dissemination
 Systems (CWDS) for predicting the contours of the cyclone is yet to be achieved. The recent devastating cyclone in Orissa
 can be seen as an example, besides past experiences. The country has witnessed the fury of weather Gods in the form of

 cyclones and other weather extremes resulting in tremendous loss of life and property in some states. There is thus an
 imperative need to perfect the system. The projects therefore need to be taken up with sense of urgency and, if necessary, in
 cooperation with other Departments and agencies. The Committee feels that the constraint of funds should not be allowed to
 stand in the totality of these projects.
(Para 16.4)
8.  The Committee notes that operationalisation of GSLV would result in India's future INSAT satellites being launched by
 this vehicle. This is expected to result in substantial savings of foreign exchange and rid the country of its dependence on
 foreign technology. Further the capability to launch the INSAT class of communication satellites, it should enable the
 country to sell the GSLV to other countries for launching their INSAT-type satellites.
(Para 17.2)
9.  The Committee observes that there is imperative need for the country to perfect its cryogenic capabilities. Sustained
 effort and perseverance should help in that direction. Added to this the analysis of past experiments would act as a guidance
 to the future.
(Para 18.4)
10   The Committee feels that the Government should clear the fog on the issue as early as possible or else its credibility to
 spread information technology is bound to suffer. DTH is a part of information technology and Government should clear the
 hurdles on the subject keeping the interest of the viewers uppermost while enacting any taw on the subject.
(Para 19.1)
11.  The Committee feels that as the number of launches per year increases, the need to have a second launch pad cannot be
 underestimated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the development of second launch pad should be accorded
 priority keeping in view the requirements in this regard.
(Para 20.3)
12. The Committee observes that the Department is progressing well in its plan to extend the       TDCC/JDCP       projects
        to       other      States      as     well.    The   Committee, however, observes that before opening new fronts, the
 Department should evaluate  the results of the projects already in hand.
(Para 23.3)
13. The Committee recommends that apart from initiating the research projects in the academic institutions, the Department
 should constantly monitor the performance of these projects so that country could be benefited by the completion of these
 projects. It should be the endeavour of the Department to complete the projects within the stipulated time frame.
(Para 24.2)
14.  The Committee appreciates the efforts being made by the Department of Space for rendering services to farmers,
 fishermen, for urban area town planning, etc. and for publicising its activities, particularly in the developmental and socio-
economic sectors.

 multi faceted space programme. Effort should be made to secure the wider involvement of the industry in marketing and

 The mandate of the Ministry of Environment and Forests entails planning, promotion and coordination of environment
 and forestry programmes. The main activities of the Ministry relate to conservation and control of pollution,
 afforestation and regeneration of forests in degraded areas, protection and conservation of forests, wildlife and
 protection of environment. The tasks are sought to be achieved through environmental impact assessment, eco-
regeneration, assistance to organisations implementing environmental and forestry programmes, enactment of
 environmental legislation, formulation of environmental policies, promotion of environmental and forestry research,
 extension, education and training to augment the requisite manpower, dissemination of environmental awareness
 among all sectors of the country’s population. The activities of the Ministry are divided in four major sectors, i.e.
1. Environment,
2. National River Conservation Directorate,
3. Forests and Wildlife and
4. National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board.

IMPACT OF BIOTIC PRESSURE
26. According to the Forest Survey of India (FSI), 40% of forest area comes under the category of degraded forests. The
 main causes of degradation are excessive grazing and excessive fuel wood collection. Illegal felling for timber and
 encroachments contribute to the problem. According to statistics available, the forest cover in India forms only 1.8% of
 the Global Forest Area. As against this the Forests are required to support 17% of human population and 16-17%
 livestock population. The estimated number of livestock that graze within the forests is estimated at 270 millions. At
 least 30% of the fodder requirement for the livestock is met from the forests. The number of people who are dependent
 on forests for their fuel wood supply is around 226 millions.
27. According to the report entitled "Demand and Supply of fuel wood, timber and fodder in India", published by Forest
 Survey of India, against a demand of 946 Million tons dry and 1136 Millions tons of green fodder, the availability of
 fodder is only 440 Million tons and 292 Million tons respectively. This yawning gap between demand and supply of the
 fodder is instrumental in excessive biotic pressure on forest. Likewise, there is a wide gap between the demand and
 supply of fuel wood in our country. Indian forests today are in a position to supply 17 million tons fuel wood on
 sustainable basis but the actual removal is around 86 million tons.
28. The Committee was apprised of the consequences of grazing on forest Eco-system. Forest grazing has several direct
 effects of which the effect on regeneration of the land is particularly injurious to the small regeneration because of the
 browsing of tender shoots and buds. The indirect damage caused by grazing is mainly on the forest soil itself, the effect
 being in varying proportion depending on the size or weight of the animals, each kind behaving in its own way as it
 moves from one place to another. The foot marks of different species affect differently on the forest land according to
 the light or reverse movement in each case.
29. The Committee was also informed that the removal of excessive fuel wood leads to removal of young saplings and
 poles in the forest area. Excessive lopping affects the crown of the trees and reduces their growth. The resultant over
 exposure of the floor of the forest leads to deterioration of the soil and there is over all decline in the fertility of the
 land. Grazing and excessive removal of saplings and poles also lead to invasion of the forest area by weeds like
 Lantana, Parthenium and Azeratum species. The growth of these weeds further affects the regeneration of forest

 species and also reduces the availability of fodder to the wild animals and to the livestock.
30. The Committee recommends that in order to augment the household income in rural areas and reduce their
 dependence on forests the Ministry should take effective measures towards development of non-timber forests
 resources and also fund projects for carrying out afforestation programme on private lands.
31. The Committee does not fully share the findings of the Survey of India for nature has its own regulatory
 system. Seen in proper perspective, the fuel wood collection by villagers or tribals living near the forests is an
 activity which has been going on ever since the man set its foot on the earth. This activity by tribals or villagers,
 the Committee feels, only helps in the regeneration of the land thus adding indirectly to the growth of the forests.
 Likewise the dry leaves also contribute to the process for they ultimately convert into a kind of manure that is
 conducive to the growth of forests. The Committee does not agree to the view the animal footing and grazing
 affects the tender plants. On the other hand there is a remote possibility of such tender plants being there in a
 dense forest unless they are planted as a part of the planned forestry. In fact, a forest is nothing but a wild
 growth which has sprung up as a part of normal process of the nature. Again, seen in a proper perspective, the
 grazing by animals is indirectly an activity equal to the filling of land which should help the reproductive
 process.
32. The Committee observes that as a result of persistent recommendation of the Committee or otherwise on
 merits the rights of tribals and villagers etc. living near the forests to collect the fuel wood have at least being
 recognized by no less a person than the Prime Minister of the country. The Ministry should therefore fall in line
 and recognize these rights which only help, as stated above, in the growth of forests as part of a natural activity.
33. Animal grazing is also not an activity which would affect the growth of the forests. Apart from what has been
 said above, the animal excreta ultimately converts itself into a kind of manure which would help the growth of
 forests.
34. The Committee further observes that the Ministry should in fact concentrate on organized felling of trees
 undertaken on a large scale by timber smugglers in connivance with the forest authorities. If checked properly,
 this alone would go a long way in saving the forests.
WILDLIFE (PROTECTION) ACT,1972
35. The Committee was informed that the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 in its present form is quite effective,
 particularly, in dealing with persons violating the provision of the Act. According to Section 51 of the Act, punishment
 for violating any of the provisions of the Act may extend to 3 years of imprisonment or with a fine which may extend
 up to Rs.25,000/- or both. In case an offence is committed in relation to any animal specified in Schedule I or Part II of
 Schedule II of the Act or whether the offence relates to hunting in or altering the boundaries of a Sanctuary or a
 National Park, such offence is punishable with imprisonment for a term not less than one year and also with a fine not
 less than Rs.5,000/-. The term of imprisonment can extend up to six years In case of a second or subsequent offence,
 the term of imprisonment can extend to 6 years and shall not be less than 2 years and the amount of fine shall not be
 less than Rs.10,000/-. The term of imprisonment for persons indulging in illegal trade or species included in Schedule I
 or Part n of Schedule II can extend up to 7 years and also with a fine which shall not be less than Rs.5,000/-. In addition
 to the above deterrent measures, there is a provision to forfeit to the State Government any trap, tool vehicle, vessel or
 weapon used in committing the offence.
36. The Committee is of the view that the above mentioned provisions should constantly be kept in view taking
 into account the experiences gained in operation of these provisions. While the Wildlife needs to be protected
 from the onslaughts of the man, a balance has also to be maintained in the penal provisions of the law. The penal
 provisions if they are made more stringent will only encourage corruption. There is a need to discourage the
 tendency of amending the Act on the basis of individual incidents. On the other hand the experience gained over
 a period of time should form the basis of a review of various provisions.

45. The Committee further observes that the situation needs to be monitored continuously and steps such as ban

Recommendations/Observations at Glance
 
1. The Committee recommends that as the schemes under GAP Phase II and NRCP now have an integral

 in water), where standards have been fixed in respect of this parameter in treated sewage. The Committee is of

 towns is a constraint in this regard) which are capable of addressing the microbial pollution adequately should
 be adopted. Treated sewage which is rich in nutrients should be used for irrigation. The Committee feels that

3. The Committee observes that one of the reasons for failure of the Ganga Action Plan Phase-II has been that

 involved on a priority basis in the implementation of GAP Phase II and NRCP. State Governments should be

4. The Committee recommends that as the major problem with regard to the pollution of River Yamuna has
 been lack of minimum flow of water, the Ministry should devise ways and means to constantly monitor the

79th Report on the Information Technology Bill, 1999
 
 The Chairman, Rajya Sabha in pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
 Committees, referred* the Information Technology Bill, 1999**, as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16 th December,
 1999 and pending therein, to the Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment & Forests for
 examination and Report.
2. In the present day world it has been the electronics and now the Information Technology (IT) which influence our life
 the most. There is hardly any area of human endeavour where electronic gadgets have not reached. There is barely any
 industry which does not depend, for its efficiency and productivity, on the application of electronics in its different
 manifestations. Technology has emerged as the vehicle of rapid change in the work culture and the way mankind
 communicates in the century. India has been no exception to this phenomenon. Whether in the field of
 telecommunications, roads, ports or air travel, the hallmark has been more efficient and cost effective technology. Thus
 from slow-moving majestic automobiles the country has moved to smart and fast technologies which have given us
 much more advanced vehicles, coal guzzling steam locomotives which have been replaced by electric traction engines.
3. Information Technology is a product of information age and technology. It is a vehicle for future development,
 opportunities, challenges and competition that enables faster collection and dissemination of information. In the history
 of civilization, no work of science has had so comprehensive an impact on human development as IT. Undoubtedly, IT
 has been the greatest changing agent of this century and promises to play its role even more dramatically in the times to
 come. IT is changing every aspect of human life, breaking old barriers and building new inter connections in the
 emerging global village and becoming the chief determinant of progress of nations and that of individuals. IT is being
 meaningfully employed in railways and airlines, banking, insurance, weather forecasting, radio astronomy, molecular
 biology, aerodynamics, etc. thereby reducing the fatigue and increasing the productivity and efficiency. And in
 education too, IT has a vital role. A large variety of software is available to cater to self-learning and evaluation on
 various subjects.
4. IT is a broad term covering the entire gamut of managing and processing information. Computer hardware, software
 and internet are the tools for the systems that have been designed, developed, supported or managed by IT
 professionals. The discovery of computers and subsequent development of the technology popularly known as
 information technology is one of the most significant achievements of the 20
th century. The role of IT as an instrument
 for progress and development has been acknowledged widely and is expected to bring in major social and economic
 benefits for the mankind and accelerate the process of development.
 
 
 
* Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II, dated the 14
th January, 2000
** Annexure

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/79report.htm[29-08-2018 16:16:19]
5. Andhra Pradesh is an example of how the States in the country can incorporate IT in the day-to-day functioning of the
 Government and re-engineer the manner in which services are provided to citizens. Under its ‘One-stop non-stop’
 approach, a pilot project called Twin cities Integrated Network Service (TWINS) integrated 18 services of six
 departments over one counter. It provides fast and easy access to Government services, makes the access to
 Government much simpler and can also cut down on corruption. It would be naive, of course, to suggest IT as the
 ultimate panacea for corruption, which may find ingenious ways to beat new technology.
6. Today, among the major Asian industrialized countries, India has abundant technically skilled manpower towards
 global IT development. IT is the fastest emerging industrial segment in the country. During the last decade, IT sector
 has registered an unprecedented growth. All the renowned global brands have either established production facilities in
 the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus giving consumer a wider choice
 of products in terms of features, quality and prices.
7. A special Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development involving several agencies at Central
 and State levels has been constituted with a view to keep pace with the latest technology developments abroad. To that
 end Government have taken two major initiatives, one, the formation of IT Ministry at the Central level and second the
 establishment of a Rs.100 crores National Venture Fund for software and IT industry. The IT industry is thus expected
 to play a lead role and serve as a nodal point to facilitate further development of IT industry.
8. Member countries of the United Nations have recognised the need for "Uniformity of laws applicable to alternatives
 to paper-based methods of communications and storage of information". A model law on e-commerce was adopted in
 1996 by the U.N. Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITAL) and the U.N. General Assembly recommended
 to its members in 1997 to give due consideration to this Model Law while enacting or revising their respective Laws.
 The IT Bill, 1999 is a sequel to this U.N. resolution. Malaysia has introduced new comprehensive legislation whereas
 countries like USA, European Union, Singapore, Korea, Japan, UK and Germany have brought out multiple
 amendments to the in existing laws as well as enacted new legislation. Italy, Japan, South Korea, Sweden and UK have
 also introduced Digital Signature laws recently.
9. In India, an Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee under the Chairmanship of the Secretary to the then Department of
 Electronics was set up on 15
th September, 1997 to take stock of draft legislation and formulate a draft Bill on electronic
 data transfer and transactions having regard to international practices. The interim report of the Standing Committee
 recommended amendments in the existing core laws such as the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; the General Clauses Act.,
 1897 and the Indian Penal Code and that there should be a single comprehensive cyber law covering digital signature,
 data protection and computer offences. Hence, the Information Technology(IT) Bill.
10. The IT Bill provides a peripheral framework for e-commerce regime, which comprises of 93 sections divided into
 13 chapters. It includes four schedules which lay down the relative amendments sought to be made to the Indian Penal
 Code, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the Banker’s Evidence Act, 1891, and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The
 13 chapters respectively deal with preliminary matters, digital signature, electronic governance, attribution,
 acknowledgement and dispatch of electronic records, secure electronic records and secure digital signatures, regulation
 of certifying authorities, digital signature certificates, obligations of subscribers, penalties and adjudication, the cyber
 regulations appellate tribunal, offences, network service providers not to be liable in certain cases and miscellaneous
 provisions.
11. The Committee observes that the Bill provides: -
i. to facilitate electronic communication by means of reliable electronic records;
ii. to facilitate electronic inter-action in trade and commerce, eliminate barriers to electronic commerce resulting
 from uncertainties over writing and signature
requirements, and to promote the development of the legal and business
infrastructure necessary to implement secure electronic commerce;

iii. to facilitate electronic filing of documents with government agencies and statutory corporations, and to promote
 efficient delivery of government services by means of reliable electronic records;
iv. to minimise the incidence of forged electronic records, intentional and unintentional alteration of records, and
 fraud, forgery or falsification in electronic commerce and other electronic transactions;
v. to help establish uniformity of rules, regulations and standards regarding the authentication and integrity of
 electronic records or documents; and
vi. to promote public confidence in the integrity and reliability of electronic records and electronic commerce, and to
 foster ‘the development of electronic commerce through the use of electronic signatures to lend authenticity and
 integrity to correspondence in any electronic medium.
vii. To provide for a Cyber Regulations Advisory Committee consisting of a Chairperson and such other number of
 official and non-official members as may be prescribed by rules to be made by the Central Government.
viii. to provide for penalties for contravention of the regulations made under the Act.
ix. To provide for the establishment of Cyber Regulations appellate Tribunal with the same composition and powers
 as that of the appellate Tribunal constituted under the Securities Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 and to hear
 appeals from the decisions of the Adjudicating Officers.
x. to provide for the deposit of the penalty amount as a prerequisite for filing of appeal before the Appellate
 Authority.

13. The Secretary and the Representatives of the Ministry of Information Technology apprised the Committee about the
 need to provide legal recognition to transactions carried out by
means of electronic data interchange and other means of electronic communication and the developments leading to the
 drafting of the Bill.
14. In the meetings of the Committee, Chairman, Telecom Commission made a presentation on the subject matter of the
 Bill and expressed their concern on the issue of "Convergence" of the Telecommunication, Broadcasting and
 Information Technology, as intended to be covered under the Bill. According to him, the convergence of technologies
 will result in the dilution of the boundaries between different sectors and it may be difficult to distinguish the computer
 networks’ as defined in the Bill from the telecom network. Therefore, the issues and concerns relating to security and
 privacy of information in the Bill would be more or less similar to the concerns in the area of telecommunications and
 distribution of encrypted TV or Radio programmes. The Secretary, Ministry of Information & Broadcasting also
 echoed the same apprehension. The Chairman, Telecom Commission also suggested for inclusion of word "voice" in
 the definition of "information" as given in clause 2(u) of the Bill to avoid any overlapping with the provisions of the
 Indian Telegraph Act; and to fix a time limit for retention of electronic records in clause 7 of the Bill. In response to the
 latter, Member Secretary, Law Commission of India submitted that the provision of Public Records Act will mutatis
 mutandis apply to this Act. Moreover, the electronic records automatically start vanishing after 5-6 years.
15. The Representatives of the Indian Music Industry and the National Association of Software and Service Companies
 (NASSCOM) also appeared before the Committee on the subject matter of the Bill. Both the representatives expressed
 the need for deletion of clause 78 of the Bill as the same appears to be in conflict with the provisions of the Copyright
 Act. Moreover, in view of the defence of due diligence and knowledge being available under clause 78, representatives
 were of the view that it was difficult to book the violators as clause 78 merely required a Network Service Provider
 with knowledge of an offence to prove that it exercised due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence. The
 Indian Music Industry submitted that the tests of lack of knowledge or of due diligence as stipulated in clause 78 of the
 IT Bill were not precise and objective and a Network Service Provider (NSP) or intermediary could rely upon clause 78

Recommendation

      As a nodal agency for the National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), Department of Space
has been interacting with the user agencies through various Standing Committees under NNRMS to co-ordinate

and private entrepreneurs.  The responsibility of DOS is limited to helping the users in generating appropriate
information using satellite remote se nsing and collateral data for optimum  exploitation of natural resources. 
Ultimately, it is the user department s, which have to make use of the information made av ailable from remote
sensing for ground level implementation.  It is the end eavor of DOS to lay emphasis on mapping of natural
resources and assist in sustainable utilisation of the resources.  For example, in the area of ground water resources,
which are fast depleting, the Ministry of Rural Deve lopment under the National Dr inking Water Mission, has

 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Eighty-fifth Report on the Action
 Taken by the Department of Ocean Development on the recommendations contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Committee on
 Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Ocean Development.
 
            The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Ocean Development  on the recommendations
 contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology,
 Environment & Forests on the Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Department of Ocean Development  which was presented to
 the Rajya Sabha on 24th April, 2000.
 
            There are fourteen recommendations contained in the Seventy-sixth Report of the Committee.  Action Taken Notes on the
 recommendations of the Committee, were received from the Department on 20th  December, 2000.
