SPACE TRANSPORTATION
34.        Space Transportation system includes the satellite launch vehicles to place satellites like INSAT and IRS and scientific
 satellites in the required orbits as well as the sounding rockets for carrying out short duration scientific experiments.  India made a
 modest beginning in this area with the launch of a 75 mm diameter sounding rocket in 1963 for investigation of ionosphere over the
 geo-magnetic equator over Thumba, near Thiruvananthapuram.  Since then, the country has established a substantial capability in the
 design, development and operationalisation of a series of sounding rockets for scientific investigations, Polar Satellite Launch
 Vehicle (PSLV), for launching Indian remote sensing satellites and Geo-synchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV), for
 launching geo-stationary communication satellites.
            The maiden developmental flight of GSLV-D1 on April 18, 2001 which successfully injected the GSAT-1 satellite in Geo-
synchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO) is a historic milestone for the Indian Space Programme.  This has validated the complex vehicle
 and mission design aspects, soundness of a number  of new vehicle systems such as cryo stage, liquid strap-ons, hot separation of
 first stage,  large diameter payload firing, launch hold release mechanism, launch pad facilities for handling and filling earth storable
 and cryogenic stage has been completed and based on its outcome the preparation for the second developmental flight of GSLV is in
 progress.  The subsequent flights, GSLV-D2 and GSLV-D3, respectively carrying G.SAT-2 and G.SAT-3, are targeted for launch in
 the timeframe 2002-2003.
35.        The objective Cryo Upper Stage (CUS) Project is to realize an indigenous cryogenic stage employing liquid oxygen and
 liquid hydrogen as oxidizer and fuel respectively for upper stage of GSLV.  In this technologically complex area, significant
 developmental efforts have been carried out resulting in the realization of the second cryogenic engine.  A series of ground
 qualification tests are planned to evaluate the engine.  The first flight of indigenous cryo stage is targeted for flight-testing by GSLV
 in 2003-2004.
The budgetary allocation amounting to Rs.16.38 crores for Cryogenic Upper Stage Project (CUSP) in BE 2002-03 are less as
 compared to Rs.21.30 crores and Rs.20.31 crores at BE and RE stages respectively in 2001-02. Asked whether this would affect the
 project adversely the Department informed  that the total budget approved for the Cryogenic Upper Staged Project was  of Rs.335.89
 crores. The cumulative expenditure of the project till March 2002 is Rs.288.48 crores i.e. Rs.85.9%. As substantial part of the total
 project cost has already been incurred, the budget sought in BE 2002-03 is relatively less compared to RE provision of last year. The
 budget provision in 2002-03 is based on the planned progress in engine and stage fabrication activities and hence does not affect the
 project’s progress, though it appears less compared to RE of last year.
36.        The successful launch of PSLV-C3/TES mission on October 22, 2001, was a significant milestone in the operational PSLV
 programme.  The mission met all its objectives by placing into desired orbit the main satellite – Technology Experimental Satellite
 (TES) of India and in addition two auxiliary satellites, Project for on-Board Autonomy (PROBA) of Belgium and Bispectral and
 Infrared Remote Detection (BIRD) of Germany, on a commercial basis.  With  this, PSLV has once again demonstrated the multiple
 satellite launching capability.  One significant feature of this mission was the orbit-raising manoeuvre carried out for PROBA for
 placing it in an elliptical orbit, different from the orbit of the main satellite.  A high-performance composite solid propellant upper
 stage motor for PSLV has been successfully test fired.  The PSLV C4-C6 flights are targeted for completion in 2002-2004.
37.        The Secretary informed the Committee that DOS was working on several critical technologies, which are related to Reusable
 Launch Vehicle System.  This would bring down the cost of space transport.  In this direction the Department is currently working on
 the concepts of the Reusable Transportation Vehicle, including engines, air breathing and so on.  The Secretary further informed that
 the Department has also started working on Space Capsule Recovery Module.  Explaining this he said that the idea was to place a
 Capsule in space and use it for some experiments and then retrieve it back to earth. 
38.        In the area of Launch Vehicle Development, the Committee desires that DOS should strive to complete the development
 flights and operationalise the GSLV (with indigenous cryogenic upper stage) for launching 2T INSAT class of satellites. 
 Considering the trend towards going for bigger and heavier spacecraft for satellite communications, the Department should  initiate
 development of an advanced GSLV Mk III capable of launching 4T INSAT class of satellite.  Besides, in tune with the long-term

 technology demonstrator in the areas of air breathing propulsion technology and space capsule recovery missions could be planned.

50.        International co-operation has been an important aspect of India’s Space Programme.  DOS has entered into agreements or
 signed memoranda of understanding with several countries and space agencies.  These include: Australia, Brunei, Canada, European
 Space Agency, France, Germany, Hungary, Indonesia, Peru, Russia, Syria, Sweden, Italy, Norway, U.K., U.S.A, and Ukraine.
 During the year, MOU’s were signed with China and Thailand and the MOU with European Space Agency (ESA), renewed.
            ISRO and the French National Space Agency (CNES) have entered the Phase-B of the joint satellite mission, “Megha
 Tropiques”, which is aimed at the study of the tropical atmosphere and climate.  The mission envisages joint development of
 scientific instruments to be carried on a French satellite platform (Proteus) and the satellite is programmed to  be launched by India’s
 PSLV in 2006.
            The Modular Opto-electronic Scanner (MOS) instrument from the German Aerospace Centre (DLR) which was flown on the
 Indian Remote Sensing Satellite, IRS P3, launched on India’s PSLV continues to provide valuable data.  The data was being received
 and analysed  by scientists in India.
51.          India plays an active role in several international bodies such as the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of
 Outer Space (UN-COPUOS).  United Nations Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (UN-ESCAP), the
 international COSPAS-SARSAT system for search and rescue operations, the International Astronautical Federation (IAF), the
 Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS), the Committee on Space Research (COSPAR), the Inter Agency Debris
 Coordination Committee (IADC), the Space Frequency Coordination Group (SFGC), the Coordinating Group on Meteorological
 Satellites (CGMS), the International Global Observing Strategy (IGOS), the International Space University (ISU), the Asian
 Association for Remote Sensing (AARS) and the International Society for Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing (ISPRS).
52.        India has been selected by the United Nations for establishing the Centre for Space Science & Technology Education in Asia
 and the Pacific (CSSTE-AP) which was formally inaugurated on November 1, 1995, at New Delhi.  The centre has been established
 around the facilities of the Indian Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS), Dehradun, Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad and
 Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), Ahmedabad.  The Centre offers Post-Graduate education courses, leading to award of
 M.Tech/M.Sc(Tech) degrees in Remote Sensing and Geographical Information Systems, Satellite Communications, Satellite
 Meteorology and Space Sciences to students of different countries in the region.

 spin-off applications, which could be of direct relevance to the common man.  Also, the moon is going to be the target of

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred-First Report of the
 Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Department of Ocean Development
 (Demand No.91).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 9
th April, 2002 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of Ocean
 Development gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects
 of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the Members
 and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean
 Development.
 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on  2
nd May, 2002.
 
NEW DELHI;                                                                                                   C.RAMACHANDRAIAH,
May 2, 2002                                                                                                                               Chairman,
                                                                            CommitteeonScience&Technology,Environment & Forests.
       
R E P O R T
           
            India has a long maritime history.  The peninsula is surrounded by the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean.  The

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/101streport.htm[29-08-2018 16:20:40]
 vast coastline of the mainland and islands is about 7,500 kms.  It’s territory includes, 1,256 islands.  The area of Exclusive Economic
 Zone (EEZ) of the country is 2.02 million sq. km. the vast coastal and offshore environment support a wide variety of marine
 ecosystem rich in species diversity and multifarious economic development activities.  The sea has tremendous influence on the
 physical and meteorological conditions of the country.  Appreciating the importance of the subject, Government of India established
 Department of Ocean Development in 1981 with an aim to create a deeper understanding of the oceanic regime of the northern and
 central Indian Ocean and also to develop technology and technological aids for harnessing of resources and understanding of various
 physical, chemical and biological processes.  The Ocean policy statement was also enunciated in 1982.
2.The Department of Ocean Development is the nodal Department for organising, coordinating and promoting development activities
 relating to ocean development in the country.  The national level R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the
 Department in carrying out its multi-disciplinary plans and programmes of national importance.  Further, marine research and
 capacity building is one of the key areas of the Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance. Hence, the
 activities of the Department are targeted towards scientific research and technology development with orientation towards its
 applications and harnessing ocean resources. The Department has also mandate towards international programmes arising out of
 international obligations and bilateral and multilateral cooperative ventures to create a technological capacity building and human
 resource development for self-reliance.
3.The programmes of the Department are directed towards:
Technology Development for future applications with strategic, industrial and economic significance.
Society with direct/indirect benefit for the community by technology applications and pilot project demonstration with the
 participation of the community for their socio-economic prosperity, and for coastal area development.
Marine Resource for exploration of marine living and non-living resources, techno-economic studies to evolve strategies for
 sustainable exploration and utilization, and resource enhancement.
Multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary Polar Science Programmes and Antarctic Expeditions with scientific and geo-political
 significance.
Capacity Building towards self-reliance through basic scientific research in ocean sector, human resource development and
 establishing Centres of Excellence in academic institutions.
Creation of pubic awareness of ocean development, its immense potential and diverse uses.
 
 BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
4.         A sum of Rs.142 crores was allocated as B.E. to the Department of Ocean Development for the year 2001-02.  This was
 reduced to Rs.120 crores at RE stage which forced the Department to scale down most of its activities last year except in the case of
 National Institute of
Ocean Technology (NIOT) where more funds were required to carry out the task of operationalising 1 MW Ocean Thermal Energy
 Conversion (OTEC) plant. However, for the year 2002-03, total budget allocation for the programmes and activities of the
 Department has been placed at Rs.199.28 crores which includes Rs.175.00 crores (Plan) and Rs.24.28 crores (Non-plan). The plan
 outlay is Rs.33 crores more than the plan outlay of the last year. The following areas have been identified to be focussed in the year
 2002-03:-
The approved outlay for the Antarctic Research is placed at Rs.26.50 crores, which  would be given as Grants-in-aid to National
 Centre for Antarctic & Ocean Research (NCAOR) for launching the 22
nd Scientific Expedition to Antarctica, carrying out scientific
 experiments, maintenance of the permanent research station “Maitri” at Antarctica and operation and manning of the NCAOR, Goa.
In the case of Poly Metallic Nodules (PMN) programme, an outlay of Rs.20 crores has been provided.
For the mission mode programmes of National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) including Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion
 (OTEC), an outlay of Rs.7.80 crores has been provided. The Expenditure Finance Committee has approved an outlay of Rs.35.25
 crore for OTEC programmes which was revised to Rs.61.13 crores. The pilot plant which was scheduled for commissioning in
 March, 2001, could not be done due to an operational mishap in the sea and will now be implemented by December, 2002. The
 activities of OTEC and other programmes on Technology for sea bed mining, coastal engineering and marine instrumentation will be
 continued in this year.
An outlay of Rs.7.10 crores has proposed for Marine Living Resources Programme.  Besides, an amount of Rs.2 crores is proposed to
 be allocated for the ongoing Drugs from Sea programme. During the year 2002-03, a provision of Rs.1.15 crore has been made for
 Marine Non-Living Resources. An outlay of Rs.25.00 crores has been provided for the Ocean Observation & Information Services.
 Out of this, the provision for the Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad is Rs.11 crores and
 for the National Data Buoy programme and the other Ocean Observing System programmes, a sum of Rs.10 crores has been
 provided.
An outlay of Rs.2 crores and Rs.5 crores has been made for Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction Systems (COMAPS) and
 Coastal Research Vessel (CRV) respectively during the Annual Plan 2002-03. For the Integrated Coastal and Marine Area
 Management (ICMAM) Programme, an outlay of       Rs.5 crores has been provided for 2002-2003. 
In line with the guidelines provided by the Island Development Authority the Department has made a provision of Rs.0.75 crores for

POLAR SCIENCE (ANTARCTIC RESEARCH) PROGRAMME
11.       The objectives of Antarctic research programme is to identify and initiate programmes of scientific and economic significance
 besides establishing infrastructure. The Programme, which was initiated in 1981, has culminated into a major national programme
 that has a distinct multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary approach.  The objective of the Antarctic mission is to plan, promote, co-
ordinate and execute the entire gamut of polar science and logistic activities of the country, in order to ensure a perceptible and
 influential presence of India in Antarctica. So far 22 scientific expeditions have been launched on a regular basis including two
 expeditions to the Southern Ocean one to Weddel Sea and another one for assessment of Antarctic Krill, which have carried out
 research work in the thrust areas of polar science.  Till date, more than 55 national institutions have participated in the scientific and
 logistic components of the expedition thereby putting about 1425 Indians to the icy continent. With this year’s allocation of Rs.26.50
 crores, the Department proposes to augment the research facilities at Indian Antarctic Station and also to actively undertake research
 in the Southern Ocean Oceanography area.
12.The Committee was informed that a modern and indigenously build station ‘Maitri’ established in Schirmacher Oasis in 1988 has
 replaced the first Indian station, Dakshin Gangotri that was established on the ice-shelf in 1984.  Maitri is equipped to provide
 comfortable living facilites for 25 persons on a year round basis and has eight permanent observations and several laboratories to
 carry out research in the frontier areas of Antarctic Science.  Since ‘Maitri’ has already withstood 12 years of Antarctic weather and
 gradually a number of shortcomings were being noticed with the station, the Department was planning to establish a new station
 during the Tenth plan, replacing the ‘Maitri’,  with an estimated cost of  Rs.75 crores. 
13.The success of the Antarctic Programme and sustained capabilities in Antarctic science and logistics promoted the Department to
 establish the first polar research lab of the country at Goa namely the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) since
 1998 which is responsible for carrying out all the activities relating to Antarctic expeditions. The research on polar science and
 expeditions to Antarctica was being planned, executed and launched annually on behalf of DOD by the Centre.  The Centre has a
 specific R&D mandate in the realms of polar science and to coordinate and launch Indian Antarctic expeditions.  The Centre has a
 unique laboratory for low-temperature research on ice cores retrieved from Antarctica and the Himalayas.  It would also have the
 facility for the application of remote sensing techniques aimed to understand the sea-ice-atmosphere interaction in the Polar Regions. 
 It would also have an Antarctic museum and a database repository on polar sciences. During 2002-03, the Centre would co-ordinate
 all the activities related to launching of the XXII Indian Antarctic Expedition.
14.During the year 2002-03, NCAOR plans to coordinate and launch the XXII Indian Scientific Expedition to Antarctica through a
 multi-institutional and multi-disciplinary approach. Moreover, efforts would be made to induct state-of-the-art experiments in
 accordance with the long-term science strategy for the Antarctic expeditions.
15.The Secretary, DOD informed the Committee that Scientific research in Antarctica was of  National and global importance. 
 Besides, important research work had been done in the areas of Earth Sciences, Atmospheric Sciences etc.  which were of
 significance to the country,  for example the research in meteorology and atmospheric sciences helped in understanding the
 relationship between Polar weather and the Indian monsoon.  Biotechnology research helped in identification of low temperature
 genes available in Antarctic microorganisms that would be coned to mesophilic bacteria.  The Antarctic programme had also helped
 the Indian Army in acquiring skills and knowledge relating to operations of vehicles and machineries under extreme cold conditions.
16.The Committee is of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National Centre for
 Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as assessment of
 biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial consortium and productivity and
 ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes. It should also envisage initiating meaningful logistics operation with other countries
 which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
17.The Committee is further of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR), being the nodal
 Department to execute the Antarctic Programmes should strive to further expand its infrastructure facilities for carrying out research
 in the realms of Polar Sciences and Southern Ocean Oceanography. Besides, the Centre should also initiate its activities related to
 establishing the  Country’s first ice-core repository and analytical facilities with focus on high-resolution histories of fact changes in
 climate, atmospheric composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
18.The Department should pass on the data collected about the impact of cold climate on human body to defence establishments to
 facilitate treatment of soldiers stationed in cold regions or for such other uses as might be required in the national interest.

 of  Mumbai which was due to  treatment of sewage as well as disposal of sewage in the deep sea through out falls.  Similarly, in Puri,

DRUG FROM SEA
29.The major objectives of the programme include:–
Systematic exploration of the entire coastline and collections made from deep sea as well for identification of more flora and fauna
 having potential for extraction of drugs and chemicals.
Collection, extraction and biological evaluation of 150 species, and evaluation of biologically potential organisms, leading to possible
 development of new drug(s).
Isolation of bioactive constituents and development as possible drugs.
Development of suitable models for biological activity in certain priority areas.
Undertaking regulatory pharmacology and toxicology of 2-3 extracts.
Initiation and completion of clinical trials for at least two drugs.
Development of at least 2 herbal drugs from the samples and marketing.
Industrial participation in drug development and marketing.
30.The Committee was informed that drug development takes nearly 8-10 years as there were several phases in drug discovery and
 development that costs about 600 million USD for each drug developed.  The ‘Drugs from Sea’ programme was initiated in 1990,
 while the  developed countries initiated this programme in the early ‘60s.  Even then, so far not even a single drug has been put in the
 market by any country.  6 to 7 products were currently in Phase II clinical trials of drug development but none of these have yet
 entered the Phase III clinical trials i.e., the final development stage. 
31.  Under the programme one lead was taken up for product development in 1996-97, but after two years of intensive research
 activities; it was found that the preparation had an unanticipated toxic effect leading to faecolith formation in the monkeys during
 chronic toxicity studies.  Therefore, efforts were made to detoxify the preparation, which took considerable time.  Finally a
 preparation  was  isolated  which  demonstrated  antidiabetic  activity  and  was  also  found  to be largely safe.  This new preparation
 is free from any side effect and has wide margin of safety.  This antidiabetic preparation was now entering clinical safety-cum-
efficacy in humans.  If found safe and effective in humans, we should be ready with this drug for marketing in next 2-3 years.   CDRI
 might also succeed in coming out with one more drug with cholesterol-lowering properties. Under the programme, so far no antiviral
 preparations have been developed.  Instead, it was only antifungal lead that has been taken up.
32.       The Committee feels there is need to concentrate efforts on the project with a view to develop the drugs as expeditiously as
 possible.

 containing the activities, namely (i) Development of Geographic Information System (GIS) based information system for 11 critical
 habitats in the coastal and marine Areas in India (II) Determination of Waste Assimilation Capacity at selected estuaries along

47.       During the year 2002-2003, more activities like shore line management and ecosystem modeling would be initiated apart from
 the continuation of the ongoing activities.  An allocation of Rs.5 crores has been made for this purpose.
48.       The Committee observes the need to focus on programmes aimed at imparting training to coastal states on use of geographic
 information system (GIS) for management of critical habitats.
GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (GIS) FOR CRITICAL HABITATS
49.       The Department seeks to develop an information system using GIS for 11 critical habitats namely, Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of
 Khambat, Malvan, Kadamat, Karwar Islands, Cochin Islands, Gulf of Mannar, Pitchavaram, Coringa, Gahirmatha and Sunderbans. 
 The tasks involved in the development of such an information system include, review of data on the habitats available; preparation of
 methodology manual; field data collection; creation of GIS database; and designing of a GIS module and integration of database.
50.       The Committee was informed that after collection of field data and development of database, a GIS based information system
 for Pitchavaram mangrove, namely Critical Habitat Information System (CHIS) has been completed and a compact disc has been
 produced and released. Use of GIS in the CHIS helped detection of the areas of degradation of mangrove and areas of recovery. The
 CHIS for Kadmat Island of Lakshadweep, 7 islands off Karwar and 21 islands of Gulf of Mannar were nearing completion.
 Development of GIS for the other 7 habitats was in advanced stages and would be completed by the end of the year.
OCEAN OBSERVATIONS AND INFORMATION SERVICES (OOIS) 
51.       During the examination of Demands for Grants (2002-03) the Committee was informed that in order to generate user-oriented
 data products and provide services to cater the needs of the coastal and ocean sectors, an integrated programme called “Ocean
 Observations and Information Services (OOIS)” was being implemented by the Department. The OOIS envisages generation and
 dissemination of reliable coastal and ocean data products such as waves, winds, temperature, current, salinity, upwelling, potential
 fishing zone information, coastal maps, etc. to support coastal and off-shore development activities and for furthering quality
 oceanographic research. Besides, it seeks to provide ocean information services for various applications in the ocean section. 
52.       The programme consists of four major components viz. Ocean Observing Systems, Ocean Information Services, Satellite
 Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) and Indian Ocean Dynamics & Modeling (INDOMOD).
53.       The Ocean Observing Systems envisage collection of sea truth data using moored data buoys, drifting buoys, expandable
 bathythermographs (XBT), current meter arrays and tide gauges, and designed particularly for acquisition of real-time sea surfaces,
 meteorological land upper oceanographic parameters from the coastal and deep waters.  Validation of the satellite sensors has also
 been undertaken using the sea truth data generated under this programme.  The Data Buoy Programme was initiated in 1996 with
 partial financial assistance from Norwegian Agency for Development (NORAD) and National Institute of Ocean Technology
 (NIOT).  It has been entrusted with the responsibilities for deployment, operation and maintenance of the data buoys.  A set of 12
 buoys were procured from M/s OCEANOR, Norway out of which, seven were moored in the coastal waters and five in the off-shore
 waters.  The buoys were equipped with state-of-the-art sensors for accurate measurement of winds, waves, currents, atmospheric
 pressure, atmospheric temperature, sea surface temperature, dissolved oxygen, chlorophyll, radioactivity, hydrocarbon and turbidity.
 The data Buoy will continue as Govt. of India (GOI) programme.
54.       The Ocean Information Service envisages generation and dissemination of ocean data/data products on an operational basis. 
 Data products in the form of Sea Surface Temperature maps, Potential Fishing Zone maps, wind vector maps, mixed layer depth-
maps, at least on heat-budget are proposed to be made available.  It is also planned to develop ocean state forecasting system; initially
 on an experimental basis.  Services will be offered in the form of coastal wetland maps, shoreline change maps, and close contour
 coastal area maps etc.  which were needed for coastal zone management activities.  The Indian National Centre for Ocean
 Information and Services (INCOIS) at Hyderabad is working as an autonomous society for efficient development and dissemination
 of Data products.
The Satellite Coastal and Oceanographic Research (SATCORE) component envisages development of regional algorithms, data
 assimilation techniques and operational models which would be transferred to the Ocean Information and Service Centre for
 operational use.  The Ocean Modeling and Dynamics (INDMOD) project addresses basic issues on the ocean dynamic, climate
 variability, ocean state forecast, sea level variations, ocean flux studies etc.  These R&D projects are expected to provide basic
 models that could explain the dynamics of the Indian ocean and form an essential input in designing system for ocean state forecast.
56.       The budgetary allocation of Rs.25 for the year 2002-2003 crores would be utilized for procurement of new buoys,
 maintenance of existing buoys, modeling of oceanic phenomena and setting up of infrastructure at the Indian National Centre for
 Ocean Information Services, Hyderabad.
57.       The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), being the nodal agency for providing coastal and ocean
 data and value added products to the users, the Department should monitor the performance and work-mechanism of the INCOIS to
 process and disseminate ocean data and data products to user communities like fisheries, weather, climate, ports, shipping etc. on a
 regular basis so that ocean weather forecasting is precise.
MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING
58.       The objectives of the programme are to foster the concept of stewardship through education, training and human resource
 development and increasing awareness at all levels. The activities proposed in the programme include promotion of research under
 the basic categories of marine  ecology,  marine biology,  marine  microbiology,  marine benthos,  coastal marine culture systems,
 marine geology/geophysics and ocean engineering & underwater robotics. Besides the ongoing programme of award of fellowships
 to students for pursuing higher studies in academic/educational institutions in various disciplines of ocean science and technology,
 and organizing exhibitions and fairs to create awareness among the public on ocean would continue.

59.       The Committee feels that the Department should focus its efforts in assisting Universities to create infrastructure facilities and
 building up a skilled human resource base in Marine Sciences. Moreover, the Department should also participate and showcase its
 activities in national and international level exposition, exhibition, fairs etc. from time to time. Inter-active computer generated
 information on Ocean Science & Technology could perhaps help educate the public on the ocean and its resources.
ARRAY FOR REAL-TIME GEOTROPIC OCEANOGRAPHY (ARGO) PROGRAMME
60.       The array for Real-time Geotropic Oceanography (ARGO) is an internationally coordinated programme for deployment of an
 array  of 3000 profiling floats at a spatial resolution of 3” X 3” (300km X 300 km) to measure temperature and salinity profiles of the
 upper ocean (up to a depth of 2000 m), periodically.  These temperature and salinity profiles are expected to improve the
 understanding of the oceanic processes and contribute to improved prediction of climate variability.
61.       The ARGO floats, equipped with pressure, temperature and salinity sensors, would drift up to a depth of about 2000 m and
 popup to the surface every 10 days for a short period to transmit the data in near real-time via Satellite to ground stations.  The
 expected life of an ARGO float is four years.
62.       Data from the global array of profiling floats would be put on GTS immediately to enable it use in operational forecasting. 
 Delayed mode data, after detailed quality control checks by the ARGO Data Centres, would be available within a few months via
 internet.  The expected life of each float is about 4 years.
63.       India is participating in the ARGO Programme and plans to deploy 150 floats in the North Indian Ocean (north of 10 S). 
 INCOIS was assigned the overall responsibility for implementation of India ARGO Programme.  A Canadian ARGO float deployed
 successfully by INCOIS onboard FORV Sagar Sampada Vessel in December 2001 is providing good quality data.  Data from 20
 ARGO floats currently deployed in the Indian Ocean by different countries are being archived at INCOIS.  This data would be made
 available to the scientific community through INCOIS ocean portal.  INCOIS participated in the International ARGO Science Team
 meeting.  Study on “Analysis and Synthesis for Indian Ocean ARGO Programme” was initiated jointly by Indian Institute of Science
 and INCOIS.  A Project Report for the Indian ARGO Programme (150 Floats) by INCOIS.
64.       The International Argo programme, endorsed by World meteorological Organisation (WMO) and intergovernmental
 Oceanographic Commission (IOC) is directed by an International Argo Science Team.  The international ocean community plans to
 deploy 3000 ARGO Floats in a phased manner by the year 2002 to give a global coverage at a spacing of 300 km.
65.       The Indian Ocean would be covered by about 450 Argo floats.  Of this, India plans to contribute 150 Floats, Australia,
 Canada, China, France, Germany, Japan, UK and USA have committed to deploy Argo Floats in the Indian Ocean Region.
66.       The Implementation planning meeting for Argo in the Indian Ocean was held in Hyderabad, India in July, 2001 where
 representatives from 17 countries and 6 International Organisations participated.  India was identified as (i) the Regional Coordinator
 and (ii) the Regional Data Centre for the Indian Ocean.
67.       The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), an autonomous body under the Department of Ocean
 Development (DOD) is the implementing agency for the programme.
68.       After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and assessing the progress of various
 important programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the budgetary allocation of Rs. 199.28
 crores, as sought by the Department for the year 2002-2003, under Demand No. 91, may be approved.
RECOMMENDATIONS / OBSERVATIONS AT GLANCE
 
1.         The Committee observes that there were major variations in the budgetary allocations and their utilization.  The non-utilisation
 of the allocation meant less or reduced activities of the Department.  The Committee is not happy with the reasons advanced by the
 Department for the non- utilization of funds which includes delay in transfer of foreign consultation, change of priorities, delay in
 initiating discussion with the neighbouring countries, non approval and uncertainty of elements.  The Committee feels that the
 Department should have foreseen these difficulties before asking for budgetary allocation and should have evolved suitable
 mechanism to monitor the budgetary proposal and its allocations.
(Para 7)
2.         The Committee commends the efforts being made by the Department in utilising the services of two vessels. However, in view
 of decommissioning of existing vessels after another 10 years, it is time to plan for acquiring new vessels  which can cater to shallow
 water survey, data buoy maintenance and provide a platform for various coastal and deep ocean activities and other requirements
 which could reasonably be foreseen in the years ahead . The new vessels would not only serve as a platform for the programmes
 envisaged in the Tenth plan but also serve as a utility vessel which might augment the capacity requirements for programmes on the
 marine living and non-living resources.
(Para 10)
3.         The Committee is further of the view that in addition to on-going programmes in various domains of polar sciences, National
 Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR) should also initiate cutting-edge experiments in such frontier areas as assessment of
 biotechnological potential of Antarctic microbes, biodegradation of organic wastes using microbial consortium and productivity and
 ecosystem dynamics in the Antarctic lakes. It should also envisage initiating meaningful logistics operation with other countries
 which could lead to operational and financial cooperation.
(Para 16)
4.         The Committee is of the view that the National Centre for Antarctic Ocean Research (NCAOR), being the nodal Department
 to execute the Antarctic Programmes should strive to further expand its infrastructure facilities for carrying out research in the realms
 of Polar Sciences and Southern Ocean Oceanography. Besides, the Centre should also initiate its activities related to establishing the 
 Country’s first ice-core repository and analytical facilities with focus on high-resolution histories of fact changes in climate,
 atmospheric composition and ice-cover in Antarctica.
(Para 17)
5.         The Department should pass on the data collected about the impact of cold climate on human body to defence establishments
 to facilitate treatment of soldiers stationed in cold regions or for such other uses as might be required in the national interest.

 INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, Environment &
 Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this One Hundred-Second Report of
 the Committee.  This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2002-2003) of the Department of Science &
 Technology (Demand No.70).
 
2.         In the meeting of the Committee held on the 10
th  April, 2002 the Secretary and other Officers of the Department of
 Science & Technology gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on
 various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants.
 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by the
 Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the
 Department of Science & Technology.

       R E P O R T
 
            The Department of Science and Technology (DST) was established with the primary objective of promoting new areas of
 Science and Technology and to play the role of a nodal department for organising, co-coordinating and promoting S&T activities
 in the country.  The mandate given to DST includes, among others:Formulation of policy statements and guidelines on
 S&TPromotion of new areas of scientific researchCo-ordination of inter-departmental S&T effortsSupport basic and applied
 research in universities and other institutionsInternational S&T Co-operationSupport high quality research in autonomous
 bodiesCatalyzing S&T interaction in societal programmes, and entrepreneurship development Science popularisation,
 communication and S&T Management Information SystemPromotion of Commercialisation of home grown technologySupport
 to technology development programmes, technology information andassessmentProviding services in the areas of:Surveying &
 Mapping by Survey of India & National Atlas & Thermatic Mapping Organisation. Meterology by India Meteorological
 Department & National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting. Technology Development and Application by
 Technology Development Board. The Committee was apprised of the recent initiatives taken by the Department for Innovation
 Foundation in order to promote grass root level invention, Swarnajayanti Fellowships for outstanding young scientists, Fund for
 Improvement of S&T Infrastructure (FIST) in universities and related Institutions, Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan, Technopreneur
 Promotion Program (TePP), Indian Climate Research, Establishing high performance computing network facilities for research
 purposes Executed Joint Technology Development projects with industry and socio-economic Ministries, Strengthen Seismcity
 programme, Modernizing autonomous research institutions, Setting up of a National Accreditation Board for Testing and
 Calibration (NABL), Setting up a Patent Facilitating Cell in order to provide support to scientists and technologists on all aspects
 of patenting.
2.

 assured an increased allocation to Science & Technology up to two percent of GNP in a period of five years.

4.         It was further stated that the increase in Plan provision of 2001-02 as compared to R.E. 2001-02 was mainly due to
 increased allocation for ‘Research and Development Support’ as also Aided Institutions.  Two new Mission Mode Projects viz.
 Seismology and Technology for Bamboo Products were also to be taken up with an allocation of Rs.30.00 crores.  Similarly,
 under Non-Plan, there were increases largely under Survey of India; India Meteorological Department; Autonomous Institutes
 and Professional Bodies; Secretariat and National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation mainly to cater to the enhanced
 level of expenditure under Salaries, Traveling Expenses and Other Expenditure viz; Telephone, Postages, Stationery,
 Petrol/Diesel, etc.
5.         It appears that there is no allocation in the current year for  R&D programmes.  When asked to explain this phenomenon,
 the department informed that all programmes of R&D have been integrated under the scheme ‘Research & Development
 Support’. Besides, the activities like Instrument Development has been merged in Technology Development Programme (TDP)
 for which a plan provision of Rs.23.00 crores has been proposed for the year 2002-03.
6.         When asked about increase in allocation by Rs.3.14 crores to Indian Association for Cultivation of Science (IACS),
 Calcutta, the Department informed the Committee that IACS was a premier institute working in the advanced areas of science
 like Molecular Science, Physics and Chemistry of Materials and Biological Sciences.  The research programmes for which
 additional grants have been allocated include:
(a)        Programmes in advanced nano-materials and condensed matter physics were critical dependent on the ready availability of
 liquid Helium.
(b)        Biocomputing and computational genomics were two major programmes to be taken up which require setting up of
 parallel computing facility and replacing the present low speed LAN by a high speed one.
(c)        Femto Chemistry and Single Molecule Spectroscopy are topmost priority to the ongoing activities in the area of
 spectroscopy requiring fresh fiscal in puts and also funds for modernization of essential old facilities.

SCIENCE AND ENGINEERING RESEARCH COUNCIL (SERC)
9.Science and Engineering Research Council (SERC) seeks to promote research in  emerging and frontier areas of science and
 engineering including multidisciplinary fields, promote the general research capability in relevant areas of science and
 engineering taking into account capability of the  institute, encourage young scientists to take up challenging R&D activities, give
 special encouragement  to projects from less endowed university departments, encourage patenting facilities to scientists  and
 technologists in the country for Indian and foreign patents on a sustained basis.
10.The Committee was informed that during the year 2002-03 the emphasis would be on supporting more fundamental research
 projects in the academic sector, particularly in the Universities with a view to tap the expertise available.  Based on the inputs
 provided by the various Programme Advisory Committees about 350 programmes were likely to be approved.  Some of the
 programmes might be in the areas of agricultural sciences, new areas of boundary layer modeling, crystal engineering, Earth
 Sciences application for societal needs, Mathematical Sciences application to industry etc.
11.Support was being provided to 100 scientists and science students through SERC fellowships during the year.  In order to train
 manpower in critical areas of S&T, 20 SERC schools/training workshops, were likely to be organized along with few contact
 programme for Young Scientists. Apart from the above projects and Centres/Facilities support would be continued for on-going
 projects and programmes like the Kishore Viagyanik Protsahan Yojana (KVPY), DST-JNC Summer Student Fellowship, SERC
 Visiting Fellowship, Integrated Science Olympiad Programme etc.
12.The allocation for Multi Disciplinary Research in Science and Technology (SERC) has been increased to Rs.212.00 crores for
 the year 2002-2003 from Rs.87.10 crores in B.E. and Rs.84.90 crores in R.E. stage.  The Department was asked to give the details
 of the programmes to be undertaken with this increased allocation, the Committee has been informed that this was mainly for
 catering to the need of supporting large number of approved proposals which could not be supported last year and new
 projects/programmes and Centres of Excellence being evolved in frontier areas such as organic light emitting display systems,
 Laser Physics, non-destructive testing related activities, high priority areas in organic chemistry, NMR facilities, low-temperature
 high magnetic field facilities, Gamma Detector Array, Aspheric Lense facility etc.  In addition, a major new initiative was the
 launching of a National Programme on “Nano Materials Science & Technology Initiatives”.   Besides, the enhanced allocation
 2002-03 would be utilized for providing support to a large number of already recommended departments of Universities etc.,
 which could not be supported last year.
13.The Committee notes with satisfaction the  increased allocation for SERC. The Committee feels that there should be a periodic
 review of the Programmes in order to avoid wasteful expenditure.
OPPORTUNITY FOR YOUNG SCIENTISTS
14.The programme seeks to provide Opportunity to Young Scientists (OYS) for pursuing exciting and innovative research ideas,
 provide opportunities for interaction and exchange of ideas with the scientific community  both at  the national and international
 levels,  involve Young Scientists in national S&T development process, encourage S&T institutions, professional bodies and
 other agencies including State S&T Councils for development of  S&T programmes involving Young Scientists.
15.The Committee observes that very few talented students are  motivated to come forward to take-up R&D as career.   It is
 necessary that efforts should, therefore, be made not only to increase the number of schemes/projects, the schemes should also be
 innovative and students should be provided with the state of art laboratory facilities and expert care should be provided to
 encourage them to test their ideas.  In case there is dearth of ideas, suggestion could be invited from all & sundry and a list could
 be drawn up to keep it handy for those who need it.
INSTRUMENT DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME
16.The Committee has been informed that the objective of this programme is to  formulate coordinate and implement programmes
 leading to indigenous development and upgradation of instruments. During the year the Department aims to pursue the  following
 Programmes :
(i)         Major projects in areas of  Portable urea sensor & measuring system for detection of adulteration in milk, Strain gauge
 force transducer to measure applied force etc.
Besides, the Department proposes to initiate programmes in mission mode in the areas of Analytical/Scientific instrumentation: X-
ray based instruments; Mass spectroscopy based instruments; chromatography based instruments; Laser based analytical
 instruments etc. Medical instrumentation: Diagnostic instruments; Instruments for patient care/treatment; Fibre optic laser based
 instruments; Image processing and visualization etc. Instruments for Environment/Pollution monitoring & control; Food
 processing; Energy monitoring & control etc; imaging technologies & instrumentation including MRI system for healthcare &

NATIONAL ACCREDITATION BOARD FOR TESTING AND CALIBRATION LABORATORIES (NABL)
18.The Board seeks to provide, coordinate, guide, implement and maintain an accreditation system for laboratories suitable for the
 country in accordance with the relevant national and international standards and guides.
19.The Laboratories ensure that all measurements, either during calibration or testing by accredited laboratories, conform to
 appropriate national/international standards maintained at National Physical Laboratory (NPL) and at Bhabha Atomic Research
 Centre (BARC) through an unbroken chain of comparisons; encourage Proficiency Tests/Inter-laboratory comparisons in order to
 ensure accuracy, reliability and reproducibility of test results; establish and maintain strong linkages with international and
 regional laboratories such as International Laboratory Accreditation Conference (ILAC), European Accreditation Cooperation for
 Laboratories (EAL), Asia Pacific Laboratory Accreditation Cooperation (APLAC) etc. and to achieve Mutual Recognition
 Arrangement through international peer evaluation so that test results of NABL accredited laboratories are accepted across the
 frontiers of the countries and thereby promote international trade.
20.       The Committee has also been informed that during 2002-03 number of accredited laboratories would be increased from the
 current level of 366 testing and 120 in the field of calibration to around 450 testing and 150 calibration laboratories. Joint
 assessment of Forensic Science Laboratory by NATA would be intensified.
21.       NABL would organise seminars and workshops on Uncertainty in Measurement, Inter-Laboratory Proficiency Testing,
 Calibration and Traceability, Validation of Test Method and Accreditation of Clinical/Food Testing/Drug Testing etc. for creating
 better awareness in the  months to come.
22.       The Committee feels that the large-scale food and drug adulteration can be prevented only if sufficient number of food and
 drug testing laboratories are available  in all major cities. Besides that training of staff involved in testing and calibration
 processes about the new standards is necessary for better results.
PATENT FACILITATING CELL (PFC)
23.       The PFC has been engaged in many activities related to intellectual property rights (IPR) with the objective of introducing
 patent information as a vital input in the process of promotion of R&D programmes, Provide patenting facilities & secretarial
 support to scientists and technologists of the country for Indian and foreign patents on a sustained basis, keep a watch on
 developments in the area of IPR and provide knowledge of important  issues  to policy makers, scientists, industry etc, Create
 awareness and understanding relating to patents and in sight of  challenges and opportunities in this area, undertake study and
 analysis of policy and operational matters emanating from the TRIPs agreement and other agreements under the World Trade
 Organisation and  act as a focal point in this matter within DST.
24.       The Committee was informed that Twenty four patent awareness workshops were organized during last year, which were
 attended by about 2,500 scientists and  technologists.  Regular “Patent Clinics” were being conducted with IIT, Delhi, to advise
 and guide the IIT scientists on individual basis on various aspects relating to patenting their inventions.
25.       The Committee is of the view that Patent Facilitating Cell should be reorganised into a vibrant nodal and referral agency
 for developing countries in Asia and Africa which could provide consultancy services for industry, universities, R&D institutions,
 government, NGOs and individuals, databases, video and multi-media products, undertake and support research and futuristic
 studies on IPR related topics. Besides, efforts should be made to develop Patent Facilitating centres at state levels in State S&T
 Councils, Universities, colleges; industry association for easy access to IPR related information at the local level.
DRUGS & PHARMACEUTICALS RESEARCH
26.       The Department initiated the scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research in 1994-95 for promoting R&D in drugs and
 pharmaceuticals sector.  The thrust of the programme is on enhancing capabilities of the Indian Drugs and pharmaceuticals
 industry  towards development of new drugs by synergising the strength of National Institutions and drug industry. Financial
 support is provided to national labs and academic institution for the research projects which are conceived jointly by the industry
 and public funded R&D institutions.  An important feature of this programme is that it supports drug development for all types of
 medicinal systems, be it traditional Indian medicinal  system or the modern one.
27.The Committee was informed that the Department would continue its efforts to support collaborative research projects  for
 drug development in the area of diseases like Tuberculosis, Leprosy, Malaria, Skin disorders like Leucoderma, Gastrointestinal
 disorder like Diarrhoea, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardio-vascular disorders and other prevalent infectious diseases, which
 involves an expenditure of 3.5 crores.
28.Development of “Veterinary Drugs” would be promoted by financially supporting collaborative projects for development of
 “Drugs for various veterinary diseases” during 2002-03 on a pro-active mode. An amount of Rs.2.50 crores was to be utilized to
 sustain ongoing projects.
  29.Asked about the progress made under the   activities for  “facility for screening of anti-viral activity” and on “transgenic and
 knock out mice”, the Department replied that, in addition to the new projects sanctioned during the year, committed expenditure
 made for a number of on-going collaborative projects/national facilities sanctioned in the previous years have to be met.  B.E. and
 R.E. for the programme was Rs.3.5 crores during 2001-2002. The  facilities earlier proposed needed heavy investment.  In view
 of this, the National Facility for Transgenic and knock-out mice had been taken up during the financial year (2001-02).  The
 overall approved cost of this project was for Rs.5.77 crores, out of which DST’s share was for Rs.2.30 crores and the rest had to
 be borne by CSIR.  With the limitation on the budget provision, only a part of the overall commitment for this facility could be
 released during that year. The establishment of National Facility for screening of anti viral activity would be taken up in the

30.The Committee observes that given the recent scare of anthrax and reappearance of plague in some parts of India efforts must
 be renewed to counteract these diseases.  With its traditional knowledge the country can perform pioneering role in tackling these
 diseases.
31.       The Committee is constrained to note the snails pace in the development of herbal medicines when they have the potential
 to cure dread disease like AIDS & Cancer besides the disease like diabetes, Hypertension etc.  Not only the herbal medicines,
 there is need to open big hospitals based on the Indian System of medicines.  The Committee is given to understand that the
 Indian System of medicine notably ayurveda did miraculous healing to the victims of Chernobyl disaster.  This lead the Russians
 to take more interest ink this system of medicine so much so that they evinced interest in the learning of the system.  Likewise the
 United States America is reported to have set up a very big hospital in one of its states based on the Indian System of medicine. 
 If it really be so, it is indeed unfortunate we have not used our system of medicine in such a big way to set up hospitals of that
 scale.  The Committee feel it is time Government thinks over the matter irrespective of the fact whether Department of Science &
 Technology is individually concerned in the matter.
TECHNOLOGY INFORMATION, FORECASTING AND ASSESSMENT COUNCIL (TIFAC)
32.Technology Information Forecasting and Assessment Council (TIFAC), a registered society under Department of Science and
 Technology, was set up in 1988 to look ahead in Technologies and energize action in the select areas.         The main objectives
 of TIFAC include generation of Technology Assessment (TA) / Techno-Market Surveys (TMC) reports, providing technology
 related information, promotion of  technology and evolving suitable mechanism for testing of technology, technology transfer and
 commercialization as well patent  information system.
33.TIFAC activities & achievements have emerged as a knowledge network in action, covering all facets of technology
 development to commercialization and to delivery.  Its focus has been to make technology work for people in various sectors like
 Agriculture and Agro Food Sector, Road Construction and Transportation Equipment, Textile Machinery upgradation, Health
 Care Services, Upgradation of Science & Engineering Colleges & Targeted Programme in Other Important Areas.
34.The Committee is of the view that effective technology transfer process to industry may also help in challenging the
 technologies coming from abroad.  Besides, the technology transferred to the industry is to be cost effective and also retain
 certain safeguards to prevent industry from exploiting the research.
SPECIAL COMPONENT PLAN FOR SCHEDULED CASTE
35.The Department informed the Committee that a special plan was undertaken  with a view to promote research, development
 and adaptation of technology for improving the life of the economically weaker sections such as scheduled castes in urban/rural
 areas,  to promote activities such as workshop, seminars, publications, jathas, etc. which would help in achieving the objectives as
 above.  
36.It was further informed that the Department undertook an All India Coordinated Programme on waste recycling and
 management; nine individual projects were funded in different municipalities and town areas.  Projects have been initiated  for
 improving skill and efficiency of occupations like leather tanning & carcass utilization to make value added products; optimizing
 the design of cycle rickshaws to reduce drudgery and increase income and improving competence of target beneficiaries in
 maintenance and management aspects, low cost self-help habitat upgradation programme  for the benefit of Scheduled Caste
 Bastis in rural areas through low cost construction technique and use of locally made building materials.  Training programmes
 were conducted for  rural Scheduled Castes for setting up low investment micro-enterprises both in rural & urban areas based on
 local resources like manufacturing of briquettes from agricultural waste.  Introduction of improved methods/tools used by the
 scavenging community for managing night soil including introduction of rapid composting techniques for income generation and
 for improving the quality of life of scavenger was also under implementation.
37.The Committee notes with satisfaction the programme undertaken for the benefit of weaker sections of the society.  The
 Committee desires that the benefits of these programmes should reach the large population living in rural areas and smaller towns
 who might be unaware of these programmes.The Committee feels that effective coordination should be established with other
 Departments who are involved in similar activities to prevent overlapping of schemes.
SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY FOR WOMEN
38.The Committee was informed that Science & Technology Programmes for Women were being undertaken to promote
 research, development and adaptation of technology, improve the working conditions and opportunities for gainful employment
 of women especially in rural areas, to increase the contribution of women to science and technology and development, to
 motivate scientists and technologists for applying their expertise to solve the problems of women in rural areas,   to improve
 existing tools/implements and equipment used by women and introduction of new  techniques,  to replicate successful 
 technology  models  relevant to women, to  establish the two-way referral system for identifying felt needs at the grass root level
 and linking it to proactive R&D, aimed at formulating future programme for location specific intervention and take up relevant
 activities which were conducive to attainment of the above objectives. 
39.Some of the technology areas identified for attention are fuel & energy, ergonomically designed and user friendly tools and
 implements for women in agriculture, drinking water management, post harvest technology, horticulture, organic farming, pest
 control, essential oil extraction, occupational health vermicomposing, biopestcides, hydroponic, low cost diagnostic kits, paper
 technology, and IT software.
40.The programme on cultivation of medicinal plants will be enlarged to include preparation of herbal formulation and quality
 control by women cooperatives.  Women’s Health intervention programmes will continue to be the focus of support to include
 women in the adolescent, child bearing and post menopausal age.  Development of health & hygiene products for women and
 their popularization will be a part of all the health initiatives.

VIGYAN PRASAR
42.This programme aims to undertake, aid, promote, guide and coordinate efforts in popularisation of science and inculcation of
 scientific temper among the people and to enhance the knowledge, awareness and interest about science and technology among
 all segments of the society.
43.The Committee was informed that over the years, the activities of Vigyan Prasar have ranged from development of a variety of
 software for Science & Technology communication and popularization to national campaigns, the use of various media and 
 providing information services on various aspect of Science & Technology.  An effort has been made to promote effective
 linkages on a continuing basis among various scientific institutions, agencies, educational and academic bodies, laboratories,
 museums, industry, trade and other organizations for effective exchange and dissemination of S&T information.
44.While commending the Department for accepting its recommendation for an increased allocation for Vigyan Prasar from
 Rs.1.00 crores during B.E. & R.E. in the year 2001-2002 to Rs.2.00 crores for the year 2002.2003, the Committee asked the
 Department the areas where enhanced allocation would be utilised the Department  informed that the existing
 programmes/activities viz., publication programme, Vigyan Prasar Information System, Vigyan Prasar Network of Science
 Clubs, Training Programmes, use of Media for S&T popularization, production of Radio/TV programmes etc., would be
 reinforced.  In addition, new initiatives in the North-East and S&T communications through satellite Radio and Television have
 been taken up.  The development & dissemination of S&T software was to be further strengthened and expanded.  HAM radio
 activity, especially in the disaster prone areas, was to be promoted.
45.The Committee is of the view that the young generation should be encouraged to take up the study of science through easy-to-
do practicals and other innovative ways, incentives, ‘earn while you learn’ schemes etc. to help build scientific temper.
46.The Committee is also of the view that use of HAM radio should be popularized in regions/areas prone to natural disasters and
 this can be done if in schools training of HAM radio’s taken up as an extra curricular activity.
NATURAL RESOURCES DATA MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (NRDMS)
47.Natural Resource Data Management System (NRDMS) is a Multi – Institutional and multi disciplinary Science & Technology
 programme of DST to develop methodologyand techniques for operationalising the concept of local level planning.It provides for
 creation of a database on natural resources and construct a socio-economic profile on district and sub-district levels to meet the
 information needs of the local administration forimplementing integrated micro level  planning.  The Geographic Information
 System (GIS) technique is adopted for storage, retrieval, analysis of the data collected from different sources on natural resources
 and socio-economic pattern of the area under investigation to produce useful information that helps in decision making.  Several
 national R&D and academic institutions are being involved for evolving the Decision Support Systems (DSS) in areas like
 watershed development, energy management, infrastructure development and land-use planning, by extending financial support
 to short duration research projects in spatial data management technology with focus  on following areas:
GIS Data Bases Centres
            The programme Strengthened the existing centres by updating them with state-of-the-art technologies like integrated
 database design, spatial decision support system for the identified sectors etc.  Supported creation of new databases centres in
 Lucknow in UP and Jallpaiguri in West Bengal.
Software Development
            An interface between indigenously developed GIS package, GRAM++ and hydrological model Soil Water Assessment
 Tool (SWAT) has been tested for land management in selected Upper Gandheswari Watershed in Bankura and Rampatna
 Watershed in Kolar.
Landslide Studies
            Landslide hazard zonation mapping have been completed in parts of Chamoli and Pithoragarh District of Uttaranchal State
 using remote sensing and GIS techniques.
            The Committee has been informed that during the year the Department proposes to Create  new NRDMS Database Centres
 to have a better coverage of variation states such as Tamilnadu, Nagaland, Uttar Pradesh and Uttaranchal. Development and
 dissemination of spatial data management tools for integrated rural development planning, evolve R&D projects in the area of 
 software development and upgradation of GRAM ++ and GIS software.
48.       The Committee observes that even though the country has  made  technological advances there are frequent cases of
 landslides.  In order to prevent this, it is necessary to have a complete hazard zonation map clearly demarcating landslide prone
 areas similar to the  one for earth quake prone areas.       Besides GIS data received from GRAM ++ should be utilized for the
 agricultural development

NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MEDIUM WEATHER FORECASTING (NCMRWF)
53.         The  objectives of the project include setting up of major infrastructure facilities like super computer, front-end
 processors and communication network and the on-line linkages with IMD and other Agro-meteorological research centres,
 development of global and regional numerical weather prediction models for medium range weather forecasting, and  
 development of appropriate data assimilation techniques for preparing initial conditions for the model. Preparation of NWP
 model  output and dissemination of the same to IMD for preparation and issue of medium range weather forecasts (3 to 10 days
 in advance) and development, preparation and dissemination of Agro-meteorological operation advisories including advisories
 for contingency crop practices to the end users through the Agro-meteorological research centres to be designated as
 experimental Agro-meteorological field units (AMFUs). Besides the project seeks to Promote and undertake studies on region
 crop-weather relationship and impact of  weather and climate on pest and diseases.
 
54.       The Committee feels that the thrust of weather forecasting should be on its accuracy.  The Committee observes that
 Department should consider enhancing the spatial resolution, range and accuracy of forecasts and advisories by constantly
 improving forecast models with use of available satellite data and techniques.
GUJARAT EARTHQUAKE – MISSION INITIATIVES IN REBUILDING & REHABILITATION
55.       In the wake of disastrous damages by the earthquake in Gujarat on 26
th January, 2001 the Advanced Composites Mission
 of TIFAC has come forward to contribute to the national efforts of re-building and rehabilitation.  A wide array of innovative
 composite products suitable for low-cost building & construction sector and bio-medical appliances has been developed by the
 Advanced Composites Mission.  Jute-coir composite boards, rice husk particle boards, FRP toilet blocks, multipurpose FRP
 handcarts and composite artificial limbs etc. address the crucial need of the hour – post-disaster relief at the quickest possible
 time.  The TIFAC Rehab Project at Bhuj was now fully operational in terms of complete occupancy of 400 shelters (20’12’). 
 Besides, 128 community toilet units constructed by the Mission were also in service.
56.       The Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department for rebuilding and Rehabilitation of Quake victims in
 Gujarat.  However it feels that in view of the massive destruction that took place there as a result of  the quake Department should
 involve certain financial agencies like Housing Urban Development Corporation (HUDCO)/ National Housing Bank (NHB) etc.
 for providing low interest loans for rebuilding so that these missions are a success. Besides, effective coordination and
 management of relief measures was very necessary.
Besides, these products must be popularized   for use in building and other similar activities in other quake prone areas in India to
 prevent loss of life and property.
SURVEY OF INDIA
57.       Survey of India, a national surveying and mapping organization acts as adviser to the Government of India on all Survey
 matters viz. geodesy, photogrammetry, mapping and map reproduction.  The main functions and responsibilities are
 establishment and maintenance of geodetic plan and height control network in the country, gravity and geomagnetic surveys, tidal
 surveys including tide predictions etc. topographical control surveys and mapping,   production of geographical map and other
 special maps, spelling of geographical names, demarcation of external boundaries of Republic of India, their depiction on maps
 and advice on the demarcation of interstate boundaries.
It transpires that an allocation of Rs.17.75 crores made in B.E. for the year 2001-2002 was increased to Rs.21.80 crores in R.E.
 last year for Publication of Map/Charts etc., and Rs.21.60 crores allocated for the year 2002-2003 did not seem justified. To this,
 the Department justified. The Committee has been informed that the activities of the Survey of India  relate to Publication of
 Maps, Charts and Reports etc., were carried out throughout the year.  The B.E. 2001-2002 was Rs.22.60 crores and the allocation
 in R.E. was raised to Rs.26.65 crores, in anticipation of increased work orders from client Departments.  It was also explained
 that the anticipated increases in work orders had not materalised. 
58.       The Committee feels it is time that Survey of India thought  of diversifying its activities.  Apart from preparing and
 bringing out political & physical maps of the country, it should endeavour to bring out maps of tourist interest of National
 Highways, towns and cities to meet the local needs.

INDIA METROLOGICAL DEPARTMENT (IMD)
59.       IMD is engaged in forecasting of Storms, Cyclones and severe weather conditions and provide climatological statistics for
 operation and Planning in the field of Agriculture, Aviation, Water Conservation, Oceanography etc.; maintaining of Network of
 large number of observations for acquisition of surface and upper air weather data; issue of forecast and timely disaster warning
 of severe weather conditions/phenomena including tropical cyclones, monitoring of Seismic activities and to locate intensity and
 center of earthquakes to understand their processes and mechanism;  to carry out and promote research and development in
 Atmospheric and Meteorological Sciences;  imparting of Meteorological training to persons of developing countries under World
 Meteorological Organisation (WMO) programmes and to Departmental persons;  monitoring and Forecasting of Occurrence of
 Snow & Avalanche over Himalayan Mountainous region at 10 km resolution, Monitoring & Analysing the air pollutants in
 sample survey observations; monitoring of Ozone depletion.
            During the Year, of the  two Doppler Radars received, one has been installed at Chennai and other is likely to be installed
 and commissioned at Kolkata in  2002,  procurement of three Doppler Radars, High Wind Speed Recorders (HWSR), Digital
 Cyclone Warning Dissemination Systems (DCWDS) were being finalized under World Bank Assisted Project for Andhra
 Pradesh.  High Wind Speed Recorder (HWSR) have already been installed.
Action was in progress for upgradation of existing Earth Station for METSAT and one complete Receiver Earth Station for
 INSAT-3.  Establishment of Seismo  Observation at Sihor & Bhavanagar and digitization of seismic charts were in progress,
 three  Seismographs has been installed under Seismological Telemetry System.
60.       The Committee expresses its concern over delay in commissioning of Doppler Radars which are needed for accurate
 weather forecasting.  Besides, In India occurrence of cyclones is a regular feature every year, the Commissioning of Digital
 Cyclone Warning Dissemination System (DCWDS), should be given a priority. The Committee would appreciate if these could
 be installed before the beginning of Monsoon Season.

 the countries.

 Japan to various Department/institutions in India.  It identified institutions undertaking advanced scientific research and conveyed

 delegation took part in the three-day event as an outcome of which joint projects were being worked out.

st century in Indo-US collaborations in science and

 be made available to the Committee.

TECHNOLOGY FOR BAMBOO PRODUCT
66.       The Committee has been given to understand that Technology for Bamboo Product is   a programme at the national level
 meant to impart a significant boost to the usage of bamboo, promote specialized products for commercialization and generate
 good employment opportunities. New tools and techniques would be introduced to enhance the manner in which the bamboo
 resources are used in the country leading to greater and sensitive use of new materials.
67.       When asked  whether a critical assessment has been made about bamboo, its growth & the employment potential it holds
 for rural areas/North East Region, the Committee has  been informed that the allocation for National Mission on Bamboo
 Applications (NMBA) reflects the growing realization that bamboo can be an important vehicle to support & catalyse economic
 activity along with employment & income generation, in particular in rural areas and in regions with substantial resources of
 bamboo such as North East India, the Andaman & Nicobar islands, the Western Ghats, Uttaranchal, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and
 Orissa.  Technology developments in recent years in many parts of the world have positioned  bamboo as an excellent wood
 substitute for building & construction and resource & support agencies.   The Committee has  been informed that all these
 assessments have highlighted the significant potential of the sector through the promotion of new value-added applications,
 technologies and markets.  Also, while developing and promoting environment friendly, value-added bamboo based product,
 practices, process technology & processing machinery under several sub-projects, the Mission would aim to empower people at
 the grass-root level encompassing farmers, artisans and other stakeholders for better employment generation with improved
 remunerative opportunities.
68.       The Committee is happy to note the Mission in Bamboo products.  However, it would like the states like Madhya Pradesh
 and  Maharastra, where sizable quantity of Bamboo is produced, have not been included in the Mission.   Besides,  the Quality of
 Bamboo needs to be improved by improving cultivation techniques.  The Committee has been given to understand that Chinese
 Bamboo is of superior quality, the Committee therefore recommends that areas like N.E. Region, which have weather conditions
 similar to those in the countries abroad must be chosen for cultivation of better variety of bamboo.
The Committee feels that the wood should be replaced by use of Bamboo for construction purposes particularly in quake prone
 areas or for making agricultural tools and for furniture.
69.       The Committee would like to add that more such mission modes could be considered for products like Jute & Coir, which
 have suffered due to cheaper substitutes available in the market and have a great potential to provide gainful employment to the
 masses.

 various programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs.1014.25
